arguments.body:
Cross-Service Failure-Case Intake Template

Purpose

Use this template for a concrete cross-service failure case. The intake is a routing and bounded-review record; it is not a new approval gate, central approval process, program-owner role, or replacement for existing implementation, release, rollback, or incident ownership.

Current intake rule — all four parts are required

1. Component: name the concrete component or service involved.
2. Mapped implementation/release owner: name the person or mapped operating owner responsible for ordinary implementation and release. This owner remains responsible for implementation, release, rollback, and operations through the existing path; do not leave this field blank.
3. Selected boundary: select exactly one boundary for this intake — invariant, provenance, failure_mode, ownership, or escalation — and state the precise boundary being reviewed. Do not select multiple boundaries; split genuinely separate cases into separate intakes.
4. Observed failure/risk: describe the concrete observed failure or risk, including evidence, conditions, impact or exposure, and the relevant version/environment. Do not submit a hypothetical concern without an observed fact or bounded evidence.

Intake

- Component:
- Mapped implementation/release owner:
- Selected boundary (exactly one: invariant | provenance | failure_mode | ownership | escalation):
- Precise boundary statement:
- Concrete observed failure/risk:
- Evidence and provenance:
- Version/environment and date:
- Affected services and cross-service dependency:
- Incident clock, stop conditions, and escalation route, if applicable:
- Related runbook, alert, incident, change, or test:

Routing and review

- A complete intake has all four required parts: component; mapped implementation/release owner; exactly one selected boundary; and concrete observed failure/risk.
- Incomplete requests return to the submitting owner for the missing information. Do not infer an owner, boundary, approval, or risk.
- Complete requests route to the mapped implementation/release owner for ordinary implementation, release, rollback, and operations decisions. The intake does not transfer those responsibilities.
- Boundary review is limited to the one selected boundary named in the intake. The boundary reviewer does not become the final release approver, does not replace the mapped implementation/release owner, and does not approve unrelated work.
- Nadia triages asynchronous cross-service exception intake and returns incomplete requests or routes complete requests to the mapped owner. Nadia makes no implementation, release, rollback, or operations decisions.
- Alex sees only boundaries that require Alex’s review under the existing routing; Alex owns the captured cross-service failure case and its bounded boundary review, not the implementation, release, rollback, or program-wide process.
- Wes owns and teaches responder-path scenarios. Nadia owns the postmortem section and material. Existing responder, postmortem, implementation, release, rollback, escalation, and operations paths remain unchanged.

Submission check

- [ ] Component is named.
- [ ] Mapped implementation/release owner is named.
- [ ] Exactly one selected boundary is named and stated precisely.
- [ ] Concrete observed failure/risk and supporting evidence are included.
- [ ] The request is routed to the mapped owner for ordinary implementation/release/rollback/operations decisions.
- [ ] Boundary review is not being used as ordinary release approval.
- [ ] No separate rollback-owner field is created.
- [ ] No separate invariant-owner, provenance-owner, failure-mode-owner, ownership-owner, or escalation-owner fields are created.
- [ ] Wes/Nadia/Alex role split and existing escalation paths are preserved.

Historical scenarios

2026-04-27 — April Lantern migration preflight: blocked pre-authorization candidate

In staging, an undeployed migration candidate performed 20 unauthorized lookups. All 20 were ultimately denied, but each lookup constructed and initialized the incident-load adapter before authorization completed; 2 of the 20 also accessed the source. This was a blocked pre-authorization candidate, not a deployed customer incident; existing customer access remained unchanged while the candidate was undeployed.

Required analysis and acceptance conditions were authorization before adapter construction/initialization or source access; denial regressions showing zero adapter constructions and zero source calls for unauthorized lookups; and an affected LPS-001 rerun before migration acceptance. Product Engineering remained the implementation and release owner. Alex maintained the cross-service case and reviewed the shared safety/failure-mode boundary; Wes owned and taught responder paths; Nadia retained the postmortem section.

2026-10-16 — paired shard-keeper staging drill

The old holder closed its serving gate on lease loss. The replacement remained out of routing during catch-up. Routing began only after the replacement opened its serving gate. Failure triggers were overlapping serving holders, routing to a closed serving gate, or a request without exactly one terminal result.

This was a staging training case with no production or ownership change. Wes owned and taught the responder path; Nadia retained the postmortem material; Alex maintained only the cross-service failure case. Shard-keeper remained outside Wes’s solo scope.

2026-11-10 — quarterly incident-practice training result

Participants correctly kept the replacement holder out of routing until its serving gate opened and recognized that lease ownership alone does not establish serving eligibility. In 2 of 4 response timelines, responders initially treated closing the old listener as sufficient and omitted the terminal outcome for a request accepted before lease loss. After the facilitator inject, both corrected the timeline and accounted for that request exactly once.

Training only: no production drill and no system change. Existing ownership and Wes’s solo shard-keeper scope were unchanged.

2026-11-10 — facilitator-only shard-keeper handoff exercise

The timed sequence transferred the lease before the replacement serving gate opened, then revealed one request accepted by the old holder before lease loss that remained in flight. Participants had to state routing eligibility separately from terminal request accounting. Lease ownership or listener closure alone was insufficient. The scoring covered handoff ordering, gate behavior, exactly-one-terminal-result accounting, failure triggers, and ownership boundaries. This was training, not a production drill, and did not expand Wes’s solo shard-keeper scope; Cyrus covered the Data Platform boundary.

2027-01-28 — facilitator-only ingest-edge shutdown with accepted work still queued

Two hundred requests had already been accepted into tenant queues. Readiness turned false and the ingest listener closed, so the edge had to refuse new work. The dispatch loop then exited with 37 requests still queued, leaving only 163 terminal outcomes. The gap was unresolved accepted work, not refused work.

The exercise required separating refusal of new work from responsibility for accepted work; requiring every accepted request to drain or receive exactly one explicit terminal result; reconciling all 200 request identities without duplication; and engaging the secondary under the established incident-clock rule if isolation failed. The timed sequence, facilitator prompts, 10-point scoring, and passing standard treated listener closure as insufficient and prohibited claims that old-owner remediation or a production change had completed. Training only; Alex contributed only this cross-service failure case, Wes taught the responder path, and Nadia reviewed the postmortem section.

2027-04-05 — PR 2141 staging readiness behavior

In staging, ten replacement instances compiled a 40,000-route fixture in 25–34 seconds against a fixed 30-second readiness timeout. Eight joined on the first attempt. Two correctly remained unready, were terminated, and restarted before joining. Production was unchanged.

The responder exercise required identifying Wes and the mapped metrics-router owner path; classifying the restart-loop exposure as a failure-mode exception rather than a production incident or release approval request; and naming evidence required before release: reproducible staging runs covering the 25–34 second compile range; readiness/join, termination, and restart-loop metrics and logs for all ten instances; confirmation that the two unready instances were terminated and recovered on restart; timeout/retry behavior and failure-mode disposition; and explicit owner sign-off through the mapped metrics-router path. Alex’s role was limited to the bounded failure-mode exercise and intake framing. Alex was not the release approver; the mapped metrics-router owner retained implementation, release, rollback, and operations responsibility. No production change was implied.

2027-05-06 / May 20 practice contrast — PR 2141 production evidence

The earlier staging candidate exceeded the fixed readiness budget, terminated, and joined only on retry. A restart was recovery activity, not acceptance evidence. In the May 6 production rollout, every instance remained unroutable until compilation finished, and every cold start stayed within the fixed readiness budget without restart. Acceptance required readiness and serving eligibility to remain aligned throughout startup; the production case passed on that basis.

Facilitator contrasts for the May 20 practice were: an over-budget replacement remains unroutable and restart is not acceptance evidence; terminal-state selection and its matching accounting contribution must come from the same winning path; and replay samples or missing source classification cannot be presented as live rollback criteria. Live rollback decisions require live, release-relevant evidence and the mapped owner’s existing rollback path.

Wes maintained and taught the responder path; Nadia reviewed postmortem framing; Alex maintained only these cross-service cases. The practice material created no new approval gate, release-approver role, or broader ownership for Alex.

Historical-scenario scope note

These scenarios are retained as historical training and evidence records below the current intake template. They do not alter current ownership, imply production completion, or create a new approval gate. Apply the current four-part intake rule and exactly one selected boundary to new submissions.

messages.content:
Sustained August 6–30 sample

Nadia’s 38-request audit shows that front-door enforcement is operating consistently over a meaningful sample:

- 24 requests contained all four required elements: the affected component, a mapped implementation/release owner, exactly one exception class, and a concrete observed failure or at-risk condition. Each was routed to the named boundary owner.
- 14 requests were stopped before bounded review:
  - 7 had only placeholder conditions
  - 3 omitted the affected component
  - 2 selected multiple exception classes
  - 2 omitted the mapped owner
- No ordinary implementation or release approval entered Alex’s lane.
- Nadia performed triage and routing only; she made no implementation, release, rollback, or operations decision.

Contrast with the initial 12-request snapshot

The initial August snapshot was directionally positive but too small to establish sustained performance: 7 requests proceeded to bounded review, while 5 were returned before review—3 for placeholder-only conditions, 1 for a missing component, and 1 for combining two exception classes.

The 38-request sample strengthens that evidence in two ways:

- It demonstrates that the gate continued to reject the same classes of incomplete or mis-scoped requests across a larger time window, rather than reflecting a one-off result.
- It makes the enforcement boundary more explicit: a request must contain a concrete observed condition, one selected boundary, a named component, and a mapped owner before it can reach review.

This supports “front-door enforcement is operating as intended,” but it does not establish universal or production-wide effectiveness, and it does not change the ownership model.

Responsibilities remain unchanged

- Mapped service owners retain responsibility for ordinary implementation, release, rollback, and operations for their services. A complete intake routes to that owner; bounded review is not release approval and does not transfer those responsibilities.
- Alex owns the captured cross-service failure case and reviews only the named, triggered boundary assigned to Alex. That review is limited to the selected boundary; Alex is not the implementation, release, rollback, or program-wide approval owner.
- Nadia owns asynchronous front-door triage: she returns incomplete requests and routes complete requests to the mapped owner. She does not make implementation, release, rollback, or operations decisions. Nadia retains the postmortem section and material.
- Wes retains responder-path ownership and teaching, including the associated bounded failure-case exercises; this does not expand his authority into other mapped services.
- Other mapped owners retain their respective service-specific implementation, release, rollback, escalation, and operational responsibilities. No owner is displaced by the intake or review process.

# Lantern March 25 continuation decision pre-read

Prepared: March 19, 2027

Purpose

This pre-read separates completed evidence from the decision still to be made at the March 25 review. It records evidence and boundaries; it does not recommend, imply, or record a continuation outcome.

Decision status and current authorization

- The existing authorization remains unchanged through March 31, 2027.
- No post-March-31 outcome exists yet. No continuation or later authorization has been decided or recorded.
- This pre-read does not extend, renew, narrow, or otherwise modify the authorization through March 31.
- Alex remains exception-review only. No different ownership or handoff is established by this document.

Completed evidence

Frozen reconciliation scope and results

- Scope: January 1–March 15, 2027. The cutoff is closed and the query is pinned.
- Frozen population: 2,684 sessions.
- Frozen logical-request count: 512, comprising:
  - 342 combined requests
  - 111 separate requests with timestamps more than 24 hours apart
  - 59 requests with explicit unknown status
- Iris and Alex completed the two-person reconciliation.
- The frozen record contains zero instances of:
  - renderer failures
  - authorization bypasses
  - post-denial calls
  - cross-tenant material
  - missing provenance or timestamps
  - unpublished ownership
  - excluded fields
  - read-only losses
- Follow-ups remaining in the frozen record: Harbor Health — 10; Mosaic Commerce — 9.
- PR 2094 remains a known evidence/implementation consideration: the stale-present/N+1 issue remains open, and the hash currently omits priority and fallback policy.

Internal reference-only integration checks — Harbor Health

These are completed evidence checks, not an authorization decision:

- Request check: zero internal reference-only integration requests for Harbor Health.
- Artifact check: zero internal reference-only integration artifacts for Harbor Health.
- Output check: zero internal reference-only integration outputs for Harbor Health.
- Result: the internal reference-only integration remained outside the Harbor Health customer path in the frozen record.

Internal reference-only integration checks — Mosaic Commerce

These are completed evidence checks, not an authorization decision:

- Request check: zero internal reference-only integration requests for Mosaic Commerce.
- Artifact check: zero internal reference-only integration artifacts for Mosaic Commerce.
- Output check: zero internal reference-only integration outputs for Mosaic Commerce.
- Result: the internal reference-only integration remained outside the Mosaic Commerce customer path in the frozen record.

Interpretation of the clean evidence

The zero findings above describe what was observed in the frozen evidence period. They do not authorize any new use or imply that any future use is approved. In particular, the clean evidence does not authorize:

- CSV access, ingestion, export, or use;
- cost data access, presentation, or use;
- writeback or mutation of any source or customer system;
- release-readiness judgments or production-readiness decisions; or
- customer exposure of internal reference navigation, including any internal reference-only request, artifact, or output.

The internal reference-only integration remains reference-only and outside both customer paths unless a separate, explicit authorization states otherwise. No customer-path integration, rollout, or production use is authorized by this pre-read.

Decision still open for the March 25 review

1. Post-March-31 authorization

   Decide whether anything should be authorized after the existing March 31 boundary. If so, specify the exact scope, permitted inputs and outputs, duration, named owner, evidence requirements, monitoring, stop conditions, and exit criteria. If not, record that no continuation is authorized.

2. Decision standard and unresolved evidence

   Decide what standard and additional evidence, if any, are required before considering continuation. Establish the disposition and accountable owner for the 10 Harbor Health and 9 Mosaic Commerce follow-ups, the 59 explicit-unknown requests, and the known PR 2094 stale-present/N+1 and hash-policy issues.

3. Boundary and prohibited uses

   Confirm that any future decision must separately address and explicitly prohibit or authorize CSV, cost data, writeback, release-readiness judgments, and customer exposure of internal reference navigation. Clean historical evidence must not be treated as approval for any of these uses.

4. Ownership and operating responsibility

   Decide whether Alex's exception-review-only boundary remains appropriate and assign explicit owners for any separately approved implementation, release, rollback, and operations work. No ownership handoff is recorded here.

Review

Scheduled review: March 25, 2027, 10:30–11:15 ET, with Hema, Iris, Theo, Product Engineering, and Alex.

No post-March-31 outcome is recorded here.

arguments.body:
Purpose

Carry the approved Q1 2027 structure into planning as three linked workstreams—not as one Lantern backlog. Each workstream keeps its own implementation, release, rollback, and operational accountability while collaborating through a narrow, read-only reference contract. The current approval is for bounded internal operating use by Infra and Product Engineering; Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce remain out of scope unless separately authorized.

Linked workstreams and mapped ownership

1. Lantern — explanation and navigation
Purpose: Help staff understand a situation and navigate to the authoritative owner-map or Cardinality Guardrails record without becoming another authority, copying authority payload values, or providing mutation capability.
Mapped owner: Product Engineering owns Lantern implementation and the associated release, rollback, and operations. Iris owns interpretation and adoption criteria. Routine implementation decisions stay with Product Engineering’s mapped reviewers.

2. Cardinality Guardrails — pipeline limits and cost semantics
Purpose: Remain authoritative for pipeline-limit behavior and cost semantics, including the meaning of measured limits versus missing, malformed, or stale inputs.
Mapped owner: Cyrus owns the Guardrails authority interface and cost semantics; the mapped Guardrails team owns implementation, release, rollback, and operations for its area. Wes owns the metrics-router operating-limit mapping where it connects to the published operating view.

3. Owner map — published responsibility
Purpose: Remain authoritative for published responsibility and canonical service ownership; Lantern may point to this record but may not reproduce or change it.
Mapped owner: The owner-map team owns publication, implementation, release, rollback, and operations for the owner-map authority. Wes owns the mapped operating-responsibility handoff for metrics-router; Product Engineering implements Lantern’s read-only navigation to the record.

Shared five-field reference contract

Internal cards may carry only these reference fields when navigating to an authoritative record:

- tenant_id
- canonical_service_id
- authority_type
- authority_record_id
- source_timestamp

The fields identify and locate an authoritative record; they are not a copy of its authority payload. Each authority remains separate, including when owner-map and Cardinality Guardrails records refer to the same canonical service. Source timestamps must remain the authority’s timestamps, not export or render time. No card or navigation path may create, update, delete, or otherwise mutate an authoritative record.

Handoff points

- Contract changes: the affected authority owner proposes the change; Product Engineering assesses the Lantern interface impact; Alex reviews only the shared-contract and cross-system failure boundary.
- Authority updates: the owner-map or Guardrails owner publishes and operates its own authoritative record. Lantern consumes the five-field reference and preserves separate authority identity and provenance.
- Lantern implementation: Product Engineering owns the build, routine implementation choices, tests, release, rollback, and operations. Alex is not an approval gate for every implementation decision.
- Cross-workstream verification: before release of a contract-affecting change, the mapped owners verify tenant isolation, authority separation, stale/missing behavior, provenance, no payload duplication, no mutation capability, and customer-path isolation.
- Failure or boundary violation: the affected workstream owner leads response and rollback for its area; the other mapped owners are engaged where the shared contract or a cross-system boundary is implicated. Alex reviews that shared boundary and failure mode, not every local remediation choice.

Alex’s review scope

Alex is the shared-contract and cross-system failure-boundary reviewer. That scope covers the invariants and seams that cross workstream boundaries: the five reference fields, authority separation, provenance, tenant isolation, mutation and payload-copy prohibitions, stale or unavailable authority behavior, and continued exclusion from Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It does not make Alex the sole implementation gate or require review of routine Lantern, Guardrails, or owner-map implementation decisions. Mapped owners remain accountable for their own delivery and operations.

Planning rule

Plan and track work under the three named workstreams, with explicit owner handoffs at the contract and boundary points above. Do not create a single Lantern backlog that absorbs Guardrails semantics or published owner-map responsibility.

Effective date: January 1, 2028

Purpose

Operate Lantern only as the approved, reference-only navigation path for internal staff. Lantern explains a situation and navigates an eligible internal user to the authoritative owner-map or Cardinality Guardrails record; Lantern is not an authority store and must not reproduce the authority payload.

Approved path

1. An eligible Infra or Product Engineering user uses Lantern for an internal operating use case.
2. Lantern creates or displays an internal card containing only these five reference fields:
   - tenant_id
   - canonical_service_id
   - authority_type
   - authority_record_id
   - source_timestamp
3. Lantern preserves the authority record identity and the authority's source_timestamp.
4. The user follows the reference to the authoritative owner-map or Cardinality Guardrails record.
5. The authoritative system remains responsible for the record's contents, published responsibility, pipeline limits, and cost semantics. Lantern may explain and navigate, but must not copy authoritative values into the card or become a second authority.

Hard prohibitions

- Do not copy, cache, summarize as authoritative, or otherwise reproduce authority payload values in Lantern.
- Do not create, update, delete, or otherwise mutate an owner-map or Cardinality Guardrails record through Lantern.
- Do not use Lantern for CSV access, export, ingestion, cost-data presentation or use, writeback, or release-readiness or production-readiness judgments unless separately and explicitly authorized.
- Do not treat a clean historical check or an internal reference as authorization for any broader use.

Customer-access boundary

The approved path is internal-only and remains completely outside customer access. No Lantern request, artifact, or output may enter Harbor Health or Mosaic Commerce. Do not connect Lantern to either customer renderer, expose internal reference navigation to a customer, add a customer-path integration, roll out customer-facing behavior, or use Lantern in a customer production path. Any expansion beyond this boundary requires a separate explicit authorization with a named owner and handoff; this runbook entry does not grant that authorization.

Ownership and handoff

- Product Engineering owns Lantern implementation, tests, release, rollback, and operations.
- The owner-map team owns published responsibility and its authoritative records.
- The Cardinality Guardrails team owns pipeline-limit behavior and cost semantics and their authoritative records.
- The shared-contract and cross-system failure-boundary reviewer reviews the five-field contract, authority separation, provenance, tenant isolation, mutation and payload-copy prohibitions, stale or unavailable authority behavior, and customer-path isolation. That reviewer is not the sole gate for routine implementation decisions.

Checks before release or contract-affecting change

Verify tenant isolation, separate authority_record_id values where authorities are distinct, preservation of source_timestamp, absence of payload duplication, absence of mutation capability, correct behavior for stale or unavailable authority records, and zero customer-path requests, artifacts, and outputs for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce.

Boundary violation response

Stop the affected path immediately. Do not continue, broaden, or repair through a customer-facing route. Preserve the request, artifact, and output evidence; notify Product Engineering and the affected authority owner; engage the shared-contract and cross-system failure-boundary reviewer; and roll back through the accountable workstream owner. Reauthorization and any customer-path change require a separate explicit decision and owner handoff.

input.body:
Cold Spring Weekend Plan
February 18–20, 2028
Start and finish: South Slope home
Travelers: Alex, Devika, and Kibo

Purpose
A low-stress winter weekend with one substantial outdoor outing, flexible indoor time, and enough margin for traffic, weather, and Kibo’s comfort.

Working assumptions
- Use a car or dog-friendly rental as the default. Do not rely on Metro-North unless its current pet rules explicitly accommodate Kibo’s size; a 53.7 lb dog will not fit the usual carrier requirement.
- Reserve two nights at a dog-friendly property in Cold Spring or a nearby Hudson Valley town. Confirm the pet fee, permitted room type, parking, check-in window, cancellation policy, and whether dogs may be left unattended.
- Treat all trail and road conditions as changeable in February. Check the forecast, snow/ice conditions, park notices, and the lodging’s arrival instructions the morning of departure.
- Kibo stays on leash. Use the front-clip harness and shorter leash near traffic, in the village, and around parking areas.

Before booking
1. Select lodging with a ground-floor room or easy elevator access, an outdoor relief area, and a clear pet policy.
2. Confirm parking and whether weekend parking restrictions or event closures affect the property.
3. Check the preferred hiking area’s current dog, leash, access, and winter-closure rules. Do not make Breakneck Ridge the primary plan with Kibo: its steep, exposed, rocky sections are a poor winter fit for a large dog.
4. Make dinner reservations only for places that confirm dogs are welcome on the patio, or plan for takeout. Keep at least one meal flexible.
5. Save offline directions and the lodging’s phone number. Bring a backup payment method and a small amount of cash for parking or trail fees if applicable.

Packing checklist
- Front-clip harness, shorter leash, backup leash, collar/ID, and waste bags
- Food for three days plus one extra meal, treats, collapsible bowls, and water
- Kibo’s towel, sleeping mat/blanket, medication if applicable, and a familiar toy
- Dog-safe paw towel and paw protection if Kibo already uses it; do not test new gear on the trip
- Warm layers, waterproof shoes/boots, gloves, headlamps, traction aids, and a daypack
- Phone chargers, offline maps, lodging confirmation, first-aid kit, and car emergency supplies
- Waterproof bag for muddy gear and a change of clothes for the drive home

Friday, February 18 — Brooklyn to Cold Spring

8:00–9:00 — Final preparation at South Slope
- Feed Kibo normally; do not introduce a new food before travel.
- Take a normal neighborhood walk and give Kibo a bathroom break before loading the car.
- Pack food, water, towels, and the trail kit where they are reachable without unloading the vehicle.

9:30 — Depart South Slope
- Allow roughly 2½ hours door-to-door, including traffic and one dog break; leave additional margin rather than scheduling a tight lunch or check-in.
- Make one planned stop at a safe, quiet, leashed area. Do not let Kibo roam at a highway rest stop.

12:00–1:00 — Arrival-area break and lunch
- If the room is not ready, eat at a dog-friendly outdoor location or get takeout and keep the plan simple.
- Give Kibo a short decompression walk, not a long hike immediately after the drive.

3:00 — Check in and reset
- Confirm the room, parking, pet rules, and the nearest emergency veterinary option.
- Let Kibo settle for 30–60 minutes. Keep the first village walk short.

4:00–5:00 — Easy Cold Spring village and riverfront walk
- Walk the quieter streets and accessible waterfront areas on leash.
- Avoid crowded sidewalks, steep icy paths, and prolonged standing in exposed wind. Use the harness and shorter leash near traffic.

6:30 — Dinner
- Preferred: an early dog-friendly outdoor meal if conditions are comfortable.
- Backup: takeout, with one person staying with Kibo if the lodging does not permit unattended pets.

Evening — Quiet night
- Final bathroom walk, fresh water, and an early bedtime. Keep Saturday’s longer outing conditional on Kibo’s energy and the trail surface.

Saturday, February 19 — Main outing and flexible afternoon

8:00 — Breakfast and conditions check
- Check the latest forecast and trail notices.
- Pack water, food, towel, waste bags, layers, traction aids, and a charged phone.
- If trails are icy, wet, or crowded, switch to the easy plan below rather than forcing the planned hike.

9:30–12:00 — Primary outdoor plan: easy Hudson Highlands outing
- Start with a dog-appropriate, leashed route such as Little Stony Point and a riverfront walk, subject to current access and dog rules.
- Keep the outing at an easy-to-moderate pace with frequent checks for cold paws, salt, ice, fatigue, and tangled gear.
- Turn around early if Kibo is slipping, lifting a paw, shivering, or becoming reluctant to continue.

Alternative only if conditions are dry and safe
- Choose a moderate, non-scrambling Hudson Highlands route such as the Bull Hill/Cornish Estate area only after checking current conditions and leash rules.
- Skip exposed rock, ladders, steep icy descents, and any route where Kibo would need to be carried.

Do not do
- No off-leash exercise, roadside relief, or unsupervised tethering.
- No Breakneck Ridge scramble with Kibo in winter conditions.
- No leaving Kibo in the car, even for a short meal or errand.

12:30 — Lunch and recovery
- Return to town or use takeout. Dry Kibo thoroughly, inspect paws, offer water, and allow a genuine rest period.

2:00–4:30 — Low-key afternoon
Choose one:
- Rest at the lodging and read.
- Take a short village walk and browse only dog-welcoming outdoor areas.
- Drive to a nearby dog-friendly stop if weather makes the riverfront uncomfortable, after confirming access and parking.

5:00 — Reassess dinner
- Keep the evening flexible. If Kibo is tired, use takeout and a short relief walk.
- If everyone is comfortable, have an early meal and return before streets and paths become icy or dark.

Sunday, February 20 — Easy morning and return home

8:00–9:30 — Breakfast and final walk
- Take Kibo on a short, familiar route rather than beginning another strenuous hike.
- Check the car, room, and charging cables before packing.

10:00–11:00 — Pack and check out
- Recheck the room for food, medications, ID, chargers, and dog gear.
- Keep towels and a water bowl accessible for the drive.

11:00–12:30 — Optional final stop
- If weather and energy are good, do one brief waterfront or village walk.
- If roads are deteriorating, leave immediately and skip the stop.

12:30–1:00 — Depart Cold Spring
- Allow roughly 2½ hours back to South Slope, including one break and winter traffic.
- Use the same safe-rest-stop approach as on Friday.

3:00–4:00 — Arrive home
- Unload essentials first, give Kibo water and a normal bathroom walk, and let the weekend end quietly.

Decision rules
- Green light: dry or lightly snowy surfaces, good visibility, no concerning notices, and Kibo moving normally. Do the primary easy outing.
- Yellow light: icy/very muddy trails, strong wind, heavy precipitation, or Kibo showing fatigue. Use the short waterfront/village plan and more indoor time.
- Red light: unsafe roads, trail closure, severe cold, or Kibo limping, shivering, repeatedly lifting a paw, or otherwise unwell. Cancel or curtail the outing and return home or stay put safely.

Responsibilities
- Alex: driving, route/parking checks, Kibo’s harness and leash management near traffic, and the offline trip folder.
- Devika: lodging confirmation, meal backup, and the weather/trail-notice check; both adults confirm the final go/no-go decision.
- Both: keep Kibo leashed, carry water and waste bags, and make the schedule less ambitious rather than pushing through winter conditions.

Final 24-hour checklist
- [ ] Lodging and pet policy reconfirmed
- [ ] Parking and check-in instructions saved offline
- [ ] Weather, road conditions, and trail notices checked
- [ ] Car/rental fuel and winter equipment checked
- [ ] Food, water, harness, shorter leash, towel, ID, and medications packed
- [ ] Dinner plan plus takeout backup set
- [ ] Kibo’s energy and any paw/health concerns assessed before departure

Cold Spring Weekend Plan
February 18–20, 2028
Start and finish: South Slope home
Travelers: Alex, Devika, and Kibo

Purpose
A low-stress winter weekend with one substantial outdoor outing, flexible indoor time, and enough margin for traffic, weather, and Kibo’s comfort.

Working assumptions
- Use a car or dog-friendly rental as the default. Do not rely on Metro-North unless its current pet rules explicitly accommodate Kibo’s size; a 53.7 lb dog will not fit the usual carrier requirement.
- Reserve two nights at a dog-friendly property in Cold Spring or a nearby Hudson Valley town. Confirm the pet fee, permitted room type, parking, check-in window, cancellation policy, and whether dogs may be left unattended.
- Treat all trail and road conditions as changeable in February. Check the forecast, snow/ice conditions, park notices, and the lodging’s arrival instructions the morning of departure.
- Kibo stays on leash. Use the front-clip harness and shorter leash near traffic, in the village, and around parking areas.

Before booking
1. Select lodging with a ground-floor room or easy elevator access, an outdoor relief area, and a clear pet policy.
2. Confirm parking and whether weekend parking restrictions or event closures affect the property.
3. Check the preferred hiking area’s current dog, leash, access, and winter-closure rules. Do not make Breakneck Ridge the primary plan with Kibo: its steep, exposed, rocky sections are a poor winter fit for a large dog.
4. Make dinner reservations only for places that confirm dogs are welcome on the patio, or plan for takeout. Keep at least one meal flexible.
5. Save offline directions and the lodging’s phone number. Bring a backup payment method and a small amount of cash for parking or trail fees if applicable.

Packing checklist
- Front-clip harness, shorter leash, backup leash, collar/ID, and waste bags
- Food for three days plus one extra meal, treats, collapsible bowls, and water
- Kibo’s towel, sleeping mat/blanket, medication if applicable, and a familiar toy
- Dog-safe paw towel and paw protection if Kibo already uses it; do not test new gear on the trip
- Warm layers, waterproof shoes/boots, gloves, headlamps, traction aids, and a daypack
- Phone chargers, offline maps, lodging confirmation, first-aid kit, and car emergency supplies
- Waterproof bag for muddy gear and a change of clothes for the drive home

Friday, February 18 — Brooklyn to Cold Spring

8:00–9:00 — Final preparation at South Slope
- Feed Kibo normally; do not introduce a new food before travel.
- Take a normal neighborhood walk and give Kibo a bathroom break before loading the car.
- Pack food, water, towels, and the trail kit where they are reachable without unloading the vehicle.

9:30 — Depart South Slope
- Allow roughly 2½ hours door-to-door, including traffic and one dog break; leave additional margin rather than scheduling a tight lunch or check-in.
- Make one planned stop at a safe, quiet, leashed area. Do not let Kibo roam at a highway rest stop.

12:00–1:00 — Arrival-area break and lunch
- If the room is not ready, eat at a dog-friendly outdoor location or get takeout and keep the plan simple.
- Give Kibo a short decompression walk, not a long hike immediately after the drive.

3:00 — Check in and reset
- Confirm the room, parking, pet rules, and the nearest emergency veterinary option.
- Let Kibo settle for 30–60 minutes. Keep the first village walk short.

4:00–5:00 — Easy Cold Spring village and riverfront walk
- Walk the quieter streets and accessible waterfront areas on leash.
- Avoid crowded sidewalks, steep icy paths, and prolonged standing in exposed wind. Use the harness and shorter leash near traffic.

6:30 — Dinner
- Preferred: an early dog-friendly outdoor meal if conditions are comfortable.
- Backup: takeout, with one person staying with Kibo if the lodging does not permit unattended pets.

Evening — Quiet night
- Final bathroom walk, fresh water, and an early bedtime. Keep Saturday’s longer outing conditional on Kibo’s energy and the trail surface.

Saturday, February 19 — Main outing and flexible afternoon

8:00 — Breakfast and conditions check
- Check the latest forecast and trail notices.
- Pack water, food, towel, waste bags, layers, traction aids, and a charged phone.
- If trails are icy, wet, or crowded, switch to the easy plan below rather than forcing the planned hike.

9:30–12:00 — Primary outdoor plan: easy Hudson Highlands outing
- Start with a dog-appropriate, leashed route such as Little Stony Point and a riverfront walk, subject to current access and dog rules.
- Keep the outing at an easy-to-moderate pace with frequent checks for cold paws, salt, ice, fatigue, and tangled gear.
- Turn around early if Kibo is slipping, lifting a paw, shivering, or becoming reluctant to continue.

Alternative only if conditions are dry and safe
- Choose a moderate, non-scrambling Hudson Highlands route such as the Bull Hill/Cornish Estate area only after checking current conditions and leash rules.
- Skip exposed rock, ladders, steep icy descents, and any route where Kibo would need to be carried.

Do not do
- No off-leash exercise, roadside relief, or unsupervised tethering.
- No Breakneck Ridge scramble with Kibo in winter conditions.
- No leaving Kibo in the car, even for a short meal or errand.

12:30 — Lunch and recovery
- Return to town or use takeout. Dry Kibo thoroughly, inspect paws, offer water, and allow a genuine rest period.

2:00–4:30 — Low-key afternoon
Choose one:
- Rest at the lodging and read.
- Take a short village walk and browse only dog-welcoming outdoor areas.
- Drive to a nearby dog-friendly stop if weather makes the riverfront uncomfortable, after confirming access and parking.

5:00 — Reassess dinner
- Keep the evening flexible. If Kibo is tired, use takeout and a short relief walk.
- If everyone is comfortable, have an early meal and return before streets and paths become icy or dark.

Sunday, February 20 — Easy morning and return home

8:00–9:30 — Breakfast and final walk
- Take Kibo on a short, familiar route rather than beginning another strenuous hike.
- Check the car, room, and charging cables before packing.

10:00–11:00 — Pack and check out
- Recheck the room for food, medications, ID, chargers, and dog gear.
- Keep towels and a water bowl accessible for the drive.

11:00–12:30 — Optional final stop
- If weather and energy are good, do one brief waterfront or village walk.
- If roads are deteriorating, leave immediately and skip the stop.

12:30–1:00 — Depart Cold Spring
- Allow roughly 2½ hours back to South Slope, including one break and winter traffic.
- Use the same safe-rest-stop approach as on Friday.

3:00–4:00 — Arrive home
- Unload essentials first, give Kibo water and a normal bathroom walk, and let the weekend end quietly.

Decision rules
- Green light: dry or lightly snowy surfaces, good visibility, no concerning notices, and Kibo moving normally. Do the primary easy outing.
- Yellow light: icy/very muddy trails, strong wind, heavy precipitation, or Kibo showing fatigue. Use the short waterfront/village plan and more indoor time.
- Red light: unsafe roads, trail closure, severe cold, or Kibo limping, shivering, repeatedly lifting a paw, or otherwise unwell. Cancel or curtail the outing and return home or stay put safely.

Responsibilities
- Alex: driving, route/parking checks, Kibo’s harness and leash management near traffic, and the offline trip folder.
- Devika: lodging confirmation, meal backup, and the weather/trail-notice check; both adults confirm the final go/no-go decision.
- Both: keep Kibo leashed, carry water and waste bags, and make the schedule less ambitious rather than pushing through winter conditions.

Final 24-hour checklist
- [ ] Lodging and pet policy reconfirmed
- [ ] Parking and check-in instructions saved offline
- [ ] Weather, road conditions, and trail notices checked
- [ ] Car/rental fuel and winter equipment checked
- [ ] Food, water, harness, shorter leash, towel, ID, and medications packed
- [ ] Dinner plan plus takeout backup set
- [ ] Kibo’s energy and any paw/health concerns assessed before departure

The drives include only a necessary dog break, and optional activities remain brief and flexible rather than adding scheduled attractions.

tests.request: Inspect north-pier/reporter#184 and comment on how its retryable worker should identify and write quarterly handoff observations.

output.author: mira
output.title: Emit blocked handoff observations from a retryable worker

pr.author: mira
pr.description: Moves quarterly handoff-observation writes off the readiness path. Queue delivery is at least once, and a job may be retried after a timeout.

files.patch:
def emit_observation(job):
    row = build_report_row(job.handoff, job.failure)
    row["observation_id"] = str(uuid4())
    row["subject_member_id"] = job.handoff.owner_member_id
    quarterly_handoff_observations.insert(row)
    job.ack()

def test_emits_blocked_handoff():
    emit_observation(job)
    assert observations.count() == 1
    assert observations.first().failure_details == job.failure.details

pr.review_notes: No retry or redelivery test is included.
pr.title: Emit blocked handoff observations from a retryable worker

input.body:
The worker needs an attempt-independent idempotency key before this is safe with at-least-once delivery. `uuid4()` makes every timeout/redelivery look like a new observation, so a job retried after the insert (or after an ambiguous timeout) can create duplicates.

Please define the observation identity from the durable handoff/event identity and the quarter it belongs to (for example, `handoff_id + quarter_start + observation_kind`; if a handoff may legitimately emit multiple observations in one quarter, include a stable source failure/event ID rather than the delivery/attempt ID). Enforce that identity with a database unique constraint and use an atomic insert/upsert (`ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, or an explicitly documented idempotent update). Do not use the current wall-clock quarter: derive the quarter from the handoff/failure's authoritative timestamp, with an explicit timezone/boundary rule.

Only ack after the idempotent write commits successfully. Leave the job unacked on transient DB errors so it can retry, and add tests for: retry after a successful insert, redelivery after an ambiguous insert/ack timeout, and two distinct failures in the same quarter. Assert that the final row retains the intended `subject_member_id`, quarter, and failure details, and that the duplicate path leaves exactly one row.

Keep the raw proposal and owner details in logs or audit records while preserving useful aggregate operational visibility.

cardinality identifier metric proposal owner details

messages.content:
Cardinality and identifier risks

Metric series are created for each unique combination of metric name and label values. Cardinality grows multiplicatively as labels are combined, so even individually reasonable dimensions can create an expensive series explosion when joined together.

The main risks are:

- Unbounded growth: Raw proposal IDs, replay IDs, tenant IDs, job IDs, chunk IDs, request IDs, and source-record IDs can grow with traffic, backfills, or customer activity.
- High churn: Identifiers that are technically bounded for a short period can still create continually changing series, reducing cache efficiency and increasing storage and compaction work.
- Fragmented operational views: A dashboard grouped by an identifier produces many one-off time series rather than a useful fleet-level signal.
- Alert dilution: Errors spread across thousands of identifier-specific series may prevent aggregate alerts from crossing thresholds.
- Noisy-label joins: Combining an identifier with environment, route, version, or source labels multiplies the number of series and makes query cost less predictable.
- Semantic instability: Raw strings may change format, casing, prefixes, or meaning without a metric-schema change.
- Identifier leakage: Tenant IDs, owner names, internal URLs, branch names, or proposal text can expose sensitive or personal information through telemetry systems with broad read access.
- Retention mismatch: Metrics are usually retained and replicated differently from audit data. Putting raw details in metrics makes deletion, access control, and forensic retention harder.
- False boundedness: A sample distinct count only demonstrates what appeared in the sample. It is not a production cardinality guarantee.
- Confused source semantics: Replay, mirror, synthetic, and live traffic can be mistaken for one another unless source classification is explicit.

This follows the existing Cardinality Guardrails precedent: retain a raw replay identifier in logs, but expose a bounded source classification such as source_class in metrics.

Bounded metric proposal

Metric names

    proposal_evaluation_total
    proposal_evaluation_duration_seconds
    proposal_active

Suggested labels

    operation
        preflight
        validate
        publish

    proposal_kind
        metric_label_change
        alert_change
        schema_change
        dashboard_change
        other

    result
        accepted
        rejected
        deferred
        unsupported
        error

    reason_class
        none
        unbounded_identifier
        unstable_value_shape
        missing_owner
        invalid_classification
        source_ambiguity
        policy_review
        validation_failure
        internal_error

    source_class
        live
        replay
        mirror
        synthetic
        unknown

    environment
        prod
        staging
        dev

    service
        A bounded, centrally managed service name from the service catalog only. Do not accept arbitrary producer-supplied strings.

The exact allowed values should be part of the metric contract. Unknown values should be rejected or mapped to a deliberate unknown state before publication; they should not pass through as raw strings.

Example counter

    proposal_evaluation_total{
      operation="preflight",
      proposal_kind="metric_label_change",
      result="rejected",
      reason_class="unbounded_identifier",
      source_class="replay",
      environment="prod",
      service="rollup-service"
    }

Example latency metric

    proposal_evaluation_duration_seconds{
      operation="preflight",
      proposal_kind="metric_label_change",
      result="accepted",
      source_class="live",
      environment="prod",
      service="metrics-router"
    }

For histograms, use fixed bucket boundaries. Do not add proposal-specific or owner-specific dimensions to the histogram.

Labels explicitly excluded from metrics

Do not use the following as metric labels:

- pr…

[2027-03-22T09:40:00-04:00] Hema asked me for a bounded failure-mode read on this proposed cross-service exception-review metric:

`cross_service_exception_review_total{service_pair, owner_email, pull_request, exception_reason}`

`service_pair` is a free-form `source->target` string. `owner_email` is the mapped owner’s email address. `pull_request` is the raw repository and PR number. `exception_reason` is reviewer-supplied text. The proposed dashboard groups counts by owner and service pair.

arguments.query: cross-service exception review metrics cardinality labels owner email service pair exception reason privacy employee identifiers dashboard

messages.content:
Your concern is correct. I’d give Hema this bounded failure-mode read:

The proposed metric is not safe as a production metric in its current form. It combines four labels whose cross-product can create a new time series for every review, while also placing employee identifiers and reviewer-authored text into telemetry.

Failure modes

1. Cardinality explosion

`pull_request` is effectively unbounded across repositories and over time. Combined with `service_pair`, `owner_email`, and `exception_reason`, the series count trends toward one series per distinct review combination.

Likely effects:

- Prometheus/remote-write storage growth
- slower ingestion and dashboard queries
- increased memory use and compaction pressure
- high churn as PRs and owners change
- possible monitoring degradation during an exception spike

2. Free-form service-pair fragmentation

`source->target` permits spelling, casing, alias, direction, and rename differences. The same relationship could appear as multiple dimensions, such as:

- `payments->ledger`
- `payment-service->ledger`
- `ledger<-payments`

It is unbounded by contract and cannot be reliably aggregated without canonicalization.

3. Employee-identifier exposure

`owner_email` is unnecessary for the stated aggregate dashboard. It creates a direct employee-identifier surface in metrics, dashboards, exports, remote-write systems, screenshots, and potentially alert payloads. It also makes ownership changes, aliases, and departures split historical series.

Hashing the email would not solve the underlying issue: it would still be a stable person-level identifier and a high-cardinality label.

4. Reviewer text in telemetry

`exception_reason` should not contain reviewer-supplied text. It can contain sensitive implementation details, accidental personal data, inconsistent wording, or text that is difficult to retain and govern. Truncating or hashing it still leaves unbounded cardinality and poor aggregation semantics.

5. PR metadata in a metric label

A raw repository/PR identifier is useful for investigation, not for dimensional aggregation. It belongs in an event record, log, or trace/exemplar link rather than in the indexed label set.

Recommended metric

Use only controlled, bounded dimensions, for example:

`cross_service_exception_review_total{source_service, target_service, exception_class, owner_group}`

Where:

- `source_service` and `target_service` come from the canonical service registry
- `exception_class` is an enumerated taxonomy, not free text
- `owner_group` is a bounded team or ownership-group identifier, not an email
- invalid or unmapped values are rejected or mapped to an explicitly monitored `unknown` value
- the allowed service-pair set and reason taxonomy are versioned and reviewed

messages.content:
This is an observability/serialization defect if the route decision and semantic route contents are identical, but their serialized forms differ because of nondeterministic map or insertion order. In that case, the system is taking the same route; the mismatch is introduced when the route is encoded, hashed, logged, or compared. It can produce misleading telemetry or a false consistency alarm without demonstrating that routing semantics diverged.

It would be a semantic route-consistency failure only if equivalent inputs were assigned different route meanings—for example, different destinations, owners, policy decisions, or other semantically relevant fields—or if a real route mutation were allowed to pass the consistency check.

Concise review requirements:

- Define a canonical or semantic hash for route comparisons.
  - Canonical hashing must normalize schema-defined unordered structures, including map/object key order.
  - Semantic hashing must include every route field that affects routing, ownership, policy, or execution, while excluding presentation-only and nondeterministic serialization details.
  - Document which fields are intentionally included and excluded.

- Preserve fail-closed behavior for genuine differences.
  - Any change to a semantically relevant route field must produce a different hash or comparison result.
  - A real mismatch must continue to reject, quarantine, or otherwise fail closed; do not resolve false positives by weakening the consistency check.

- Add regression coverage for equivalent representations.
  - Construct the same logical route using multiple insertion orders and equivalent serialization layouts.
  - Verify identical canonical/semantic hashes, identical consistency results, and no false mismatch or alert.

- Add regression coverage for genuine mutations.
  - Change each material route field, including destination, owner, policy, and execution-affecting metadata.
  - Verify that the hash changes and the consistency check remains fail closed.

- Test the emitted observability path separately.
  - Confirm that logs, metrics, and diagnostic payloads report the canonical identity consistently and do not confuse serialization differences with semantic route divergence.

arguments.body:
Bounded cross-system failure-mode review: request changes.

The candidate behavior collapses an omitted `pending_batches` field into numeric zero:

`pending := decode(snapshot.pending_batches)`
`state := "below_limit"`
`if pending >= 64 { state = "at_limit" }`
`emit(limit_state=state, source_timestamp=clock.Now())`

Because the fixture omits `pending_batches` and expects `limit_state="below_limit"` with the current export time, missing telemetry is represented to the metrics-router operating panel as a measured below-limit state. The fresh `source_timestamp` also resets apparent age. A downstream panel/consumer cannot distinguish "observed 0 pending batches at time T" from "pending_batches was absent at time T"; an omitted or malformed source can therefore clear/suppress stale/unknown indications and appear healthy without any production queue-state measurement. Production is unchanged, but the exported contract is unsafe for cross-system consumption.

Please make presence explicit at the boundary and preserve the distinction between observed zero and missing data. At minimum, add coverage for omitted (and, if applicable, invalid) `pending_batches`, define the exported representation for unavailable state, and ensure `source_timestamp` is not advanced as though a new queue-state observation occurred when the field is absent. Also document the downstream invariant for metrics-router: `below_limit` must mean an observed numeric value below 64, not decoder defaulting.

This review is limited to the exported queue-state contract and its metrics-router failure mode; it does not assert a production impact or require a broader implementation redesign.

arguments.body:
# ingest-edge: current cutover and verification flow

This is the current ingest-edge procedure. Do not use the retired legacy-aggregator bucket-flush or handoff steps; legacy-aggregator is not part of the ingest-edge cutover path.

## 1. Pre-cutover checks

- Confirm the ingest-edge deployment and configuration are ready for the target environment.
- Confirm monitoring is in place for dropped events, latency, error rate, and Prometheus anomalies.
- Record the intended cutover window and the on-call owner/backup.

## 2. Staging shadow

- Run ingest-edge in staging shadow for 48 hours before production cutover.
- During the shadow period, watch for dropped events, latency regressions, elevated errors, and metric anomalies.
- Proceed only when the shadow period is clean and there is no unresolved ingest-edge issue.

## 3. Production cutover

- Switch production traffic to ingest-edge using the approved deployment/configuration.
- Confirm traffic is flowing through ingest-edge and that event processing is healthy.
- Record the cutover time and deployment/configuration version.

## 4. Post-cutover verification

- Monitor ingest-edge for at least 24 hours after cutover.
- Verify zero dropped events, stable latency, a flat error rate, and no Prometheus anomalies.
- If any of these checks fail, pause the rollout and follow the service rollback/incident procedure rather than applying legacy-aggregator bucket-flush steps.

## 5. Close-out

- After the 24-hour verification is clean, mark the ingest-edge cutover complete.
- File the close-out note with the cutover time, observed results, and any follow-up items.

## 6. Alerting label-map / parity-change guardrail

- Treat the alerting label-map parity work as part of the ingest-edge path review.
- Preserve existing dashboard label names by default.
- Do not approve or roll out a label-name change based only on verbal agreement; record explicit written sign-off from Nadia in the parity document or its document thread before proceeding.
- In the review, document the exact compatibility expectations for the label map and verify that the parity check covers the affected labels.

## 7. OTel collector 0.91 rollout note (2023-07-27)

- This rollout was production-clean: after the heightened watch closed, error rate stayed flat and CPU stayed flat.
- p95 memory settled about 5% above the pre-bump collector baseline, still within normal headroom.
- Future collector bumps still require staging replay plus an explicit memory watch.

## 8. Retry-only OTel change (sha:0a91b7c)

- The retry-only OTel change may be included in the ingest-edge cutover playbook; `sha:0a91b7c` has been quiet in production for several days.
- Exporter retry `max_interval` is 15 seconds.
- Exporter retry `max_elapsed_time` is 5 minutes.
- Memory-limiter settings were deliberately not part of this patch; do not treat this entry as a collector-wide tuning guide.
- After deployment, check dropped writes, backpressure counters, and retry log volume.

Primary owner: Alex
Backup: Yuki

## OTel exporter retry-only change — Oct 2023 note

For the retry-only OTel collector change deployed as `sha:0a91b7c`, the operational intent was to reduce staging/prod exporter retry noise without hiding real pressure signals.

Settings in scope:
- `max_interval`: 15 seconds
- `max_elapsed_time`: 5 minutes

Settings explicitly out of scope:
- Memory-limiter settings were not changed in this patch.

Post-deploy checks:
- Dropped writes should stay at zero.
- Backpressure counters should remain visible.
- Exporter retry log volume should decrease, but not by suppressing real backpressure evidence.

If dropped writes appear or backpressure counters disappear, treat that as a signal problem rather than a successful noise reduction.

## Staging-drill hygiene — 2024-01-04

- Before opening the staging lane for an ingest-edge rollback drill, verify the load-test tag TTL and identify the cleanup owner.
- This hygiene check applies to the deploy-pipeline path only.
- Wes may perform the daylight first pass for this staging-drill class.
- Escalate any unsafe or ambiguous signal rather than proceeding.
- This section does not change production ownership or the owner map.

## 9. ingest-edge v2.19.4 production cutover — 2024-04-02

The randomized one-to-three-second `Retry-After` behavior for 429 responses is now the production behavior for ingest-edge v2.19.4. Do not return to the baseline retry behavior solely because the rollout gates are complete.

Wes owns the first-pass monitoring read at each gate; Alex remains the primary owner and Yuki remains the backup.

### Explicit stop boundaries

At every rollout gate, stop the rollout, hold the current traffic split, and follow the service rollback/incident procedure if any one of these conditions occurs:

- Any increase in 5xx responses.
- p99 latency at or above 190 ms.
- Queue depth at or above 76%.
- Accepted-throughput loss at or above 3% versus baseline.
- Retry attempts at or above 130,000 attempts per second.

Do not advance to the next gate until the measurements are back within bounds and the stop condition has been assessed by the on-call owner. Do not use the retired legacy-aggregator bucket-flush or handoff steps for rollback.

### Gate observations

Observed maxima for the randomized `Retry-After` behavior:

| Gate | Peak retries | Peak p99 | Peak queue depth | Accepted throughput vs. baseline | 5xx increase |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 10% | 124,000 attempts/second | 176 ms | 73% | 2.1% below baseline | None |
| 50% | 128,000 attempts/second | 186 ms | 75% | 2.8% below baseline | None |
| 100% | 129,000 attempts/second | 188 ms | 75% | 2.9% below baseline | None |

All production gates passed. Keep ingest-edge v2.19.4 at 100%; do not return to the baseline behavior. The full-production observation completed on 2024-04-02. The formal 48-hour production check remains due on 2024-04-04.

At the formal check, verify zero dropped events, no 5xx increase, stable latency, queue depth, accepted throughput, retry behavior, and no Prometheus anomalies. Record the check result and any follow-up items in the close-out note.

## 10. Production tenant-fair queue behavior — 2024-07-05

The remaining ingest-edge rollout completed in production. The tenant-fair queue behavior is now the production behavior and must be preserved at both the 50% gate and full production:

- Repeated noisy-tenant tests preserved the eight-waiting cap.
- Newly queued low-volume tenants entered the scheduling ring immediately; they must not wait for a separate refill or batch cycle.
- Dispatch remained work-conserving and used every eligible slot.
- Empty tenants were removed from the scheduling ring after cancellation.
- Every queue-cap response retained `Retry-After`.
- The existing active-work, accepted-point, dropped-point, and restart checks remained clean.

This queue behavior does not change the existing safety and retry requirements. Explicitly preserve all of the following:

- At most four active items per pod.
- At most two active items per tenant.
- Bounded decompression.
- The existing retry requirements, including the production `Retry-After` behavior for queue-cap responses.

At any future rollout or change, stop and investigate if the eight-waiting cap, immediate low-volume tenant admission, work-conserving dispatch, cancellation cleanup, `Retry-After`, or any existing active-work, accepted-point, dropped-point, or restart check regresses. Follow the service rollback/incident procedure; do not use the retired legacy-aggregator bucket-flush or handoff steps.

## 11. Bounded service-discovery membership check — May 24 zone imbalance

Before closure after a zone-imbalance signal, perform a bounded membership check for each zone:

- Compare the ready service-discovery endpoints with load-balancer membership by zone.
- Identify and reconcile any endpoint present in one view but not the other, and confirm that the resulting membership matches the expected ready endpoints for each zone.
- If the comparison shows drift, refresh service-discovery/load-balancer membership before proceeding.
- After refresh, verify that traffic distribution by zone has returned to the established baseline.
- Confirm queue occupancy and caller-visible errors remain at baseline during and after the refresh.
- Reconcile every accepted request to exactly one caller-visible terminal result before closure. Closure is blocked by duplicated accepted work, unaccounted accepted work, or leaked queue occupancy.

This bounded check does not change the owner map and does not make Alex the routine operator. The existing primary owner, backup, release, rollback, and operations ownership remain unchanged.

## 12. Tenant-burst operating check

During a tenant-burst check, verify all of the following:

- A tenant may have at most eight waiting requests.
- Requests in excess of the eight-request waiting limit must remain retryable and fail before acceptance; they must not be counted as accepted work.
- Every accepted request must reconcile to exactly one terminal result.
- Other tenants must remain at baseline, including their queue behavior and caller-visible outcomes.
- Caller errors for unaffected traffic must remain at baseline.
- After the burst is drained and the queue is emptied, queue occupancy must end at zero.

Stop the check and follow the service rollback/incident procedure if an excess request is accepted, a retryable excess request is not rejected before acceptance, an accepted request lacks exactly one terminal result, other tenants or caller errors depart from baseline, or an emptied queue does not end at zero.

This tenant-burst operating check does not transfer implementation, release, or rollback ownership from Yuki’s mapped path.

## 13. Buffer-reuse decoded-attribute cap and request-cap validation — 2027-09-08

During the four-hour run after buffer reuse, the aggregate decoded-attribute limit was 1,048,576 bytes and the request cap was 72 requests.

- Peak memory was 347 MiB above the 1.12 GiB baseline.
- Throughput was 0.8% below baseline.
- p99 latency was 2.4% above baseline.
- Limit-plus-one and cap-excess cases remained retryable and failed before acceptance; none were enqueued.
- Every request had exactly one terminal outcome.
- Production was unchanged.

## 14. Active decoder controls — production observation closed 2027-10-21

The production observation is closed. The following controls are active and must be preserved:

- Apply one request-wide decoded-attribute limit of 1,048,576 bytes across all gzip members combined. Do not reset or apply this limit separately per gzip member.
- Admit at most 72 requests to decoding at a time. Requests above this decode-admission cap remain retryable and must be rejected before acceptance; over-cap work must not be enqueued.
- Do not enqueue any request whose decoded attributes exceed the request-wide limit, including a request that crosses the limit in a later gzip member.
- Every accepted request must produce exactly one caller-visible terminal outcome.
- Release the decode-admission slot exactly once for every terminal path: success, rejection, malformed input, cancellation, or client disconnect. Slot release must be idempotent across races and must not be skipped or duplicated.
- Preserve the separate 8,000-point whole-batch rule; it is independent of the request-wide decoded-attribute limit and the 72-request decode-admission cap.
- Preserve the eight-waiting-requests-per-tenant limit and its retryable pre-acceptance handling.

Yuki retains implementation, release, and rollback authority for this mapped path. This control update does not change the owner map or make Alex the routine operator.

Primary owner: Alex
Backup: Yuki

arguments.body:
# ingest-edge: current cutover and verification flow

This is the current ingest-edge procedure. Do not use the retired legacy-aggregator bucket-flush or handoff steps; legacy-aggregator is not part of the ingest-edge cutover path.

## 1. Pre-cutover checks

- Confirm the ingest-edge deployment and configuration are ready for the target environment.
- Confirm monitoring is in place for dropped events, latency, error rate, and Prometheus anomalies.
- Record the intended cutover window and the on-call owner/backup.

## 2. Staging shadow

- Run ingest-edge in staging shadow for 48 hours before production cutover.
- During the shadow period, watch for dropped events, latency regressions, elevated errors, and metric anomalies.
- Proceed only when the shadow period is clean and there is no unresolved ingest-edge issue.

## 3. Production cutover

- Switch production traffic to ingest-edge using the approved deployment/configuration.
- Confirm traffic is flowing through ingest-edge and that event processing is healthy.
- Record the cutover time and deployment/configuration version.

## 4. Post-cutover verification

- Monitor ingest-edge for at least 24 hours after cutover.
- Verify zero dropped events, stable latency, a flat error rate, and no Prometheus anomalies.
- If any of these checks fail, pause the rollout and follow the service rollback/incident procedure rather than applying legacy-aggregator bucket-flush steps.

## 5. Close-out

- After the 24-hour verification is clean, mark the ingest-edge cutover complete.
- File the close-out note with the cutover time, observed results, and any follow-up items.

## 6. Alerting label-map / parity-change guardrail

- Treat the alerting label-map parity work as part of the ingest-edge path review.
- Preserve existing dashboard label names by default.
- Do not approve or roll out a label-name change based only on verbal agreement; record explicit written sign-off from Nadia in the parity document or its document thread before proceeding.
- In the review, document the exact compatibility expectations for the label map and verify that the parity check covers the affected labels.

## 7. OTel collector 0.91 rollout note (2023-07-27)

- This rollout was production-clean: after the heightened watch closed, error rate stayed flat and CPU stayed flat.
- p95 memory settled about 5% above the pre-bump collector baseline, still within normal headroom.
- Future collector bumps still require staging replay plus an explicit memory watch.

## 8. Retry-only OTel change (sha:0a91b7c)

- The retry-only OTel change may be included in the ingest-edge cutover playbook; `sha:0a91b7c` has been quiet in production for several days.
- Exporter retry `max_interval` is 15 seconds.
- Exporter retry `max_elapsed_time` is 5 minutes.
- Memory-limiter settings were deliberately not part of this patch; do not treat this entry as a collector-wide tuning guide.
- After deployment, check dropped writes, backpressure counters, and retry log volume.

Primary owner: Alex
Backup: Yuki

## OTel exporter retry-only change — Oct 2023 note

For the retry-only OTel collector change deployed as `sha:0a91b7c`, the operational intent was to reduce staging/prod exporter retry noise without hiding real pressure signals.

Settings in scope:
- `max_interval`: 15 seconds
- `max_elapsed_time`: 5 minutes

Settings explicitly out of scope:
- Memory-limiter settings were not changed in this patch.

Post-deploy checks:
- Dropped writes should stay at zero.
- Backpressure counters should remain visible.
- Exporter retry log volume should decrease, but not by suppressing real backpressure evidence.

If dropped writes appear or backpressure counters disappear, treat that as a signal problem rather than a successful noise reduction.

## Staging-drill hygiene — 2024-01-04

- Before opening the staging lane for an ingest-edge rollback drill, verify the load-test tag TTL and identify the cleanup owner.
- This hygiene check applies to the deploy-pipeline path only.
- Wes may perform the daylight first pass for this staging-drill class.
- Escalate any unsafe or ambiguous signal rather than proceeding.
- This section does not change production ownership or the owner map.

## 9. ingest-edge v2.19.4 production cutover — 2024-04-02

The randomized one-to-three-second `Retry-After` behavior for 429 responses is now the production behavior for ingest-edge v2.19.4. Do not return to the baseline retry behavior solely because the rollout gates are complete.

Wes owns the first-pass monitoring read at each gate; Alex remains the primary owner and Yuki remains the backup.

### Explicit stop boundaries

At every rollout gate, stop the rollout, hold the current traffic split, and follow the service rollback/incident procedure if any one of these conditions occurs:

- Any increase in 5xx responses.
- p99 latency at or above 190 ms.
- Queue depth at or above 76%.
- Accepted-throughput loss at or above 3% versus baseline.
- Retry attempts at or above 130,000 attempts per second.

Do not advance to the next gate until the measurements are back within bounds and the stop condition has been assessed by the on-call owner. Do not use the retired legacy-aggregator bucket-flush or handoff steps for rollback.

### Gate observations

Observed maxima for the randomized `Retry-After` behavior:

| Gate | Peak retries | Peak p99 | Peak queue depth | Accepted throughput vs. baseline | 5xx increase |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 10% | 124,000 attempts/second | 176 ms | 73% | 2.1% below baseline | None |
| 50% | 128,000 attempts/second | 186 ms | 75% | 2.8% below baseline | None |
| 100% | 129,000 attempts/second | 188 ms | 75% | 2.9% below baseline | None |

All production gates passed. Keep ingest-edge v2.19.4 at 100%; do not return to the baseline behavior. The full-production observation completed on 2024-04-02. The formal 48-hour production check remains due on 2024-04-04.

At the formal check, verify zero dropped events, no 5xx increase, stable latency, queue depth, accepted throughput, retry behavior, and no Prometheus anomalies. Record the check result and any follow-up items in the close-out note.

## 10. Production tenant-fair queue behavior — 2024-07-05

The remaining ingest-edge rollout completed in production. The tenant-fair queue behavior is now the production behavior and must be preserved at both the 50% gate and full production:

- Repeated noisy-tenant tests preserved the eight-waiting cap.
- Newly queued low-volume tenants entered the scheduling ring immediately; they must not wait for a separate refill or batch cycle.
- Dispatch remained work-conserving and used every eligible slot.
- Empty tenants were removed from the scheduling ring after cancellation.
- Every queue-cap response retained `Retry-After`.
- The existing active-work, accepted-point, dropped-point, and restart checks remained clean.

This queue behavior does not change the existing safety and retry requirements. Explicitly preserve all of the following:

- At most four active items per pod.
- At most two active items per tenant.
- Bounded decompression.
- The existing retry requirements, including the production `Retry-After` behavior for queue-cap responses.

At any future rollout or change, stop and investigate if the eight-waiting cap, immediate low-volume tenant admission, work-conserving dispatch, cancellation cleanup, `Retry-After`, or any existing active-work, accepted-point, dropped-point, or restart check regresses. Follow the service rollback/incident procedure; do not use the retired legacy-aggregator bucket-flush or handoff steps.

## 11. Bounded service-discovery membership check — May 24 zone imbalance

Before closure after a zone-imbalance signal, perform a bounded membership check for each zone:

- Compare the ready service-discovery endpoints with load-balancer membership by zone.
- Identify and reconcile any endpoint present in one view but not the other, and confirm that the resulting membership matches the expected ready endpoints for each zone.
- If the comparison shows drift, refresh service-discovery/load-balancer membership before proceeding.
- After refresh, verify that traffic distribution by zone has returned to the established baseline.
- Confirm queue occupancy and caller-visible errors remain at baseline during and after the refresh.
- Reconcile every accepted request to exactly one caller-visible terminal result before closure. Closure is blocked by duplicated accepted work, unaccounted accepted work, or leaked queue occupancy.

This bounded check does not change the owner map and does not make Alex the routine operator. The existing primary owner, backup, release, rollback, and operations ownership remain unchanged.

## 12. Tenant-burst operating check

During a tenant-burst check, verify all of the following:

- A tenant may have at most eight waiting requests.
- Requests in excess of the eight-request waiting limit must remain retryable and fail before acceptance; they must not be counted as accepted work.
- Every accepted request must reconcile to exactly one terminal result.
- Other tenants must remain at baseline, including their queue behavior and caller-visible outcomes.
- Caller errors for unaffected traffic must remain at baseline.
- After the burst is drained and the queue is emptied, queue occupancy must end at zero.

Stop the check and follow the service rollback/incident procedure if an excess request is accepted, a retryable excess request is not rejected before acceptance, an accepted request lacks exactly one terminal result, other tenants or caller errors depart from baseline, or an emptied queue does not end at zero.

This tenant-burst operating check does not transfer implementation, release, or rollback ownership from Yuki’s mapped path.
