arguments.body:
# ingest-edge: current cutover and verification flow

This is the current ingest-edge procedure. Do not use the retired legacy-aggregator bucket-flush or handoff steps; legacy-aggregator is not part of the ingest-edge cutover path.

## 1. Pre-cutover checks

- Confirm the ingest-edge deployment and configuration are ready for the target environment.
- Confirm monitoring is in place for dropped events, latency, error rate, and Prometheus anomalies.
- Record the intended cutover window and the on-call owner/backup.

## 2. Staging shadow

- Run ingest-edge in staging shadow for 48 hours before production cutover.
- During the shadow period, watch for dropped events, latency regressions, elevated errors, and metric anomalies.
- Proceed only when the shadow period is clean and there is no unresolved ingest-edge issue.

## 3. Production cutover

- Switch production traffic to ingest-edge using the approved deployment/configuration.
- Confirm traffic is flowing through ingest-edge and that event processing is healthy.
- Record the cutover time and deployment/configuration version.

## 4. Post-cutover verification

- Monitor ingest-edge for at least 24 hours after cutover.
- Verify zero dropped events, stable latency, a flat error rate, and no Prometheus anomalies.
- If any of these checks fail, pause the rollout and follow the service rollback/incident procedure rather than applying legacy-aggregator bucket-flush steps.

## 5. Close-out

- After the 24-hour verification is clean, mark the ingest-edge cutover complete.
- File the close-out note with the cutover time, observed results, and any follow-up items.

## 6. Alerting label-map / parity-change guardrail

- Treat the alerting label-map parity work as part of the ingest-edge path review.
- Preserve existing dashboard label names by default.
- Do not approve or roll out a label-name change based only on verbal agreement; record explicit written sign-off from Nadia in the parity document or its document thread before proceeding.
- In the review, document the exact compatibility expectations for the label map and verify that the parity check covers the affected labels.

## 7. OTel collector 0.91 rollout note (2023-07-27)

- This rollout was production-clean: after the heightened watch closed, error rate stayed flat and CPU stayed flat.
- p95 memory settled about 5% above the pre-bump collector baseline, still within normal headroom.
- Future collector bumps still require staging replay plus an explicit memory watch.

## 8. Retry-only OTel change (sha:0a91b7c)

- The retry-only OTel change may be included in the ingest-edge cutover playbook; `sha:0a91b7c` has been quiet in production for several days.
- Exporter retry `max_interval` is 15 seconds.
- Exporter retry `max_elapsed_time` is 5 minutes.
- Memory-limiter settings were deliberately not part of this patch; do not treat this entry as a collector-wide tuning guide.
- After deployment, check dropped writes, backpressure counters, and retry log volume.

Primary owner: Alex
Backup: Yuki

## OTel exporter retry-only change — Oct 2023 note

For the retry-only OTel collector change deployed as `sha:0a91b7c`, the operational intent was to reduce staging/prod exporter retry noise without hiding real pressure signals.

Settings in scope:
- `max_interval`: 15 seconds
- `max_elapsed_time`: 5 minutes

Settings explicitly out of scope:
- Memory-limiter settings were not changed in this patch.

Post-deploy checks:
- Dropped writes should stay at zero.
- Backpressure counters should remain visible.
- Exporter retry log volume should decrease, but not by suppressing real backpressure evidence.

If dropped writes appear or backpressure counters disappear, treat that as a signal problem rather than a successful noise reduction.

## Staging-drill hygiene — 2024-01-04

- Before opening the staging lane for an ingest-edge rollback drill, verify the load-test tag TTL and identify the cleanup owner.
- This hygiene check applies to the deploy-pipeline path only.
- Wes may perform the daylight first pass for this staging-drill class.
- Escalate any unsafe or ambiguous signal rather than proceeding.
- This section does not change production ownership or the owner map.

## 9. ingest-edge v2.19.4 production cutover — 2024-04-02

The randomized one-to-three-second `Retry-After` behavior for 429 responses is now the production behavior for ingest-edge v2.19.4. Do not return to the baseline retry behavior solely because the rollout gates are complete.

Wes owns the first-pass monitoring read at each gate; Alex remains the primary owner and Yuki remains the backup.

### Explicit stop boundaries

At every rollout gate, stop the rollout, hold the current traffic split, and follow the service rollback/incident procedure if any one of these conditions occurs:

- Any increase in 5xx responses.
- p99 latency at or above 190 ms.
- Queue depth at or above 76%.
- Accepted-throughput loss at or above 3% versus baseline.
- Retry attempts at or above 130,000 attempts per second.

Do not advance to the next gate until the measurements are back within bounds and the stop condition has been assessed by the on-call owner. Do not use the retired legacy-aggregator bucket-flush or handoff steps for rollback.

### Gate observations

Observed maxima for the randomized `Retry-After` behavior:

| Gate | Peak retries | Peak p99 | Peak queue depth | Accepted throughput vs. baseline | 5xx increase |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 10% | 124,000 attempts/second | 176 ms | 73% | 2.1% below baseline | None |
| 50% | 128,000 attempts/second | 186 ms | 75% | 2.8% below baseline | None |
| 100% | 129,000 attempts/second | 188 ms | 75% | 2.9% below baseline | None |

All production gates passed. Keep ingest-edge v2.19.4 at 100%; do not return to the baseline behavior. The full-production observation completed on 2024-04-02. The formal 48-hour production check remains due on 2024-04-04.

At the formal check, verify zero dropped events, no 5xx increase, stable latency, queue depth, accepted throughput, retry behavior, and no Prometheus anomalies. Record the check result and any follow-up items in the close-out note.

## 10. Production tenant-fair queue behavior — 2024-07-05

The remaining ingest-edge rollout completed in production. The tenant-fair queue behavior is now the production behavior and must be preserved at both the 50% gate and full production:

- Repeated noisy-tenant tests preserved the eight-waiting cap.
- Newly queued low-volume tenants entered the scheduling ring immediately; they must not wait for a separate refill or batch cycle.
- Dispatch remained work-conserving and used every eligible slot.
- Empty tenants were removed from the scheduling ring after cancellation.
- Every queue-cap response retained `Retry-After`.
- The existing active-work, accepted-point, dropped-point, and restart checks remained clean.

This queue behavior does not change the existing safety and retry requirements. Explicitly preserve all of the following:

- At most four active items per pod.
- At most two active items per tenant.
- Bounded decompression.
- The existing retry requirements, including the production `Retry-After` behavior for queue-cap responses.

At any future rollout or change, stop and investigate if the eight-waiting cap, immediate low-volume tenant admission, work-conserving dispatch, cancellation cleanup, `Retry-After`, or any existing active-work, accepted-point, dropped-point, or restart check regresses. Follow the service rollback/incident procedure; do not use the retired legacy-aggregator bucket-flush or handoff steps.

## 11. Bounded service-discovery membership check — May 24 zone imbalance

Before closure after a zone-imbalance signal, perform a bounded membership check for each zone:

- Compare the ready service-discovery endpoints with load-balancer membership by zone.
- Identify and reconcile any endpoint present in one view but not the other, and confirm that the resulting membership matches the expected ready endpoints for each zone.
- If the comparison shows drift, refresh service-discovery/load-balancer membership before proceeding.
- After refresh, verify that traffic distribution by zone has returned to the established baseline.
- Confirm queue occupancy and caller-visible errors remain at baseline during and after the refresh.
- Reconcile every accepted request to exactly one caller-visible terminal result before closure. Closure is blocked by duplicated accepted work, unaccounted accepted work, or leaked queue occupancy.

This bounded check does not change the owner map and does not make Alex the routine operator. The existing primary owner, backup, release, rollback, and operations ownership remain unchanged.

## 12. Tenant-burst operating check

During a tenant-burst check, verify all of the following:

- A tenant may have at most eight waiting requests.
- Requests in excess of the eight-request waiting limit must remain retryable and fail before acceptance; they must not be counted as accepted work.
- Every accepted request must reconcile to exactly one terminal result.
- Other tenants must remain at baseline, including their queue behavior and caller-visible outcomes.
- Caller errors for unaffected traffic must remain at baseline.
- After the burst is drained and the queue is emptied, queue occupancy must end at zero.

Stop the check and follow the service rollback/incident procedure if an excess request is accepted, a retryable excess request is not rejected before acceptance, an accepted request lacks exactly one terminal result, other tenants or caller errors depart from baseline, or an emptied queue does not end at zero.

This tenant-burst operating check does not transfer implementation, release, or rollback ownership from Yuki’s mapped path.

messages.content: [2027-09-26T15:30:00-04:00] I’ve completed two ordinary bouldering sessions in the repaired right shoe. The fit and edging feel predictable, the new sole has stayed secure, and I had no foot or forearm symptoms during either session or the following mornings. Structure a 75-minute session for reintroducing harder small-edge attempts, with a progressive repaired-shoe check, a bounded number of hard attempts, adequate rests, the longer warmup, and gradual total loading. Keep the established stop rules: pain above 2/10, symptoms lasting 30 minutes, or next-morning symptoms mean stepping back and contacting the clinician.

75-minute return session

Use the two symptom-free ordinary sessions as your baseline. Reintroduce intensity by substituting harder attempts for some normal climbing rather than adding them on top of your usual volume. Keep all attempts controlled—no maximal dynos, uncontrolled falls, or repeated failure attempts.

0:00–0:12 — Longer general warm-up
- 4 minutes of easy whole-body movement and shoulder/forearm circulation.
- 4 minutes of gentle ankle, foot, wrist, and forearm mobility.
- 4 minutes of easy bodyweight movement, emphasizing quiet foot placement and relaxed gripping.
- No small-edge loading yet.

0:12–0:22 — Progressive repaired-shoe check
- Inspect the repaired shoe: sole edge, toe area, rand, and repair boundary should remain fully bonded, with no lifting, gaps, unusual movement, or new hot spot.
- Walk and rise onto the forefoot for 2 minutes.
- Do easy slab or large-hold climbing for 3 minutes.
- Add gentle edging on comfortable, positive footholds for 3 minutes.
- Finish with 2 minutes of easy climbing using deliberate, quiet placements.
- Stop the progression if the shoe feels less secure or foot symptoms appear.

0:22–0:32 — Easy climbing
- Climb 3–4 very easy problems or equivalent easy movement.
- Use large footholds and relaxed hands.
- Take approximately 1 minute between problems.
- This should feel clearly easier than an ordinary session.

0:32–0:47 — Moderate transition block
- Climb 3 moderate problems or short sections.
- Introduce smaller footholds gradually, but keep the movement submaximal.
- Use about 2 minutes of rest between efforts.
- Include only the grip and foot positions already tolerated in the two ordinary sessions.

0:47–1:02 — Bounded harder small-edge block
- Maximum: 4 hard attempts total.
- Each attempt should be a short sequence or limited number of moves, not a full session-length problem.
- Start around 80–85% effort. Only attempt the next one if the shoe remains secure and symptoms are absent or no higher than 2/10.
- Rest 3 minutes between attempts; use the full rest rather than attempting while fatigued.
- Stop the block early if movement quality declines, you begin compensating, or forearm/foot symptoms develop.
- Do not add “one last attempt.”

1:02–1:10 — Easy cooldown climbing
- Climb 2 very easy problems or easy movement.
- Return to large footholds and relaxed gripping.
- No further small-edge attempts.

1:10–1:15 — Exit check
- Reinspect the repaired shoe for lifting, separation, or changed fit.
- Note any foot or forearm symptoms, their peak intensity, and whether they settle during the cooldown.
- Do not progress based only on how the session feels; also check the following morning.

Stop rules

- Pain above 2/10: stop the current progression immediately and step back to the last symptom-free level. If it does not settle or returns, end the session and contact the clinician.
- Any symptom lasting 30 minutes: contact the clinician and do not progress the loading.
- Any next-morning foot or forearm symptom: step back to the previous tolerated session level and contact the clinician.
- If symptom-free during the session and the next morning, keep the next session at the same total duration and attempt cap before increasing either difficulty or volume.

results.title: Influenza vaccination aftercare and warning signs
results.snippet: ...If you develop any symptom that feels severe or rapidly worsening, use the more urgent option rather than waiting for the >>>usual<<< timeframe.

messages.content: [2027-09-22T08:45:00-04:00] I received the scheduled influenza vaccination after arriving at 7:55 AM. I have mild soreness at the injection site but no breathing difficulty, facial swelling, widespread rash, dizziness, fever, or other acute symptom. What’s the ordinary same-day guidance for activity, hydration, and local soreness, and which symptoms or timing would warrant urgent care or contacting a clinician?

Your described mild injection-site soreness, without other symptoms, is ordinary after an influenza vaccination.

Same-day guidance

- Activity: Resume normal activities as tolerated, including exercise. If the arm is sore or you feel tired, choose lighter activity and rest; gentle arm movement can help.
- Hydration: Drink normally according to thirst and eat normally. Extra fluids are not required, but avoid becoming dehydrated.
- Soreness: Use a cool, damp cloth or wrapped cold pack for about 10–15 minutes at a time. Move the arm gently, but avoid forceful massage or pressure on the site.
- Medication: If needed and normally safe for you, an over-the-counter pain or fever reducer can be used according to its label. Routine preemptive medication is generally unnecessary.

Expected timing

- Soreness, mild redness or swelling, fatigue, headache, muscle aches, or a low-grade fever may begin within the first day and usually improve over 1–2 days.
- If you are still at the vaccination site, follow its observation instructions—many sites recommend remaining for about 15 minutes.

Seek emergency care immediately—call emergency services—if within minutes to several hours you develop trouble breathing, wheezing, throat or tongue swelling, facial swelling, widespread hives, fainting, severe dizziness, or rapidly worsening symptoms.

Contact a clinician promptly if:

- Fever is high, symptoms are severe, or symptoms are not improving after about 2–3 days.
- Injection-site redness or swelling is rapidly expanding, very painful, hot, draining pus, or significantly limits arm movement.
- New progressive tingling or weakness, trouble walking, swallowing, or breathing develops in the days to weeks afterward; these are uncommon but warrant urgent evaluation.

If you develop any symptom that feels severe or rapidly worsening, use the more urgent option rather than waiting for the usual timeframe.

messages.content: [2027-07-21T17:35:00-04:00] During a stationary pre-ride check, I found that my bicycle’s front brake lever pulls to within about one centimeter of the handlebar and front-wheel braking force is noticeably lower than usual. The rear brake works normally, the front wheel is seated, and I see no fluid, damaged housing, loose caliper, or new wheel rub. I haven’t ridden it and will keep it out of use. Give me a concise no-ride inspection limited to externally visible checks, confirm the no-ride boundary, and draft a clear description for a bicycle shop. Don’t include instructions for opening the hydraulic system or road-testing it with reduced braking.

No-ride boundary

Do not ride the bicycle—even slowly or to the shop. Keep the front brake out of service until a qualified bicycle mechanic inspects and repairs it. Do not road-test it with reduced braking.

Externally visible, stationary checks

- Confirm the front wheel remains fully seated and the axle/quick-release is closed and secure.
- Look for cracks, bends, looseness, or movement at the brake lever, handlebar mount, hose, caliper, and caliper mounts.
- Inspect the hose and fittings for cuts, kinks, abrasion, or wetness; do not loosen or open any fitting.
- Through the caliper opening, check that the pads appear present, seated, and reasonably even.
- Inspect the rotor for heavy contamination, obvious bending, cracks, or contact with nearby parts.
- Check that nothing is touching or obstructing the lever, hose, caliper, rotor, or wheel.

If anything is loose, cracked, leaking, or damaged, leave it untouched and arrange transport.

Description for the shop

“During a stationary pre-ride check, the front brake lever pulled to within about 1 cm of the handlebar, and front-wheel braking force was noticeably weaker than usual. The rear brake works normally. The front wheel is seated. I found no visible fluid, damaged hose/housing, loose caliper, or new wheel rub. The bike has not been ridden since I noticed the issue and has been kept out of use. Please inspect and repair the complete front braking system, including the lever, hose/fittings, caliper, pads, rotor, and wheel/axle interface. I have not opened the hydraulic system or road-tested it.”

messages.content: [2027-04-01T15:20:00-04:00] I’m considering my first ordinary bicycle ride after several winter weeks off. The prior chain, cassette, rear tube, rear light, and front-wheel issues are all closed, and I haven’t noticed any new fault. Give me a concise fifteen-minute pre-ride inspection and test sequence covering tires, brakes, drivetrain, wheel retention, lights, and a short loaded test, with clear findings that mean stop and get service.

Fifteen-minute pre-ride check

0:00–3:00 — Tires and wheels
- Check both tires for correct firmness with a gauge, staying within the sidewall range.
- Inspect tread and sidewalls for cuts, embedded glass, cracks, flat spots, or bulges.
- Spin each wheel: it should turn freely without significant wobble, rubbing, or a pulsing brake rotor/rim.
- Squeeze pairs of spokes briefly; look for an obviously loose or broken spoke.

Stop and get service for: any bulge, casing cut, exposed tube, persistent soft tire, major wheel wobble, wheel rub, bearing roughness, or broken/very loose spoke.

3:00–5:00 — Wheel retention
- Confirm the front and rear axle, quick-release, or thru-axle is fully seated and firmly secured.
- With the brake released, pull each wheel sideways and forward/backward. There should be no play.
- If fitted, verify quick-release levers are closed firmly against the frame/fork—not merely resting in line.

Stop and get service for: any wheel movement, an axle that will not tighten securely, a lever that opens too easily, or uncertainty about retention.

5:00–8:00 — Brakes
- Squeeze each brake separately while stationary. The lever should feel firm and should not touch the handlebar.
- Check that pads contact the braking surface evenly and that nothing is contaminated or badly worn.
- Walk the bike and apply each brake; it should stop promptly without grinding, pulling sharply, or pulsing.

Stop and get service for: a soft lever, lever-to-bar contact, cable/hydraulic leakage, grinding, severely worn pads, contaminated pads, poor stopping, or any brake that fails to release cleanly.

8:00–11:00 — Drivetrain
- Check that the chain is present, reasonably clean, and not stiff, kinked, or excessively slack.
- Rotate the cranks by hand and shift through several gears while unloaded.
- Confirm the chain does not skip, derail, grind loudly, or contact the spokes.
- Pedal gently in a low gear, then briefly apply moderate pressure.

Stop and get service for: chain skipping under light pressure, repeated derailment, a bent or loose crank, grinding or cracking noises, or any drivetrain fault that could cause sudden loss of drive.

11:00–12:30 — Lights and controls
- Turn on the front and rear lights; verify steady and flashing modes, secure mounting, and adequate battery charge.
- Check that cables, controls, and accessories cannot contact the tires, chain, or wheels.

Stop and get service—or do not ride in darkness or poor visibility—for: a required light that will not turn on, a loose light likely to fall into a wheel, or wiring/accessories that can interfere with moving parts.

12:30–15:00 — Short loaded test
- Load the bike as usual, including your normal bag or rack load; secure everything so it cannot shift.
- In a quiet, level area, ride slowly for a few minutes. Test gentle acceleration, both brakes separately and together, several shifts, and a brief stand-on-the-pedals effort.
- Listen and feel for handling changes, steering looseness, wheel rub, brake vibration, chain skipping, or load movement.

Stop immediately and get service for: unstable steering, any wheel or handlebar looseness, unexpected braking behavior, tire contact with the frame or load, drivetrain skipping, a shifting load, or any new noise, vibration, smell, or fault.

If all checks pass, begin the actual ride conservatively and recheck after the first few minutes.

messages.content: [2026-12-31T16:20:00-05:00] The building warned us to expect intermittent neighborhood fireworks and sharp noise after dark. Devika and I will already be home at the South Slope apartment from 6:00 to 10:00 PM for dinner, a movie, and Kibo’s normal evening routine. He has no current symptoms, and there’s no known ingestion or injury. Give me a practical, non-medication plan for when to take his longer walk, how to handle brief later bathroom trips, how to set up a secure quiet area and mask noise, how to manage the apartment door, what comfort measures to use, and which signs mean we should contact an emergency vet rather than continue comforting him at home.

For tonight, make the goal “finish the outside activity before dark, then keep Kibo indoors and prevent escape.”

Before 6:00 PM

- Take the longer walk in daylight, ideally finishing by about 5:15–5:30 PM. Use his front-clip harness and shorter leash near traffic, as usual. Choose the quieter South Slope route and turn back early if you hear fireworks.
- Let him have a thorough bathroom opportunity before returning home. Do not wait for the first fireworks.
- Once inside, close and latch windows, balcony access, and exterior doors. Draw curtains or blinds so flashes are less visible.
- Prepare one quiet area away from the apartment entry and street-facing windows. Put down his usual bed or blanket, water, and a familiar item. If he already likes his crate, leave it available with the door open; do not introduce or force a crate tonight.
- Run steady background sound before fireworks begin: a fan, television, music, or white noise. Keep it at a comfortable level, not loud enough to compete aggressively with the noise.
- Keep his harness, leash, and identification accessible by the door, but do not leave him tethered unattended.

From 6:00–10:00 PM

- Keep Kibo indoors for dinner and the movie. Let him choose whether to stay near you or retreat to the quiet area.
- Offer calm, familiar enrichment such as a food puzzle, stuffed toy, lick mat, or chew that he has safely used before. Skip anything new or difficult enough to frustrate him.
- Comfort is fine: sit nearby, speak normally and quietly, and pet him if he seeks contact. Do not force cuddling, drag him out of hiding, scold him, or repeatedly check on him in a way that adds excitement.
- Keep your own movements and reactions routine. Avoid making each bang an event.
- Manage the apartment door deliberately:
  - Before opening it, put Kibo in the quiet room or have one adult hold his harness and leash.
  - Check that the hallway and exterior door area are clear.
  - Keep the door open only as long as necessary and close it immediately.
  - Do not rely on him “staying” near the doorway, even if he normally does.

Brief later bathroom trips

- Use the shortest practical trip, preferably during a quiet lull. If he is reluctant, wait rather than pulling him outside during active fireworks.
- Put the harness and leash on before opening the apartment door. Use both a secure harness and collar with identification if that is his normal setup.
- Stay close to the building, use the most familiar route, and return immediately after he urinates/defecates. No long walk or off-leash time.
- Bring a flashlight and watch for debris or unexpected people/noise. Keep the leash firmly in hand.
- If he cannot safely settle enough to go out, an indoor accident is preferable to forcing him into a frightening situation. Clean it without punishment.
- After returning, check his paws and body briefly for cuts or debris, then resume the quiet routine.

Contact an emergency vet rather than continuing home comfort if Kibo has any of these:

- Trouble breathing, blue/gray or very pale gums, collapse, fainting, inability to remain awake, or severe weakness.
- A seizure, repeated seizures, or abnormal unresponsiveness.
- Escape-related injury, uncontrolled bleeding, suspected fracture, severe pain, or a wound he will not stop worsening.
- Repeated vomiting, marked abdominal swelling, choking, or suspected ingestion of fireworks, explosives, medication, alcohol, or another toxin.
- Signs of dangerous overheating that do not improve after moving him to a cool, quiet area—especially heavy breathing with weakness, confusion, vomiting, or collapse.
- Panic so severe that he is repeatedly slamming into doors/windows, chewing through barriers, injuring himself, or cannot be safely contained.

Ordinary trembling, hiding, clinginess, pacing, or brief panting can usually be managed with the quiet-area plan if he remains responsive, can breathe normally, and is not injuring himself. If you are unsure whether an inges…

results.title: 15-minute bouldering warmup progression
results.snippet: [2025-09-04T16:18:00-04:00] Ren says the gym’s >>>usual<<< easy warmup wall is closed for route setting before our 7:00 PM session. I’m still cleared for ordinary bouldering, including underclings and hard gripping, without...

messages.content: [2025-09-04T16:18:00-04:00] Ren says the gym’s usual easy warmup wall is closed for route setting before our 7:00 PM session. I’m still cleared for ordinary bouldering, including underclings and hard gripping, without a move cap, but I want to preserve the longer forearm warmup and gradual loading. Give me a practical 15-minute substitute using floor mobility, easy traversing, and the lowest available open-hand routes, plus a first-attempt progression. Keep the existing step-back criteria: pain above 2/10, symptoms lasting 30 minutes, or next-morning symptoms mean I step back and contact the clinician.

15-minute substitute warmup

0:00–3:00 — Floor mobility
- Wrist circles: 10 each direction.
- Gentle wrist flexion/extension pulses: 10 each, no forcing.
- Forearm pronation/supination with relaxed hands: 10 each side.
- Elbow bends and shoulder circles: 10 each.
- Scapular push-ups or wall scapular protractions: 8–10.
- Finish with 2–3 easy bodyweight squats and shoulder rolls.

3:00–7:00 — Easy traversing
- Start on the biggest, most comfortable holds with an open-hand grip.
- Keep feet quiet and movement deliberate; stay well below your normal effort.
- Traverse for about 60–90 seconds, then rest 30 seconds.
- Repeat for two or three rounds.
- Let the feet do most of the work; avoid hanging or gripping hard during this phase.

7:00–11:00 — Lowest available open-hand routes
- Choose the easiest routes with large, positive holds and straightforward movement.
- Climb at roughly 50–60% effort, downclimbing when practical.
- Do 2–3 short attempts, with at least 45–60 seconds of rest.
- Use underclings or harder grips only if they occur naturally and remain easy; do not seek them out as a test.

11:00–15:00 — Gradual loading
- Choose one slightly more demanding open-hand route or an easy familiar problem.
- Make one controlled attempt at about 60–70% effort.
- Rest 1–2 minutes, then repeat only if the forearm feels normal and settled.
- After that, begin the session’s normal progression rather than jumping directly to hard gripping or limit attempts.

First-attempt progression

1. Floor mobility: confirm normal motion and no concerning symptoms.
2. One easy traverse: assess how the forearm responds during movement.
3. Two or three lowest-grade open-hand climbs: keep effort clearly submaximal.
4. One modest step up in difficulty: use controlled movement and normal rest.
5. Only then progress toward ordinary session intensity, increasing either difficulty or grip demand—not both at once.

Keep the longer warmup and gradual loading even though there is no move cap. Step back and contact the clinician if pain rises above 2/10, symptoms last 30 minutes, or symptoms appear the next morning.

- Use his secure front-clip harness and leash. Keep him leashed the entire time, avoid...

messages.content: [2025-07-04T09:00:00-04:00] Devika and I are keeping our protected local day, but intermittent neighborhood fireworks are expected from late afternoon through the evening. Kibo sometimes startles at sharp outdoor bangs, though he has no current distress, breathing problem, vomiting, collapse, or escape attempt. Give me a practical preventive plan covering an earlier long walk using his secure front-clip harness and leash, the apartment’s windows and curtains, a quiet interior resting area, food and bathroom timing, what not to improvise with human medication, and the signs that would require urgent veterinary help.

Practical fireworks plan for Kibo

Before late afternoon

- Take his longest walk earlier than usual, before fireworks are likely—ideally late morning or early afternoon.
- Use his secure front-clip harness and leash. Keep him leashed the entire time, avoid crowded or traffic-heavy routes, and do not rely on an off-leash area even if it is normally safe.
- Let him sniff and toilet thoroughly, but keep the walk calm rather than exhausting him in heat.
- Check that his ID tag and microchip information are current. Keep a recent photo available in case he bolts.
- Bring him inside before the first expected bangs. Do not wait for him to become frightened.

Set up the apartment

- Close windows, balcony doors, and exterior doors before the noise begins. Check screens and latches; screens alone are not escape protection.
- Close curtains or blinds to block flashes and reduce visual triggers. Keep balcony access unavailable.
- Choose a quiet interior room, preferably away from windows. Set up his familiar bed, blanket, water, and a favorite safe toy there.
- Use steady background sound—fan, air conditioner, white noise, or calm music—to mask intermittent bangs. Start it before the fireworks.
- Allow him to hide or move around if he wants. Do not force him out, restrain him, or introduce a crate or confinement method he has not already learned to enjoy.
- Stay relaxed and available. Calm reassurance is appropriate; avoid dramatic reactions to each bang.

Food and bathroom timing

- Feed his normal meal at the usual time, or slightly before the noise becomes active if that is more comfortable for him. Do not give a large unfamiliar meal or new treats.
- Offer high-value familiar treats, a food toy, or a lick mat if he wants them, but do not pressure him to eat.
- Keep fresh water available and monitor that he can reach it.
- Give him another brief, leashed bathroom trip before dusk. After that, use the most protected, familiar route possible and check outside for active fireworks first.
- If a later trip is necessary, use the harness and leash even in a fenced yard, keep it brief, and never open the door without first confirming that he is secured.

Medication and calming products

- Do not give human medications, alcohol, cannabis products, sleep aids, antihistamines, or leftover prescriptions unless a veterinarian has specifically prescribed and directed that exact medication and dose for Kibo.
- Do not improvise with essential oils or supplements. Some are ineffective, toxic, or can interact with medications.
- If he has had significant fireworks anxiety before, ask his veterinarian in advance about a situational medication and when to administer it. Do not wait until he is already panicking to seek dosing advice.

Watch for escalation

Contact a veterinarian promptly for persistent or worsening panic, inability to settle, repeated escape attempts, nonstop vocalizing, destructive behavior causing injury, refusal of water, or signs of overheating or dehydration.

Seek urgent/emergency veterinary care for:

- Labored, noisy, or very rapid breathing that does not settle, blue/gray or very pale gums, or choking
- Collapse, fainting, severe weakness, unresponsiveness, or inability to stand
- Seizure activity, especially a prolonged or repeated seizure
- Serious bleeding, major trauma, broken nails with uncontrolled bleeding, or injury from crashing through a door/window
- Repeated vomiting, severe diarrhea, a swollen abdomen, or suspected ingestion of fireworks, medication, alcohol, cannabis, or another toxin
- Any escape or outdoor exposure where he may have been struck, injured, or exposed to fireworks debris

Keep the nearest emergency veterinary hospital and poison-control contact information accessible, and call ahead while transporting him if an emergency occurs. Since Kibo currently has no distress or other warning signs, prevention, early exercise, secure indoor management, and calm monitoring are the appropriate focus.

arguments.body:
Q1 Staff-IC Scope

Purpose

I provide cross-service technical framing across the metrics pipeline, Cardinality Guardrails, and Lantern so teams can plan and execute with clear invariants, failure handling, and ownership boundaries.

My scope

• Define and maintain cross-service invariants across the three areas, including the contracts and data-shape expectations that must hold at service boundaries.
• Review failure modes and ensure that denial, timeout, stale-provenance, partial-material, and other material failure paths have explicit handling and observable outcomes.
• Clarify ownership and escalation boundaries: identify the mapped owner for each implementation or operational decision, define when an issue escalates, and make handoffs and non-goals explicit.

Ownership boundary

Mapped owners retain decision authority for implementation, operations, telemetry, and release readiness in their areas. I do not become a universal approval gate. My role is to make the shared invariants, failure modes, ownership, and escalation paths explicit; the mapped owners decide and execute within those boundaries.

Expected output

A concise, reviewable scope and decision record for Q1 planning, with unresolved cross-service risks routed to the appropriate owner rather than held for Staff-IC approval.

arguments.title: Metrics-router cutover plan — rollout spine
arguments.body:
# Metrics-router cutover plan

## 1. Objective and scope

Move production traffic from the current metrics-router path to the cleaned-up metrics-router implementation with a controlled rollout, clear rollback points, and no dashboard-label churn.

In scope:
- Production traffic cutover for metrics-router.
- Validation of routing correctness, event delivery, latency, error rate, and cardinality behavior.
- Preservation of existing dashboard and alert label names throughout the cutover.
- Rollback to the prior serving path if a gate fails.

Out of scope:
- Shard-keeper migration; it remains last in the migration sequence.
- A parallel dashboard-label cleanup.
- Broad refactoring of config-loader or legacy-aggregator behavior beyond what is required to cut over safely.

Context:
- ingest-edge is the first migration, metrics-router is second, and shard-keeper is last.
- ingest-edge completed a 48-hour staging shadow with zero dropped events.
- legacy-aggregator still has a known bucket-flush-timing concern. Treat that as a validation item, not as a reason to expand this document unless it affects cutover safety.

## 2. Preconditions

Before starting the production rollout, confirm:

1. The candidate metrics-router version is built, reviewed, and deployable.
2. The config-loader path is deterministic for environment/file overrides, including overlapping label predicates; the more-specific rule must win.
3. Existing dashboard and alert label names are unchanged.
4. The previous version and its configuration are available for immediate rollback.
5. Observability is live for both candidate and baseline: request volume, error rate, latency, dropped/rejected events, routing mismatches, cardinality, and bucket-flush behavior around legacy-aggregator integration.
6. An owner is assigned to watch the rollout and an owner is available to execute rollback.

Record the candidate version, config revision, start time, and rollback target in the change ticket before traffic moves.

## 3. Rollout sequence

Use one production rollout with small, reversible steps. Keep the same config and label contract at every step.

Phase 0 — deploy dark
- Deploy the candidate without serving production traffic.
- Run health checks and configuration validation.
- Confirm that startup, config loading, and downstream connectivity are clean.

Phase 1 — canary
- Send a small traffic slice to the candidate.
- Hold long enough to observe a representative request and flush window, not merely a successful health check.
- Compare candidate against baseline on all gates below.

Phase 2 — partial rollout
- Increase traffic only if the canary is clean.
- Recheck after each increase rather than assuming a clean canary proves the full rollout.

Phase 3 — full cutover
- Move the remaining traffic to the candidate.
- Keep the old path warm and rollback-ready through the observation window.

Phase 4 — stabilize
- Continue monitoring through at least one complete bucket-flush cycle and the agreed post-cutover observation window.
- Close the rollout only after the final validation checklist is complete.

Suggested traffic steps: 5% → 25% → 50% → 100%. If traffic volume is too low for meaningful percentages, use a fixed request/event count per step and document the count. Do not add more stages unless the rollout math or observed risk requires it.

## 4. Decision gates

Advance only when candidate behavior is consistent with baseline and there is no unexplained degradation.

Hard-stop / rollback conditions:
- Any confirmed dropped event or material increase in rejected events attributable to the candidate.
- Routing mismatch, incorrect label selection, or evidence that a less-specific overlapping predicate wins.
- Error rate, latency, or saturation materially worse than baseline and not explained by traffic mix.
- Cardinality growth that threatens downstream capacity or changes expected series behavior.
- Bucket-flush timing or downstream delivery behavior that causes data loss, unacceptable delay, or alerting impact.
- Dashboard or alert label names change.

At each step, record:
- Traffic percentage or fixed request/event count.
- Candidate and baseline volume.
- Error/rejection/drop counts.
- Latency comparison.
- Routing/configuration validation result.
- Cardinality result.
- Legacy-aggregator flush result.
- Advance, hold, or rollback decision and owner.

If a metric is noisy or the sample is too small to support a decision, hold at the current step. Do not advance on a green-looking but underpowered sample.

## 5. Rollback

Rollback by shifting traffic back to the last known-good metrics-router version/configuration. Preserve the candidate logs, metrics, config revision, and timestamp before changing state so the failure can be investigated.

After rollback:
1. Confirm traffic is serving from the prior path.
2. Verify errors, drops/rejections, latency, routing behavior, and downstream flush behavior return to baseline.
3. Notify the migration owner and record the failed gate.
4. Do not retry until the cause is understood or an explicitly reviewed mitigation is ready.

## 6. Final checklist

Before declaring success:

- [ ] Candidate version and config revision recorded.
- [ ] Dark deployment and health checks passed.
- [ ] Canary passed with a representative sample/flush window.
- [ ] Partial rollout gates passed at each step.
- [ ] Full traffic is on the candidate.
- [ ] No dropped events or unexplained rejection increase.
- [ ] Routing and overlapping-predicate behavior validated.
- [ ] Latency and error rate are acceptable versus baseline.
- [ ] Cardinality is within expected bounds.
- [ ] Legacy-aggregator bucket-flush behavior is acceptable.
- [ ] Dashboard and alert label names remain unchanged.
- [ ] Rollback target remains available through the observation window.
- [ ] Owner has recorded the final decision and follow-up items.

## 7. Open items before execution

- Fill in the exact canary hold time or minimum request/event sample.
- Fill in the agreed numerical alert thresholds if they are already defined in the change ticket; otherwise use baseline comparison and the hard-stop conditions above.
- Name the rollout owner, rollback owner, and communication channel.
- Confirm the expected legacy-aggregator flush window.

Keep these details in the change ticket/runbook rather than expanding this plan. The cutover document should stay focused on sequence, gates, rollback, and ownership.

Created the cutover doc spine and kept it focused enough for a roughly four-page document.

It covers:
- Scope and preconditions
- 5% → 25% → 50% → 100% rollout sequence
- Validation gates, including routing, cardinality, flush timing, and label preservation
- Rollback procedure
- Final checklist
- A short list of execution details to fill in before rollout

arguments.title: Audit results meeting — lock the owner map and shard-keeper restart path
arguments.body:
Meeting outcome target

Leave with an explicit owner map, a written deploy freeze, and a safe, executable shard-keeper restart path. Do not leave any role as “TBD,” “ad hoc,” or implied by team involvement.

1. Decisions to lock in the room

- Primary owner, named backup, and escalation path for each service.
- Whether the deploy freeze applies to all three owned services and what exact condition lifts it. Proposed default: no deploys while the audit findings and shard-keeper restart path are unresolved; lift only after the owner map, runbook changes, and canary-safe environment are explicitly recorded and acknowledged.
- A single operational owner for rollup-service. It cannot remain effectively unowned or be treated as an informal dependency.
- The approver and operator for shard-keeper restart, plus the person who can stop the restart.
- The canary-safe environment and the evidence required before production action. Laptop testing is not acceptable; staging is not acceptable unless explicitly marked canary-safe.

2. Owner map — current evidence and gaps

- ingest-edge: Alex primary; Yuki formal backup. The runbook also requires the cutover owner/backup to be recorded for the window.
- metrics-router: Alex primary; Wes backup.
- shard-keeper: Alex is the operational primary. The current material is inconsistent on backup: Nadia is listed for label-parity/status entries, while Cyrus team is listed for rollback and ownership history. Resolve this in the meeting by naming one accountable backup and separately recording Cyrus team only if it is a confirmed dependency/support role.
- rollup-service: owner must be explicitly assigned. Cyrus team is referenced as the consumer/owner since May 18 in the shard-keeper label-parity procedure, but the audit lesson says rollup-service was effectively unowned. Confirm the accountable individual or team and obtain acknowledgment.
- Nadia: explicit sign-off for alerting/dashboard label parity; do not treat verbal agreement as sufficient.
- Escalation: record who is paged first, who is paged second, and the deadline for escalation if the primary cannot isolate the issue.

Required format for the final map:
Service | Primary | Backup | Escalation | Dependencies | Acknowledged by | Runbook link/entry

3. Shard-keeper — clean restart path

Preconditions — all must be checked and recorded before action:

- Audit findings are closed or explicitly accepted by the named owner.
- Current state and partial-movement risk are captured; do not assume rollback is safe after partial state movement.
- A canary-safe environment is explicitly identified. No laptop deployment; do not use staging unless it is explicitly canary-safe.
- Alex and the named backup are present/available for the operation.
- Nadia has signed off on alerting/dashboard label-name parity.
- The rollup-service owner confirms the consumer is ready and reading the expected label map.
- The exact prior/current label map and compatibility expectations are recorded.
- Stop/abort criteria, observer, and rollback authority are written down.

Execution sequence:

1. Freeze unrelated deploys and announce the change window.
2. Record the pre-restart state, versions, label map, consumer state, and monitoring baseline.
3. Exercise the restart path in the explicitly canary-safe environment.
4. Verify shard-keeper health, state movement, consumer reads, alert behavior, and label parity.
5. Proceed only on explicit canary sign-off from the named primary, backup, Nadia, and rollup-service owner.
6. Roll forward through the approved pipeline; never deploy from a laptop.
7. If a precondition or signal fails, stop and use the hardened rollback path rather than improvising.
8. After the change, record observed results, open risks, and the exact condition for lifting the freeze.

Known runbook guardrails: the rollback entry says to re-push the prior label map, confirm the rollup-service consumer is reading, pre-coordinate with Nadia on label-name parity, and never deploy from a laptop. Treat these as guardrails, not proof that the full restart procedure is complete.

4. Audit lessons to state plainly

- shard-keeper rollback was unsafe after partial state movement.
- rollup-service was effectively unowned.
- A label-name diff was invisible to symptom alerts and looked like generic ingest trouble.

5. Doc cleanup after decisions

- Rewrite shard-keeper into separate operator-path and owner-path sections.
- Replace contradictory backup fields with the locked map and explicit dependency roles.
- Add the canary-safe environment definition and a test-evidence checklist.
- Add rollback stop conditions for partial state movement.
- Add explicit rollup-service ownership and acknowledgment.
- Record Nadia’s written parity sign-off requirement and the exact label compatibility checks.
- Remove or mark stale/historical ownership entries so they cannot be mistaken for the current map.

Close the meeting by reading the final owner map and freeze-lift condition back to the room, then recording acknowledgments in the document.

bookend_end.content:
I pulled the current runbooks and created the meeting prep doc:

Audit results meeting — lock the owner map and shard-keeper restart path

The doc is structured to force explicit decisions on:

- Primary, backup, escalation, dependencies, and acknowledgment for every service
- A named owner for rollup-service
- The contradictory shard-keeper backup entries
- A written deploy freeze and precise lift condition
- A canary-safe, no-laptop shard-keeper restart path
- Stop/abort criteria and rollback authority
- Nadia’s written label-parity sign-off
- Follow-up cleanup for operator-path versus owner-path documentation

The current evidence supports Alex/Yuki for ingest-edge and Alex/Wes for metrics-router. Shard-keeper’s backup is not actually locked yet: Nadia and Cyrus team appear in different roles across the runbooks, so that needs an explicit meeting decision rather than another inferred assignment.

input.body:
# Incident-practice case study: April 2023 metrics-router cutover canary

## Scenario

On April 7, 2023, at approximately 14:30 ET, the metrics-router cutover canary emitted an info-level alert. The alert was not a page, but the automated rollback triggered as designed. The responder investigated the canary signal, identified a regression associated with the OpenTelemetry collector’s batch window, and redeployed metrics-router cleanly. The system was healthy again within four hours.

The response preserved the intended safety properties of the rollout: the canary limited exposure, rollback was automatic and available, and the prior serving path remained usable while the cause was investigated. The team did not treat the clean redeploy as proof that the rollout was safe to accelerate. After the hiccup, metrics-router was observed at 85% traffic with no drops and normal latency before proceeding toward the next rollout step.

## What makes this useful practice

This was a contained failure rather than a customer-facing emergency, but it tested several responder habits:

- Distinguishing an informational canary signal from a paging incident without ignoring it.
- Letting the rollback mechanism reduce blast radius before debugging.
- Investigating the full telemetry path, including collector batching, instead of assuming the router code was the only suspect.
- Verifying recovery with concrete signals—drops, latency, and downstream behavior—before advancing the cutover.
- Communicating calmly and accurately: the service was healthy after rollback and redeploy, but the canary regression still warranted investigation and a measured restart.

The central lesson is that a canary is successful when it makes an unsafe change cheap to stop and easy to understand—not only when it stays green.

## Responder discussion questions

1. Which signals and checks would you require before allowing the cutover to advance beyond the post-rollback 85% observation point?
2. If the automatic rollback had not fired, what would be your first safe containment action, and who would own the decision to continue or roll back?

arguments.title: Blocking follow-up — Harbor Health customer ownership provenance
arguments.body:
Status: BLOCKED — production unchanged

Context
Product Engineering’s revised branch correctly renders explicit unknown in the visible Harbor Health card when current ownership provenance cannot be resolved. However, executed API fixtures show that customer responses still contain the hidden `cached_owner_value` field. The cached value therefore remains in the customer path, not audit-only.

Blocking requirement
Remove `cached_owner_value` and any equivalent cached-owner material from every customer response. When current ownership provenance cannot be resolved, the only customer-visible and customer-retrievable ownership result must be explicit unknown. Cached ownership may not be exposed through hidden fields, alternate response shapes, nested objects, metadata, headers, exports, or customer-facing API variants.

Required evidence before unblock
1. Executed API fixtures for every customer-facing response shape/endpoint demonstrate that `cached_owner_value` is absent, including null/empty/hidden-field cases.
2. Negative and fallback-path tests demonstrate that unresolved current provenance returns explicit unknown and no cached owner value.
3. Retrieval-level evidence—not only UI screenshots—shows that a customer querying the API cannot retrieve cached ownership through alternate fields, serialization paths, metadata, headers, exports, or equivalent endpoints.
4. UI evidence shows explicit unknown in the visible Harbor Health card for unresolved provenance.
5. Automated regression coverage is added for the response contract and the customer-retrievability boundary; test output and fixture names are attached to the follow-up.
6. Confirm audit-only behavior separately: any retained historical/cached material is accessible only to the authorized audit path and is absent from all customer responses.

Ownership boundary
Product Engineering retains ownership of implementation, release, and rollback. This follow-up does not transfer or dilute that ownership. Product Engineering must provide the code change, executed evidence, release decision, and rollback readiness. Production remains unchanged until the blocking requirement and all evidence above are satisfied.

Unblock decision
Do not approve release or treat the revised branch as complete while any cached owner value remains customer-visible or customer-retrievable. Unblock only after the full response-surface evidence confirms that unresolved customer results contain explicit unknown and no cached ownership material.

results.title: Front brake no-ride inspection
results.snippet: ...Please inspect and repair the complete front braking system, including the lever, hose/fittings, caliper, pads, rotor, and wheel/axle >>>interface<<<. I have not opened the hydraulic system or road-tested it.”

messages.content: [2027-07-21T17:35:00-04:00] During a stationary pre-ride check, I found that my bicycle’s front brake lever pulls to within about one centimeter of the handlebar and front-wheel braking force is noticeably lower than usual. The rear brake works normally, the front wheel is seated, and I see no fluid, damaged housing, loose caliper, or new wheel rub. I haven’t ridden it and will keep it out of use. Give me a concise no-ride inspection limited to externally visible checks, confirm the no-ride boundary, and draft a clear description for a bicycle shop. Don’t include instructions for opening the hydraulic system or road-testing it with reduced braking.

No-ride boundary

Do not ride the bicycle—even slowly or to the shop. Keep the front brake out of service until a qualified bicycle mechanic inspects and repairs it. Do not road-test it with reduced braking.

Externally visible, stationary checks

- Confirm the front wheel remains fully seated and the axle/quick-release is closed and secure.
- Look for cracks, bends, looseness, or movement at the brake lever, handlebar mount, hose, caliper, and caliper mounts.
- Inspect the hose and fittings for cuts, kinks, abrasion, or wetness; do not loosen or open any fitting.
- Through the caliper opening, check that the pads appear present, seated, and reasonably even.
- Inspect the rotor for heavy contamination, obvious bending, cracks, or contact with nearby parts.
- Check that nothing is touching or obstructing the lever, hose, caliper, rotor, or wheel.

If anything is loose, cracked, leaking, or damaged, leave it untouched and arrange transport.

Description for the shop

“During a stationary pre-ride check, the front brake lever pulled to within about 1 cm of the handlebar, and front-wheel braking force was noticeably weaker than usual. The rear brake works normally. The front wheel is seated. I found no visible fluid, damaged hose/housing, loose caliper, or new wheel rub. The bike has not been ridden since I noticed the issue and has been kept out of use. Please inspect and repair the complete front braking system, including the lever, hose/fittings, caliper, pads, rotor, and wheel/axle interface. I have not opened the hydraulic system or road-tested it.”

arguments.query: Mosaic Commerce chronology defect source_timestamp regression tests ordering retries missing malformed timestamps combined chronological sentence

messages.content:
Assessment

The proposed correction is directionally right and matches the defect: customer-visible ordering should be derived solely from the authoritative source_timestamp. Keeping observation, serialization, processing, render, and retry times as audit metadata prevents implementation timing from changing the customer-facing explanation.

The regression groups are also appropriate for the known failure mode. They exercise the main ways operational timing or timezone handling could incorrectly override source order:

- Delayed processing
- Repeated retries
- Midnight crossings
- Equal source timestamps
- DST spring-forward offsets
- DST fall-back offsets

This is a suitable boundary for the ordering defect, provided it remains limited to chronology selection and presentation. It should not expand into changing timestamp production, provenance, unrelated tenant behavior, or re-enabling the affected combined chronological sentence.

Gaps to close

1. Missing or malformed timestamp semantics

“Render explicit unknown” is necessary but incomplete. Define:

- What counts as malformed: null, blank, invalid format, impossible date, invalid offset, or out-of-range value
- Whether an unknown record appears at the beginning, end, or in a separate undetermined group
- That unknown records cannot fall back to processing, retry, render, or local-display time
- Whether the API, UI, export, and any sorting layer apply the same rule

2. Equal source_timestamp behavior

The equal-timestamp case needs an explicit invariant. The implementation must not invent chronological precedence from an audit timestamp. Either:

- Records remain an unordered tie group, or
- A documented stable, non-temporal tie-breaker is used solely for deterministic rendering

A retry or record identifier must not become an implicit claim about event chronology.

3. Timezone normalization

The DST cases should verify both ordering and equivalence:

- Explicit offsets are normalized to an unambiguous instant
- Spring-forward nonexistent local times are rejected or rendered unknown
- Fall-back repeated local times remain distinguishable when offsets differ
- A timestamp’s display timezone does not alter its ordering
- No host or browser-local timezone leaks into the sort

4. Retry and duplicate semantics

The retry tests should distinguish delayed reprocessing of the same logical record from a genuinely new record. They should verify that:

- A retry cannot move an existing record
- Retries do not create duplicate customer-visible chronology entries unless duplication is intended
- Idempotent replay preserves both source order and record identity

5. Cross-layer coverage

Unit tests for the comparator are not enough. Add at least one integration or contract test proving that the selected ordering survives ingestion, serialization, API response, and final rendering. Include a guard that audit fields are present for diagnostics but are never used as sort fallbacks.

6. Boundary and execution evidence

There is still no final build or executed regression count. Therefore this remains a sound proposed correction and test boundary, not an evidenced result. Before changing status, capture the exact test inventory, pass/fail output, and any cases intentionally excluded.

Recommendation

Keep the correction as proposed, retain the combined chronological sentence disabled, and add explicit contracts for unknown placement, equal-timestamp ties, timezone normalization, retry identity, and cross-layer sorting. Those are the material gaps; they can be closed without declaring the defect fixed or reopening the combined chronology.

messages.content: [2027-12-19T16:10:00-05:00] Anya sent me this North Pier proposal: mark the Q4 design-system snapshot frozen on December 23 because many staff are away the following week, then attach December 24–31 observations as amendments. North Pier’s established rule is to freeze each quarterly snapshot only after quarter close; later corrections, not in-quarter observations, become linked amendments.

Anya’s proposal conflicts with North Pier’s established rule.

December 23 is before Q4 closes, and December 24–31 observations are still in-quarter observations—not later corrections. Freezing on December 23 would make the snapshot incomplete and misclassify valid Q4 data as amendments.

Recommended approach:

- Keep the Q4 snapshot open through December 31.
- Freeze it after quarter close, beginning January 1.
- Attach only genuine post-close corrections as linked amendments.
- If staffing requires an earlier operational cutoff, label the December 23 artifact as a provisional or operational snapshot, not the authoritative frozen Q4 snapshot.

messages.content: [2027-12-14T19:10:00-05:00] One section of our indoor-rated holiday light string goes dark when the cord near its molded plug is moved. There’s no heat, smoke, burning odor, spark, discoloration, exposed conductor, wall-receptacle issue, or effect on other apartment power. Devika and I unplugged the string and put it out of Kibo’s reach instead of continuing to test it. Should we retire the whole string, and what safety markings and cord features should we check on a replacement?

Yes—retire the whole string. A section going dark when the cord near the molded plug is moved is an intermittent fault in or near the plug, cord, or strain relief. It can worsen into arcing or overheating even though there is currently no heat, odor, smoke, or visible damage. Do not bend it again to locate the fault, cut out the bad section, splice it, or replace the molded plug.

Keep it unplugged and away from Kibo, as you’ve done. If practical, return it to the retailer or manufacturer as defective; otherwise dispose of it according to your locality’s instructions for small electrical/electronic items. Do not put it back into service or donate it.

For a replacement, check:

- A genuine recognized safety certification, such as UL Listed, ETL Listed, or CSA/cUL/cETL. The mark should be on the product or its tag—not merely a vague “tested” claim on the box.
- The manufacturer, model, electrical rating, and clear “indoor use only” or “indoor/outdoor” labeling.
- An intact, flexible cord with no cuts, flattened areas, cracking, loose insulation, discoloration, or stiff sections.
- A firmly attached molded plug with substantial strain relief where the cord enters it. Avoid a plug that wiggles, twists, or allows the cord to flex sharply at the entry point.
- A polarized plug when supplied by the product design, and a built-in fuse where the product specifies one. Never bypass a fuse or substitute a higher-rated fuse.
- Clear instructions stating the maximum number of strings that may be connected end-to-end and the maximum load. Stay within those limits.
- LED lamps, preferably, because they generally produce less heat and use less current. Still keep them away from curtains, paper, bedding, and other combustible material.
- A cord and plug appropriate for the intended location. An indoor-rated string should remain in a dry indoor area; do not treat an indoor-only label as weather protection.

Before hanging the new string, inspect it while unplugged and test it once without moving or pinching the cord. Stop using it immediately if flickering, partial outages, warmth at the plug, odor, buzzing, sparking, or breaker/GFCI operation occurs.

Interview assessment draft — 2027-12-07

Ratings and observed evidence

1. Invariants before implementation — Strong
Observed evidence: Established tenant-safe admission boundaries before implementation details: limits were applied before acceptance, excess work was treated as retryable, and each accepted unit had one accepted-work identity. This demonstrated clear reasoning about admission safety, retry behavior, and identity/invariant boundaries.

2. Serving readiness versus process liveness — Strong
Observed evidence: Kept readiness closed until immutable configuration and derived routing agreed. This demonstrated a fail-before-readiness stance and a concrete consistency condition rather than equating process liveness with safe service readiness.

3. Terminal outcomes for accepted work — Mixed-positive
Observed evidence: The recovery journal and replay design were sound and accounted for durable recovery semantics. However, crash/reconnect behavior was supported by tabletop reasoning rather than executed evidence until prompted. The candidate then identified the exact executable harness needed to test it; that harness was not executed during the interview.

4. Distributed implementation, rollback, and exception ownership — Strong
Observed evidence: Separated recommendations from mapped-owner execution, release, and rollback responsibilities, demonstrating clear ownership boundaries and explicit handoff reasoning.

Overall evidence-based assessment
Mixed-positive. The interview demonstrated strong tenant-safe admission, fail-before-readiness reasoning, durable journal/replay design, and explicit implementation/release/rollback ownership boundaries. The main qualification is evidence discipline: crash/reconnect recovery was initially a tabletop claim, not demonstrated execution; after prompting, the candidate named the precise harness needed, but the harness and resulting behavior were not run or observed. Treat the design claims as credible but distinguish them from validated recovery evidence. This is a technical assessment only and does not make or imply the hiring decision.

messages.content: [2027-12-19T16:10:00-05:00] Anya sent me this North Pier proposal: mark the Q4 design-system snapshot frozen on December 23 because many staff are away the following week, then attach December 24–31 observations as amendments. North Pier’s established rule is to freeze each quarterly snapshot only after quarter close; later corrections, not in-quarter observations, become linked amendments.

Anya’s proposal conflicts with North Pier’s established rule.

December 23 is before Q4 closes, and December 24–31 observations are still in-quarter observations—not later corrections. Freezing on December 23 would make the snapshot incomplete and misclassify valid Q4 data as amendments.

Recommended approach:

- Keep the Q4 snapshot open through December 31.
- Freeze it after quarter close, beginning January 1.
- Attach only genuine post-close corrections as linked amendments.
- If staffing requires an earlier operational cutoff, label the December 23 artifact as a provisional or operational snapshot, not the authoritative frozen Q4 snapshot.

arguments.body:
Interview assessment draft — 2027-12-07
Review status: DRAFT — for Alex’s personal review and submission. Not submitted.

Ratings and observed evidence

1. Invariants before implementation — Strong
Observed evidence: Established tenant-safe admission boundaries before implementation details: limits were applied before acceptance, excess work was treated as retryable, and each accepted unit had one accepted-work identity. This demonstrated clear reasoning about admission safety, retry behavior, and identity/invariant boundaries.

2. Serving readiness versus process liveness — Strong
Observed evidence: Kept readiness closed until immutable configuration and derived routing agreed. This demonstrated a fail-before-readiness stance and a concrete consistency condition rather than equating process liveness with safe service readiness.

3. Terminal outcomes for accepted work — Mixed-positive
Observed evidence: The recovery journal and replay design were sound and accounted for durable recovery semantics. However, crash/reconnect behavior was supported by tabletop reasoning rather than executed evidence until prompted. The candidate then identified the exact executable harness needed to test it; that harness was not executed during the interview.

4. Distributed implementation, rollback, and exception ownership — Strong
Observed evidence: Separated recommendations from mapped-owner execution, release, and rollback responsibilities, demonstrating clear ownership boundaries and explicit handoff reasoning.

Overall evidence-based assessment
Mixed-positive. The interview demonstrated strong tenant-safe admission, fail-before-readiness reasoning, durable journal/replay design, and explicit implementation/release/rollback ownership boundaries. The main qualification is evidence discipline: crash/reconnect recovery was initially a tabletop claim, not demonstrated execution; after prompting, the candidate named the precise harness needed, but the harness and resulting behavior were not run or observed. Treat the design claims as credible but distinguish them from validated recovery evidence. This is a technical assessment only and does not make or imply the hiring decision.

messages.content:
[2024-10-17T09:14:00-04:00] Product Engineering revised `lantern#42` after my blocking comment. The new read path now has this form:

Revised path:
1. Read deploy-card cache tuple using tenant identity.
2. If an object exists, compare its stored provenance timestamp with the permitted source freshness limit.
3. If stale, delete the object and return `UNKNOWN_STALE_SOURCE` without calling render.
4. If fresh, render the cached object.
5. If absent, use the existing permitted-source fetch path.

Reported unit results: fresh cache hit passes; stale cache hit returns explicit unknown and does not call render; absent source returns the existing explicit unknown state. The repeated delayed-source and two-tenant integration fixtures have not yet run.

Assess whether this ordering closes the stale-hit bypass and identify the remaining fixture evidence required before the blocker can clear. Customer access remains closed, and I need a precise boundary for when a longer shadow could be considered.

Assessment

The revised ordering closes the stale-hit bypass for this read path, assuming the tenant identity is the authorized identity used to form the cache key and the provenance timestamp is mandatory and valid.

The important change is that provenance validation now occurs before render:

1. Tenant-scoped lookup prevents an unrelated tenant’s object from being selected.
2. A stale object is deleted and converted to explicit `UNKNOWN_STALE_SOURCE`.
3. The stale object cannot reach render on that request.
4. A fresh object is still rendered.
5. An absent object still uses the permitted-source path.

The reported unit results support those branch-level claims. They do not yet justify clearing the blocker because the cross-request and cross-tenant properties remain unverified.

Evidence still required

1. Repeated delayed-source integration fixture

Run the delayed-source scenario repeatedly with:

- A cached object whose provenance is beyond the permitted freshness limit.
- The permitted source delayed or unavailable.
- Multiple reads during the delay.
- A deterministic reset, followed by another run.
- A later permitted-source response, if that is part of the existing fixture.

Required assertions:

- Every stale-cache read returns `UNKNOWN_STALE_SOURCE`.
- Render is never called for the stale object.
- The stale object is actually removed, or deletion failure is handled fail-closed without rendering.
- No delayed-source condition causes the old cached object to be served as if it were fresh.
- The later fresh source follows the existing permitted-source path.
- Results are reproducible across repetitions and resets.

2. Two-tenant integration fixture

Use two synthetic tenants with deliberately similar or colliding card identifiers, for example:

- Tenant A: stale cached object.
- Tenant B: fresh cached object.

Authenticate and run the complete path independently as each tenant. Assert:

- The cache lookup is keyed by the authorized tenant identity, not merely a caller-supplied identifier.
- Tenant A receives `UNKNOWN_STALE_SOURCE` and never reaches render.
- Tenant B can render only Tenant B’s fresh object.
- Neither tenant can observe, render, or receive the other tenant’s object.
- Auth, cache, adapter, and render records retain the same synthetic-tenant correlation.
- Repeated runs after deterministic reset preserve the same isolation.

3. Evidence and stop-condition checks

The integration results should record, at minimum:

- Synthetic tenant identity.
- Cache key or tuple identity.
- Stored provenance timestamp.
- Applied freshness limit.
- Decision (`fresh`, `stale`, or `absent`).
- Render invocation or confirmed non-invocation.
- Deletion result.
- Correlation across auth, cache, adapter, and render.

The blocker should remain if there is lost correlation, any cross-tenant material, stale material reaching render, a nondeterministic reset, or an implicit/ambiguous unknown state.

Shadow boundary

A longer shadow should not be considered yet. The entry boundary is:

- The delayed-source fixture passes repeatedly.
- The two-tenant isolation fixture passes.
- Evidence recording and deterministic reset are demonstrated.
- No customer access is enabled.
- The shadow is synthetic-tenant, observe-only, and has no customer-visible render, publication, or room mutation.

Passing the longer shadow would provide additional confidence, but it is not a substitute for those fixtures and should not itself reopen customer access.

The shadow must stop immediately, with the blocker preserved, on any stale-to-render path, cross-tenant observation, missing provenance/correlation, reset failure, or unexpected non-explicit result.

messages.content:
[2024-11-14T17:25:00-05:00] The first Lantern shadow evidence slice covers 3,200 customer-shaped lookups across both synthetic tenants and selected release-review traffic. It contains no cross-tenant material. Four deliberately stale permitted-source cases render explicit unknown, 118 denied requests make no adapter calls, and sampled external fields contain no internal room links or other internal-only metadata. Iris says the four unknown-state cards remain understandable without the omitted source detail.

This is eleven days into the authorized thirty-day internal shadow using two synthetic tenants and selected Infra and Product Engineering release-review traffic. The four acceptance conditions are no cross-tenant material, explicit unknown for stale permitted sources, no source-adapter calls for denied requests, and no internal-only metadata in external fields. State what this encouraging interim evidence supports, what it does not yet establish, and what must continue to be measured through the full shadow. Customer access remains closed.

Interim evidence supports:

- In the observed 3,200-lookups slice, the four acceptance conditions are behaving as intended:
  - no cross-tenant material appeared;
  - stale permitted-source cases rendered explicit unknown;
  - all 118 denied requests avoided source-adapter calls;
  - sampled external fields contained neither internal room links nor other internal-only metadata.
- The unknown-state presentation is understandable even without exposing the omitted source detail, based on Iris’s review.
- The current shadow implementation appears directionally consistent with the agreed authorization, provenance, and external-data boundaries across the two synthetic tenants and selected Infra/Product Engineering release-review traffic.

It does not yet establish:

- That these conditions hold consistently for the entire authorized 30-day shadow.
- That the slice is representative of all relevant request shapes, traffic patterns, tenants, adapters, stale-source combinations, or failure modes.
- That the observed absence of leakage or cross-tenant material will persist at larger volume or under unusual data and authorization combinations.
- That the four stale cases are sufficient to establish reliable unknown-state behavior across the broader stale-source space.
- Production readiness, a decision to expand the shadow, or authorization for any customer access. Customer access remains closed.

Through the remainder of the shadow, continue measuring and retaining auditable evidence for:

- Tenant isolation: every lookup and rendered result, including negative checks for cross-tenant material.
- Stale permitted sources: explicit-unknown behavior across varied stale cases, with counts, rates, and any regressions.
- Denied requests: request counts, adapter-call counts, and confirmation that denied requests consistently produce zero source-adapter calls.
- External-field safety: systematic checks—not only samples—for internal room links, internal-only metadata, and other provenance or boundary violations.
- Coverage and representativeness: traffic volume and request-shape distribution by tenant, source state, authorization outcome, and release-review path.
- Failures and edge cases: retries, partial results, malformed or missing source data, authorization changes, and any discrepancies between raw material, transformed data, and rendered output.
- Unknown-state comprehension: continue collecting review evidence for varied unknown cases, while ensuring that explanatory detail does not disclose restricted source information.

The appropriate interim conclusion is encouraging evidence that the acceptance conditions are holding in the observed slice—not completion of the acceptance review and not a basis for opening customer access.
