results.snippet: ...A second interpretation case is in >>>Mosaic<<< >>>Commerce<<<: deploy movement sourced March 12 at 7:18 AM appears beside an independently current incident-load summary sourced March 11 at 2:10 AM, a spread of 29 hours and 8 minutes...

messages.content: [2025-03-12T08:10:00-04:00] The pilot is at 31 sessions, and authorization, denial ordering, tenant isolation, provenance, exclusions, and read-only controls continue to hold. A second interpretation case is in Mosaic Commerce: deploy movement sourced March 12 at 7:18 AM appears beside an independently current incident-load summary sourced March 11 at 2:10 AM, a spread of 29 hours and 8 minutes. The user asked whether these signals describe one operating window. Before choosing a final timing rule, I want to retain evidence across the remaining early sessions: tenant, published service identifier, each signal's freshness result, provenance, source timestamp, timestamp spread, and whether the user requested a combined explanation. Define the evidence fields and comparison method Iris and I should use to evaluate the remaining pilot sessions before selecting a combined-explanation timing rule.

Use two linked records for each eligible session: one record per signal and one comparison record for the signal pair. Preserve raw values and derived judgments separately so a later timing rule cannot rewrite the evidence.

Signal record

Field                         Definition
session_id                    Stable identifier for the pilot session
tenant                        Exact tenant name or ID
published_service_identifier Exact published service identifier used by the user-facing result
signal_role                   Controlled value, such as deploy_movement or incident_load_summary
signal_value_reference        Reference to the rendered signal or underlying record; avoid copying mutable text only
freshness_result              fresh, stale, missing, invalid, or unknown
freshness_rule_version        Version of the freshness check used
freshness_evaluated_at        Time at which freshness was evaluated
provenance                    Source system, record/reference ID, and provenance-backed status
source_timestamp_original     Timestamp exactly as supplied by the source, including timezone/offset
source_timestamp_utc          Normalized UTC representation used for comparison
observed_at                   Time the signal was retrieved or rendered
retrieval_result              Retrieved, unavailable, permission-denied, or other explicit result
data_exclusion_status         Included, excluded, or indeterminate, with the exclusion reason

Comparison record

Field                         Definition
session_id                    Link to the session
tenant_match                  Whether both signals belong to the same tenant
service_identifier_match      Exact match on the published service identifier
signal_pair                   The two signal roles being compared
timestamp_spread              Absolute difference between the two source timestamps
newer_signal                  Which signal has the later source timestamp
freshness_combination         The two independently recorded freshness results
provenance_combination        Whether both signals have valid, provenance-backed sources
combined_explanation_requested Boolean indicating whether the user explicitly requested a combined explanation
request_text_reference        Reference to the user request or preserved request text
same_operating_window_label   Iris’s independent judgment: yes, no, or indeterminate
alex_operating_window_label   Alex’s independent judgment: yes, no, or indeterminate
judgment_rationale             Short evidence-based rationale for each judgment
reviewed_at                    Time the judgment was recorded
reconciliation_result          Agreed label, disagreement, or unresolved
reconciliation_notes           Explanation of any disagreement
timing_rule_applied            Leave empty during evidence collection, or record only if testing a candidate rule
candidate_rule_result          Result under a named candidate rule, kept separate from the human judgment

Comparison method

1. Capture the evidence before interpreting it.

   Record each signal independently, including its original timestamp, normalized UTC timestamp, freshness result, provenance, and exclusion status. Do not infer one signal’s freshness from the other signal or from the timestamp spread.

2. Apply eligibility checks first.

   Treat the signals as comparable only when:

   - They belong to the same tenant.
   - They use the same exact published service identifier.
   - Neither signal is excluded, invalid, or missing.
   - Both source timestamps are usable.

   Retain non-comparable cases in the dataset, but mark them as indeterminate rather than forcing a combined-window judgment.

3. Compute spread only from source timestamps.

   Use the absolute difference between the two normalized source timestamps. Do not use retrieval time, display time, incident publication time, or the time the user asked the question. Preserve the original timestamps so the calculation can be reproduced.

arguments.title: Q1 2028 operating-focus working draft
arguments.body:
Purpose

Working draft for January planning. This is a bounded discussion draft, not finalized objectives and not an ownership decision.

Operating focus themes

1. Keep asynchronous exception intake measurable

- Preserve measurable intake for asynchronous exceptions, including volume, aging, disposition, and observable failure modes.
- Nadia owns front-door triage. This draft does not reassign that responsibility or decide a broader ownership model.
- Use the measures to identify patterns and trigger follow-up; do not turn routine intake into a centralized approval process.

2. Monitor Lantern’s existing authorization through March 31, 2028

- Monitor the existing Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce authorization through March 31, 2028, using the frozen Q4 package as the relevant operating baseline.
- The frozen Q4 package is not renewal approval, expansion approval, or a decision to extend scope beyond the existing authorization.
- Surface material changes, exceptions, provenance gaps, and decision-relevant evidence for the mapped review path.

3. Support triggered cross-service reviews

- Support reviews triggered by cross-service invariant concerns, provenance questions, or failure modes.
- Keep mapped owners responsible for implementation, release, and rollback authority.
- Contribute evidence, coordination, and review support without centralizing routine approvals or overriding the mapped owners’ authority.

Explicit exclusions

- People management.
- Centralized routine approval.
- Treating this draft as finalized objectives.
- Making an ownership decision through this document.
- Treating the frozen Q4 package as renewal or expansion approval.

Planning guardrails

- Keep scope bounded to measurement, monitoring, and triggered review support.
- Preserve explicit ownership handoffs and decision authority.
- Escalate only when a defined trigger or material exception warrants it.
- Revisit and finalize through the January planning process; this document records a working direction only.

arguments.title: Lantern platform-line operating handoff — April 1
arguments.body:
Lantern platform-line operating handoff — April 1

Purpose and authorization

This is a single operational handoff for the Lantern platform-line transition. It establishes implementation and operating clarity; it is not a new strategy or authorization decision. The existing authorization remains in force through March 31, and the new terms do not become active before April 1.

April 1 role split

- Iris owns the customer promise, adoption criteria, and UI interpretation.
- Alex owns freshness, tenant-isolation, authorization-denial, latency, and error monitoring, plus the shared data contract, source-registration safety gates, and failure-mode review.
- Product Engineering owns implementation.

System and responsibility boundaries

- Lantern remains the explanation layer for provenance-backed service and system state.
- Cardinality Guardrails remains the source for pipeline limits and cost signals.
- The owner map remains the source of published responsibility.
- Lantern does not produce release-readiness judgments or employee-performance interpretations.
- Per-service telemetry cost remains outside customer authorization through September 30.

Source-registration safety gates

Any new source type enters through shared registration with all of the following:

1. Tenant-scoped authorization before source access.
2. Required provenance and source timestamps.
3. Explicit unknown for stale or missing input.
4. Excluded-field checks.
5. A successful safety rerun before customer use.

Customer scope: April 1 through September 30

Only Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce—and no other accounts—continue with read-only access through the shared authorization wrapper.

Authorized customer-visible scope is limited to:

- Provenance-backed deploy movement.
- Published service ownership.
- Timestamped incident-load summaries.
- Explicit unknown states.

The following are not authorized:

- Any additional account.
- Cost data.
- CSV export.
- Raw incident text.
- Internal room metadata.
- Employee identifiers or comparisons.
- Inferred or unpublished ownership.
- Internal-only fallback data.
- Any write capability.

Immediate suspension conditions

An authorization-wrapper bypass, adapter call after denial, cross-tenant material, stale or missing source rendered as anything other than explicit unknown, deploy event without required provenance, unpublished ownership, incident-load summary without its source timestamp, exposure of any excluded field, or loss of read-only enforcement immediately suspends both accounts pending correction and a successful rerun of the affected safety check.

Latency and other errors do not independently suspend access unless they cause one of those violations.

Operating review checklist

- Confirm role ownership and handoffs for customer promise, adoption criteria, UI interpretation, monitoring, shared data contract, registration gates, failure-mode review, and implementation.
- Verify Lantern, Cardinality Guardrails, and owner-map source boundaries.
- Verify tenant-scoped authorization precedes every source access.
- Verify provenance and source timestamps are present for permitted outputs.
- Verify stale or missing input renders as explicit unknown.
- Verify excluded-field checks and read-only enforcement.
- Verify no additional accounts or unauthorized data/output/write paths are exposed.
- On any listed violation, suspend both Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce, correct the issue, and complete a successful rerun of the affected safety check before restoring access.
- Do not suspend access for latency or other errors unless they cause a listed violation.

Effective window

The April 1 terms apply from April 1 through September 30. No new terms become active before April 1.

arguments.body:
January 22, 2027 staff-only rehearsal acceptance checklist

Purpose and boundary
This rehearsal is staff-only and evaluates the first reference handoff and denial behavior. Passing it neither authorizes customer exposure nor makes Alex the routine implementation gate. Product Engineering owns Lantern implementation; mapped teams retain implementation, release, rollback, and operational ownership for their work. Alex reviews the shared contract and cross-system failure boundaries only.

Authority split to preserve
- Lantern is the explanation and navigation layer.
- Cardinality Guardrails is authoritative for pipeline limits and cost semantics.
- The owner map is authoritative for published responsibility.
- These authority lanes remain separate; Lantern must not become authoritative for Cardinality Guardrails semantics or published responsibility.

Reference-envelope acceptance
- Every reference carries exactly these fields and no others: `tenant_id`, `canonical_service_id`, `authority_type`, `authority_record_id`, and `source_timestamp`.
- No reference may carry copied authority payload values, embedded authority content, or any additional identity, version, display, or decision fields.
- The owner-map reference and the Cardinality Guardrails reference must retain separate authority identities (`authority_type` and `authority_record_id`) and separate `source_timestamp` values. Neither reference may substitute the other’s authority identity or timestamp.
- The rehearsal must demonstrate that the canonical service identity and tenant binding remain present and unchanged for every reference.

Unknown and denial behavior
- A missing authority record, stale authority record, malformed authority record, or otherwise unverifiable authority record renders as an explicit `unknown`; it must not be treated as current, valid, approved, or below-limit.
- On denial or an `unknown` authority result, the adapter must stop and make zero adapter calls afterward. The acceptance evidence must show the denial boundary and a zero-call post-denial trace.
- No fallback, retry, enrichment, mutation, or downstream adapter call may bypass the denial boundary.

Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce isolation
- The rehearsal must produce no copied authority payload value, mutation path, or customer-path request, artifact, or output for Harbor Health or Mosaic Commerce.
- The test must verify that both customer paths remain absent, including requests, artifacts, outputs, writes, and side effects; staff-only rehearsal traffic and evidence must remain outside those customer paths.

Acceptance evidence
- Capture the exact five-field reference envelopes for the owner-map and Cardinality Guardrails lanes, showing their distinct authority identities and source timestamps.
- Exercise current, missing, stale, and denied authority-record cases and record explicit `unknown` results where applicable.
- Verify zero adapter calls after denial from the call trace.
- Verify no Harbor Health or Mosaic Commerce customer-path request, artifact, output, copied authority value, or mutation occurred.
- Record any failed criterion as a rehearsal failure; do not convert a pass into customer authorization or a new routine implementation approval.

arguments.title: Lantern continuation and platform-boundary decision — September 24, 2026
arguments.body:
Decision record

Decision date: September 24, 2026
Operating handoff: October 1, 2026
Decision meeting: Lantern continuation and platform-boundary review, 10:30–11:15 AM
Decision authorities: Hema and Theo

1. Renewed authorization

After review of the June 16–September 15 operating evidence and the separate reference-only rehearsal, Hema and Theo authorized Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce—and no other accounts—to continue from October 1, 2026 through March 31, 2027 with read-only access through the shared authorization wrapper.

The renewed term does not activate before October 1, 2026.

2. Permitted scope

Access remains limited to:

- Provenance-backed deploy movement
- Published service ownership
- Timestamped incident-load summaries
- Explicit unknown states

3. Excluded scope

The authorization does not include:

- Any additional account
- Cost data
- CSV export
- Raw incident text
- Internal room metadata
- Employee identifiers or employee comparisons
- Inferred or unpublished ownership
- Internal-only fallback data
- Write capability
- Release-readiness judgment
- Employee-performance interpretation

4. Suspension conditions

The following immediately suspend both accounts pending correction and a successful rerun of the affected safety check:

- Authorization-wrapper bypass
- Adapter call after denial
- Cross-tenant material
- A stale or missing source rendered as anything other than explicit unknown
- Deploy event without required provenance
- Unpublished ownership
- Incident-load summary without its source timestamp
- Exposure of an excluded field
- Loss of read-only enforcement

Latency and other errors do not independently suspend access unless they cause one of the violations above.

5. October 1 internal platform cycle

The reference-only model is the starting point for an internal platform cycle beginning October 1, 2026. The cycle does not begin early. This is an internal-cycle start only; customer exposure of the reference-only integration requires separate later authorization.

6. Five-field reference contract and authority split

The shared integration uses canonical published service identity and exactly these five fields:

- tenant_id
- canonical_service_id
- authority_type
- authority_record_id
- source_timestamp

There is no copied authority payload and no writeback.

Authority boundaries:

- Lantern remains the explanation layer.
- Cardinality Guardrails remains the authority for pipeline limits and cost signals.
- The owner map remains the authority for published responsibility.

The authority_type, authority_record_id, and source_timestamp must identify the same authoritative record. Lantern does not copy limit or cost values from Cardinality Guardrails.

7. Ownership assignments

- Alex owns the shared cross-system contract and failure-mode boundaries.
- Iris owns interpretation and adoption criteria.
- Cyrus owns the Cardinality Guardrails authority interface and cost semantics.
- Wes owns metrics-router control mappings and operating evidence.
- Product Engineering owns Lantern implementation.

Mapped owners retain responsibility for implementation, release, rollback, and operations within their areas. Alex’s assignment is limited to the shared contract and failure-mode boundaries stated above.

8. No-early-activation and customer-exposure boundary

Neither the renewed two-account authorization nor the internal reference-only platform cycle may activate before October 1, 2026. Customer exposure is not included in this decision. It requires separate later authorization before any customer-facing activation or use.

9. Handoff acceptance

The October operating handoff is accepted only when the authorized term, Harbor Health/Mosaic Commerce account allowlist, read-only wrapper enforcement, permitted and excluded fields, provenance requirements, explicit-unknown behavior, authority boundaries, ownership assignments, and suspension checks are preserved as stated in this record. Any suspension requires correction and a successful rerun of the affected safety check before either account resumes access.

This is the durable decision record for the October operating handoff and platform boundary, separate from the completed evidence-review document.

arguments.body:
Lantern June 16–September 15 operating-evidence review prep

Purpose and review window

- Evidence period: June 16 through September 15, 2026, inclusive.

- This is a preparation record for Hema’s operating-evidence and rehearsal review.

- The corrected staff-only reference-rehearsal result remains open.
- Do not include projected counts.
- Export status: frozen.
- No access-renewal or access-expansion decision is made here.
- No platform-cycle decision is made here.

Authorized customer surface

- The only authorized customer accounts through September 30, 2026 are Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce.
- Existing access for both accounts remains read-only under the current authorization and data contract.
- No other customer account is authorized by this record.
- No rehearsal request, artifact, or result enters either the Harbor Health or Mosaic Commerce customer path.

Pending reconciliation — customer operating evidence

1. Harbor Health

Reconcile and record, without projecting counts:

- Logical explanation requests. Keep these distinct from retry rows, attempt rows, and transport rows; do not merge or relabel those categories as explanations.
- Eligible combined explanations, checked against all of the following: same tenant; published service; valid provenance; freshness; matching source timestamp; and elapsed-time requirements.
- Valid separations greater than 24 hours.
- Explicit-unknown outcomes whenever a permitted input is stale or missing. Do not render stale or missing permitted input as a known value, successful explanation, or inferred result.
- Eligible renderer failures.
- Customer-use observations for the Harbor Health release follow-up.
- Published owner-map alias-path use, with no-match outcomes and conflicting-alias outcomes recorded separately. Do not infer identity from names or from customer context.
- Harbor Health’s owner-correction request remains outside the authorized customer surface.

2. Mosaic Commerce

Reconcile and record, without projecting counts:

- Logical explanation requests. Keep these distinct from retry rows, attempt rows, and transport rows; do not merge or relabel those categories as explanations.
- Eligible combined explanations, checked against all of the following: same tenant; published service; valid provenance; freshness; matching source timestamp; and elapsed-time requirements.
- Valid separations greater than 24 hours.
- Explicit-unknown outcomes whenever a permitted input is stale or missing. Do not render stale or missing permitted input as a known value, successful explanation, or inferred result.
- Eligible renderer failures.
- Customer-use observations for the Mosaic Commerce incident handoff.
- Published owner-map alias-path use, with no-match outcomes and conflicting-alias outcomes recorded separately. Do not infer identity from names or from customer context.
- Mosaic Commerce’s metrics-router limit-and-cost request remains outside the authorized customer surface.

3. Total customer sessions

- Reconcile the total customer-session evidence for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce only, without projecting counts.
- Keep total customer sessions distinct from logical explanation requests, retries, attempts, and transport rows.
- Identify the account/tenant boundary for each included record and exclude cross-tenant material.
- Apply the same permitted-input, provenance, freshness, source-timestamp, elapsed-time, published-service, and explicit-unknown rules used for account-level reconciliation.
- Leave the final reconciled total open until the evidence review.

Cross-cutting reconciliation checks

- Logical explanation requests are a separate evidence category. A retry, attempt, or transport row is not a logical explanation request unless the evidence independently satisfies the explanation definition.
- A combined explanation is eligible only when the records are from the same tenant, reference a published service, have valid provenance, satisfy freshness, carry the required source timestamp, and satisfy the elapsed-time requirements.
- Separations greater than 24 hours are valid only when the underlying timestamps and tenant/service/provenance linkage support that conclusion.
- If a permitted input is stale or missing, the outcome must be rendered as explicit unknown.
- Renderer failures are eligible evidence only when their eligibility and relevant provenance are documented; they must not be converted into successful customer explanations.
- Owner-map alias-path use must resolve through the published owner map. Record no-match and conflicting-alias outcomes as separate outcomes. Never infer identity from names or customer context.

Automatic-stop condition checklist

Use this checklist for the entire operating-evidence export and review. Each item must be checked against the frozen export and supporting evidence; any observed condition is an automatic stop, not a pass or a recoverable customer result.

[ ] Authorization-wrapper bypass.
[ ] Adapter call after authorization denial.
[ ] Cross-tenant material.
[ ] Stale or missing permitted source rendered as anything other than explicit unknown.
[ ] Deploy event missing required provenance.
[ ] Unpublished ownership rendered or presented as ownership.
[ ] Incident-load summary missing its required source timestamp.
[ ] Excluded-field exposure.
[ ] Loss of read-only enforcement.
[ ] Any other documented automatic-stop condition applicable to this operating-evidence or customer-path contract; record the condition separately rather than folding it into an ordinary reconciliation exception.

For each checked item, retain the supporting record, affected tenant/account, service or path, relevant timestamp(s), and disposition. Do not treat an unchecked box as evidence that the condition did not occur until the review reconciliation is complete.

Corrected staff-only reference-rehearsal evidence — separate section

Scope and contract

Open reconciliation items

Reference-rehearsal disposition

- Corrected reference-rehearsal result: open.
- No customer-facing conclusion is drawn from the rehearsal.
- No copied authority value, mutation operation, authorization conclusion, tenant-isolation conclusion, source-timestamp conclusion, stale/missing-authority conclusion, alias-resolution conclusion, or customer-path-isolation conclusion is treated as settled before reconciliation.

Boundary reminders

- Harbor Health’s owner-correction request is outside the authorized customer surface.
- Mosaic Commerce’s metrics-router limit-and-cost request is outside the authorized customer surface.
- Neither request changes the authorized account set, read-only access, current authorization, or current data contract.

arguments.body:
August 18, 2026 decision and handoff

Rejection: During the 1:00–2:00 PM staff-only rehearsal, Product Engineering’s combined-payload candidate was rejected. It copied the metrics-router operating limit and estimated cost into a Lantern-owned payload and attached an owner-map mutation endpoint. This would have made Lantern a second authority for Cardinality Guardrails data and would have given Lantern a write path into published responsibility. Cyrus confirmed that cost semantics remain owned by Cardinality Guardrails. Iris confirmed that Lantern may explain and navigate to authoritative detail, but must not present copied authority values as its own.

Selected contract: The corrected platform-reference contract contains exactly these five fields:
- tenant_id
- canonical_service_id
- authority_type
- authority_record_id
- source_timestamp

Boundaries: The reference-only contract contains no authority payload values and no mutation capability. Lantern is a reference, explanation, and navigation surface only; Cardinality Guardrails remains authoritative for operating-limit and estimated-cost semantics, and published responsibility remains protected from Lantern writes. No copied values, second authority, owner-map mutation endpoint, or equivalent write path is permitted.

Customer paths: Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce customer paths remain unchanged. Neither account’s authorization expands.

Handoff and status
- Completed: The design decision is complete. The rejected combined-payload model and its authority/write-path boundary violation are recorded, and the five-field reference-only model and boundaries are selected.
- Pending Product Engineering: Implement the corrected reference-only model. Produce executable rehearsal evidence covering existing authorization, tenant isolation, source-timestamp handling, stale-or-missing authority, conflicting-alias behavior, and customer-path isolation. results.title: Review handlePolicy error handling

messages.content:
Request changes.

`log.Fatal` must not be used in an HTTP handler. It calls `os.Exit(1)`, so a single malformed client request terminates the entire metrics-router process and can interrupt unrelated requests.

Return a client error and stop processing instead:

```go
func handlePolicy(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    policy, err := decodeAndValidate(r.Body)
    if err != nil {
        log.Printf("invalid route policy: %v", err)
        http.Error(w, "invalid route policy", http.StatusBadRequest)
        return
    }

    publish(policy)
    w.WriteHeader(http.StatusNoContent)
}
```

Please add table tests verifying that:

- Invalid input returns `400`.
- `publish` is not called for invalid input.
- An invalid request does not terminate the process or affect later requests.
- Valid input is published and returns the expected success status.

If `publish` can fail, its error should also be handled and mapped to an appropriate server-side response rather than ignored.

arguments.body:
Lantern June 16–September 15 operating-evidence review prep

Purpose and review window

- Evidence period: June 16 through September 15, 2026, inclusive.
- Review: September 18, 2026, 10:30–11:15 AM ET.
- This record keeps the operating-evidence track and the completed September 8 staff-only rehearsal track separate.
- Export status: frozen.
- Operating-evidence results remain open pending scheduled reconciliation. Do not project counts or treat counts, safety findings, or customer-use results as complete or final before reconciliation.
- The September 8 rehearsal results below are observed staff-only evidence; they do not close, project, or pre-judge the operating track.

Authorized customer surface and standing boundaries

- The only authorized customer accounts through September 30, 2026 are Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce.
- Existing access for both accounts remains read-only under the current authorization and data contract.
- No other customer account is authorized by this record.
- No rehearsal request, artifact, or result enters the Harbor Health or Mosaic Commerce customer path; both customer paths remain unchanged.
- Harbor Health’s owner-correction request and Mosaic Commerce’s metrics-router limit-and-cost request remain outside the authorized customer surface.

Operating evidence — June 16–September 15, 2026

Status: OPEN pending the scheduled reconciliation.

The operating track must remain separate from the rehearsal track. Reconcile and record the following for Harbor Health, Mosaic Commerce, and the total customer-session evidence, without projecting counts:

- Logical explanation requests, kept distinct from retry rows, attempt rows, and transport rows.
- Eligible combined explanations, only when the evidence satisfies same-tenant, published-service, valid-provenance, freshness, matching source-timestamp, and elapsed-time requirements.
- Valid separations greater than 24 hours, supported by the underlying timestamps and tenant/service/provenance linkage.
- Explicit-unknown outcomes whenever a permitted input is stale or missing. Stale or missing input must not render as a known value, successful explanation, or inferred result.
- Eligible renderer failures, with eligibility and relevant provenance documented; they must not be converted into successful customer explanations.
- Customer-use observations for Harbor Health release follow-up and the Mosaic Commerce incident handoff.
- Published owner-map alias-path use, with no-match and conflicting-alias outcomes recorded separately. Do not infer identity from names or customer context.
- Account/tenant boundary for every included record; exclude cross-tenant material.
- Final operating counts, safety findings, customer-use results, and total customer-session reconciliation remain open until the September 18 review.

Automatic-stop conditions for the operating export and review

Check each condition against the frozen export and supporting evidence. Any observed condition is an automatic stop, not an ordinary reconciliation exception or recoverable customer result:

[ ] Authorization-wrapper bypass.
[ ] Adapter call after authorization denial.
[ ] Cross-tenant material.
[ ] Stale or missing permitted source rendered as anything other than explicit unknown.
[ ] Deploy event missing required provenance.
[ ] Unpublished ownership rendered or presented as ownership.
[ ] Incident-load summary missing its required source timestamp.
[ ] Excluded-field exposure.
[ ] Loss of read-only enforcement.
[ ] Any other documented automatic-stop condition applicable to this operating-evidence or customer-path contract.

For each item, retain the supporting record, affected tenant/account, service or path, relevant timestamp(s), and disposition. An unchecked box is not evidence that the condition did not occur until reconciliation is complete.

Staff-only rehearsal — September 8, 2026 (completed evidence)

Status: COMPLETED OBSERVATION, STAFF-ONLY. This section is separate from operating evidence and does not imply that the operating track passed.

Contract and model boundary

- The model carried no copied authority payload values and had no mutation capability.

- 0 cross-tenant lookups or material.

- 0 unpublished ownership renders.

Interpretation and decision boundaries

input.body:
Q1 2028 documentation-update facilitator packet

Purpose
Facilitate consistent, accurate documentation updates during Q1 2028. Use the examples below to discuss how to describe a change without overstating its scope, effect, approval status, or completion.

Use
- Keep the description factual and limited to what was observed or completed.
- Distinguish a proposed update from an approved or implemented update.
- State what remains unchanged when that prevents a misleading interpretation.
- Do not add personal, confidential, or patient-related material.

Adopted example structure

Example 1 — Clarifying an existing procedure

what happened
The procedure was revised to make the existing handoff steps easier to follow. The underlying responsibilities and required approval path did not change.

safe wording
“Updated the procedure for clarity and ease of use; responsibilities, approval requirements, and the underlying process remain unchanged.”

what the wording must not imply
- That a new process was introduced.
- That responsibilities or approval requirements were reassigned.
- That the revision has been tested, approved, or adopted if those actions have not occurred.

Example 2 — Correcting a documentation error

what happened
A documentation error was identified and corrected in the current working copy. The correction changes the recorded wording only; it does not establish that the related work was performed or change the underlying record.

safe wording
“Corrected the identified wording error in the working copy; no additional work or change to the underlying record is asserted.”

what the wording must not imply
- That the corrected wording proves an action occurred.
- That the underlying process, decision, or outcome changed.
- That the correction was reviewed, approved, or propagated to other copies unless that is separately confirmed.

Facilitator prompts
- What is directly known, and what is not established?
- Does the proposed wording separate the documentation change from any operational change?
- Which unchanged conditions should be stated explicitly?
- What approval, review, propagation, or adoption claims would require separate evidence?

Scope note
This packet contains only generic, non-patient documentation examples. It intentionally excludes patient material, identifiers, clinical details, and case-specific content.

arguments.title: Alex Q2 2027 operating focus — draft
arguments.body:
Q2 operating focus — draft

Planning material for the April 2, 2027 discussion. This is not a new ownership or product decision.

1. Monitor renewed Lantern access without expanding the authorized surface

Beginning April 1, monitor the renewed Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce Lantern access within the existing bounded authorization. Keep the shared-wrapper requirement and the explicitly allowed surface intact: provenance-backed deploy movement, published ownership, timestamped incident-load summaries, and explicit unknowns. Do not expand access or treat out-of-scope data, metadata, judgments, fallbacks, writes, or readiness/performance conclusions as authorized.

2. Maintain reusable cross-service failure cases and exception routes

Keep failure cases reusable across services, with clear provenance, known unknowns, and explicit exception routes. Capture how an exception is raised, who owns the decision, what evidence is required, and how the route is closed—without turning exceptions into informal central approval.

3. Support mapped owners without becoming a centralized implementation or release gate

Help mapped teams work from shared invariants and make explicit owner handoffs. Mapped owners retain implementation, release, rollback, and operations responsibility. I will support coordination, reusable cases, and escalation paths, but will not become a centralized implementation or release gate.

Boundaries

- Planning and operating focus only; no change to current authorization, ownership, or product scope.
- Preserve explicit owner handoffs and team-level responsibility.
- Treat unknowns as unknowns and route exceptions explicitly rather than inferring ownership or adding fallback access.

messages.content: [2025-01-11T16:30:00-05:00] My phone's encrypted cloud device backup has not completed since December 26 because the account is using 49.7 GB of its 50 GB allocation. Photo synchronization is current, but messages and device settings are included only in the stale device backup. The phone is working normally, and I have a computer with enough free space for an encrypted local backup. Give me a preservation-first sequence for creating and verifying an encrypted local phone backup before I free cloud storage or change the cloud backup scope.

Assuming this is an iPhone using iCloud Backup and a Mac or Windows computer, use this order. The key rule is: do not delete the old iCloud backup or change what it contains until the local backup has passed verification.

1. Freeze the current state

- Leave the phone powered on, unlocked when needed, and connected to power.
- Do not delete the existing iCloud backup.
- Do not change iCloud Backup, Messages in iCloud, Photos, or other sync settings yet.
- Avoid installing updates, restoring the phone, or deleting messages/photos before the local backup is complete.
- If possible, take notes or screenshots of:
  - The last successful iCloud backup date.
  - The iCloud storage usage.
  - Which iCloud services are enabled, especially Messages and Photos.

2. Prepare the computer

- Use a direct, reliable USB cable and connect the phone directly to the computer rather than through an unpowered hub.
- Make sure the computer has ample free disk space—more than the phone’s used storage, with additional room for the backup and normal system operation.
- Keep the computer connected to power and prevent it from sleeping during the backup.
- Install or update the supported Apple software:
  - macOS: Finder.
  - Windows: Apple Devices, or iTunes on an older supported setup.
- Choose a strong local-backup encryption password and save it in a password manager or another location that does not depend solely on the phone. An encrypted local backup is generally unusable if this password is lost.

3. Preserve any earlier local backup

If the computer already has a local backup for this phone:

- Do not simply overwrite it.
- In Finder or Apple Devices, open the backup-management screen and archive the existing backup if that option is available.
- Do not delete that older backup until the new backup has been verified.

4. Establish the trusted connection

- Connect the phone by USB.
- Unlock it.
- Approve “Trust This Computer” on the phone if prompted, and enter the phone passcode.
- Confirm that Finder or Apple Devices identifies the correct phone, including its name and capacity.

5. Enable encryption before starting

In Finder:

- Select the phone.
- Open the General tab.
- Under Backups, select “Back up all of the data on your iPhone to this Mac.”
- Select “Encrypt local backup.”
- Set and save the encryption password.
- Start the backup with “Back Up Now.”

In Apple Devices or iTunes:

- Select the phone.
- Open the General or Summary page.
- Select “Encrypt local backup.”
- Set and save the encryption password.
- Start the backup.

Do not start an unencrypted backup first and assume it can later be converted. Confirm that encryption is enabled before initiating the important backup.

6. Let the backup finish without interruption

- Keep the phone connected until the application reports completion.
- Do not use the phone heavily during the operation.
- Do not disconnect it merely because the progress indicator appears to pause; large backups can spend time preparing or finalizing.
- Record the completion time shown by Finder, Apple Devices, or iTunes.
- If an error occurs, retain the old iCloud backup and the original phone state. Resolve the error and retry rather than freeing iCloud space.

7. Verify the backup metadata

After completion, use the backup-management screen and confirm all of the following:

- The listed device is the correct phone.
- The backup date and time are current.
- The backup size is plausible for the phone’s used data; it should not be suspiciously tiny or unchanged from an old backup without explanation.
- The backup is marked encrypted, usually by an encryption label or lock indicator.
- The backup remains listed after closing and reopening Finder or Apple Devices.
- The computer’s backup folder has a current modification time and a nontrivial size.

Do not alter files inside the backup folder. Renaming, moving individual files, or editing its contents can make it unusable.

messages.content: [2023-07-18T09:10:00-04:00] Hema asked me this morning not to let legacy-aggregator become the undefined tail now that shard-keeper is closed. I'm pulling Cyrus and Roman into an inventory pass today. The goal is not full retirement today and not a new cardinality-control project; it's to identify whether legacy-aggregator still participates in live metrics-router or rollup-service routing, and what can be isolated without breaking mirror/replay validation. Draft me a tight checklist so the meeting doesn't dissolve into archaeology.

Legacy-aggregator inventory meeting checklist

Objective

Determine whether legacy-aggregator still participates in live metrics-router or rollup-service routing, and identify safe isolation candidates without breaking mirror/replay validation.

1. Set the boundary

[ ] Do not plan full retirement today.
[ ] Do not open a new cardinality-control project.
[ ] Treat metric-rollup as out of scope; it is deprecated/unowned and is separate from rollup-service.
[ ] Focus only on legacy-aggregator’s current production paths, dependencies, and validation role.

2. Establish ownership

[ ] Cyrus: confirm rollup-service paths and dependencies.
[ ] Roman: trace shard/replay/mirror behavior and operational dependencies.
[ ] Alex: confirm metrics-router paths, configuration, and live traffic.
[ ] Name one owner for each unresolved dependency before ending the meeting.

3. Inventory the service

For every legacy-aggregator integration, record:

[ ] Caller or upstream service.
[ ] Target service or downstream consumer.
[ ] Environment and deployment location.
[ ] Live, replay-only, mirror-only, validation-only, or unknown.
[ ] Routing/configuration reference: repo, config key, job, queue, endpoint, or dashboard.
[ ] Traffic evidence and last-seen timestamp.
[ ] Failure behavior if the path is disabled.
[ ] Whether rollback is available and tested.

4. Check live routing specifically

[ ] Search metrics-router configuration and code for legacy-aggregator references.
[ ] Verify whether metrics-router sends, receives, or merely retains compatibility handling for it.
[ ] Search rollup-service configuration and code for legacy-aggregator references.
[ ] Verify whether the path carries production traffic or only historical/replay data.
[ ] Check deployment manifests, scheduled jobs, queues, and service discovery—not just repository references.

5. Check mirror/replay validation

[ ] Identify every mirror or replay job that reads from or writes to legacy-aggregator.
[ ] Confirm whether validation requires the service to be live, or only requires retained data/schema compatibility.
[ ] Document the minimum behavior needed to preserve validation.
[ ] Do not disable anything until a replay or mirror test demonstrates the proposed isolation is safe.

6. Classify each finding

Put every reference into exactly one bucket:

[ ] Active production dependency — must remain.
[ ] Validation dependency — isolate only with an explicit replacement/test.
[ ] Historical or dormant — candidate for isolation.
[ ] Dead configuration/code — cleanup candidate, no runtime action yet.
[ ] Unknown — assign an owner and deadline; do not infer.

7. Decide only the next safe action

For each isolation candidate, record:

[ ] Exact component or route to isolate.
[ ] Expected effect on metrics-router, rollup-service, mirror, and replay.
[ ] Verification test and success criteria.
[ ] Rollback method.
[ ] Named owner.
[ ] Proposed execution window.

Meeting exit criteria

[ ] One-page dependency map exists.
[ ] No “unknown” item lacks an owner and follow-up date.
[ ] Live-routing status is explicitly confirmed or marked unverified.
[ ] Mirror/replay requirements are documented.
[ ] At least one safe isolation candidate is identified, or the blocking evidence is named.
[ ] No retirement or cardinality-control work is accidentally committed.

arguments.title: Legacy-aggregator isolation — scoping
arguments.body:
Audience: Hema, metrics-router, and rollup-service teams

Objective
Isolate legacy-aggregator from the live production path while preserving mirrored writes and replay validation until full retirement is safe.

Current state
The inventory pass traced the remaining production references. legacy-aggregator still receives mirrored writes and feeds the replay validator. It should no longer be required by live metrics-router or rollup-service routing once the last fallback path is removed cleanly.

Immediate scope
- Identify and remove the final live-routing fallback in metrics-router and rollup-service.
- Keep mirrored writes to legacy-aggregator unchanged during the transition.
- Keep replay validation running and use it to confirm equivalent behavior before and after isolation.
- Add explicit checks/alerts for any attempted live-path dependency on legacy-aggregator.
- Document rollback and the conditions for safely proceeding toward full retirement.

Out of scope for this pass
- Full retirement or deletion of legacy-aggregator.
- Stopping mirrored writes.
- Removing replay validation.
- A broader named project or effort focused on cardinality control.

Completion criteria
- No live production request or routing path depends on legacy-aggregator.
- Mirrored writes continue successfully.
- Replay validation remains healthy with no unexplained divergence.
- The fallback removal, rollback path, and follow-up retirement criteria are documented and reviewed by Hema and both teams.

Coordination
metrics-router and rollup-service owners should jointly trace the fallback, review the change, and verify production behavior. Cyrus, Roman, and Alex’s inventory findings are the starting reference; this document scopes isolation only and does not represent full retirement.

messages.content: [2023-10-25T09:06:00-04:00] I'm turning the new Cardinality Guardrails scope into first-pass acceptance checks, and my raw bullets need to become something reviewers can actually apply to a metrics-router or shard-keeper change. I don't want it to read as if every high-cardinality label is automatically forbidden, and I want the rollup-service parity check plus the live-versus-validation alert boundary embedded directly in the checklist. Turn these notes into a practical PR/review checklist for the first Cardinality Guardrails control slice, with pass/fail language and explicit non-goals.

Cardinality Guardrails — first control slice PR/review checklist

Purpose

Apply this checklist to metrics-router or shard-keeper changes that add, remove, rename, derive, or change the behavior of metric labels, routing dimensions, or related alert inputs.

The goal is not to prohibit every high-cardinality label. The goal is to ensure that cardinality is intentional, bounded where possible, observable, and consistent across services.

Review outcome

- PASS: Every applicable check passes, or an explicitly documented exception has an owner and follow-up.
- FAIL: Any applicable check is missing, ambiguous, or contradicted by the implementation.
- N/A: The reviewer records why the check does not apply.

1. Change and label inventory

[ ] PASS — The PR identifies every affected metric, label, and code path.

Evidence should include:

- Added, removed, renamed, or transformed labels
- Whether the label is emitted by metrics-router, shard-keeper, or both
- Whether the change affects production traffic, replay, mirroring, validation, or test-only paths
- Any alert or dashboard consuming the changed label

[ ] FAIL if a reviewer must infer the affected label set from implementation details or generated output.

2. Cardinality classification

For each affected label, the PR records one of:

- Bounded
- Expected high-cardinality
- Potentially unbounded
- Rejected or removed

[ ] PASS — The classification includes a short reason based on the label’s source and expected value set.

[ ] FAIL — The PR calls a label “safe” or “unsafe” without explaining its value source, bound, or expected growth.

[ ] PASS — High cardinality alone is not treated as an automatic rejection. The review evaluates whether the cardinality is intentional, bounded or controlled, and appropriate for the metric’s use.

3. Explicit label checks

[ ] PASS — customer_id, when used, is identified as expected high-cardinality and has a documented purpose, retention/use justification, and metric-specific review.

[ ] FAIL — customer_id is rejected solely because it is high-cardinality, without evaluating its intended use.

[ ] PASS — A new or newly unbounded experiment_id dimension has completed the cardinality preflight before merge.

The preflight must cover:

- Expected value growth
- Whether values are bounded, sampled, or otherwise controlled
- Estimated impact on the affected metric
- Rollout and rollback conditions
- A named owner for the decision

[ ] FAIL — A new or unbounded experiment_id is introduced without that preflight.

[ ] PASS — route_pattern is normalized and bounded before it becomes a label value.

[ ] FAIL if route_pattern can contain raw, effectively unique request paths or an unbounded set of path variants.

[ ] FAIL — Raw path IDs, error strings, exception text, payload fragments, request contents, or equivalent per-request data are used as label values.

4. Value normalization and boundedness

[ ] PASS — The implementation removes or normalizes variable components that do not represent a deliberate aggregation dimension.

Examples include:

- Resource IDs embedded in paths
- Arbitrary query parameters
- User-generated strings
- Error messages or payload-derived values
- Unbounded experiment or feature identifiers

[ ] PASS — Any remaining high-cardinality value has a documented reason to exist and an identified control, such as an explicit bound, allowlist, sampling policy, or preflight gate.

[ ] FAIL — The PR relies only on “the values are usually small” or current production volume as the control.

5. Rollup-service parity

Apply this section whenever a label is added, removed, renamed, normalized, or changes semantic meaning across a metrics-router, shard-keeper, and rollup-service boundary.

[ ] PASS — The PR compares the affected label names and meanings with rollup-service before merge.

[ ] PASS — The comparison confirms that the same label name means the same thing across the participating services, or the PR documents the intentional …

# ingest-edge: current cutover and verification flow

This is the current ingest-edge procedure. Do not use the retired legacy-aggregator bucket-flush or handoff steps; legacy-aggregator is not part of the ingest-edge cutover path.

## 1. Pre-cutover checks

- Confirm the ingest-edge deployment and configuration are ready for the target environment.
- Confirm monitoring is in place for dropped events, latency, error rate, and Prometheus anomalies.
- Record the intended cutover window and the on-call owner/backup.

## 2. Staging shadow

- Run ingest-edge in staging shadow for 48 hours before production cutover.
- During the shadow period, watch for dropped events, latency regressions, elevated errors, and metric anomalies.
- Proceed only when the shadow period is clean and there is no unresolved ingest-edge issue.

## 3. Production cutover

- Switch production traffic to ingest-edge using the approved deployment/configuration.
- Confirm traffic is flowing through ingest-edge and that event processing is healthy.
- Record the cutover time and deployment/configuration version.

## 4. Post-cutover verification

- Monitor ingest-edge for at least 24 hours after cutover.
- Verify zero dropped events, stable latency, a flat error rate, and no Prometheus anomalies.
- If any of these checks fail, pause the rollout and follow the service rollback/incident procedure rather than applying legacy-aggregator bucket-flush steps.

## 5. Close-out

- After the 24-hour verification is clean, mark the ingest-edge cutover complete.
- File the close-out note with the cutover time, observed results, and any follow-up items.

## 6. Alerting label-map / parity-change guardrail

- Treat the alerting label-map parity work as part of the ingest-edge path review.
- Preserve existing dashboard label names by default.
- Do not approve or roll out a label-name change based only on verbal agreement; record explicit written sign-off from Nadia in the parity document or its document thread before proceeding.
- In the review, document the exact compatibility expectations for the label map and verify that the parity check covers the affected labels.

## 7. OTel collector 0.91 rollout note (2023-07-27)

- This rollout was production-clean: after the heightened watch closed, error rate stayed flat and CPU stayed flat.
- p95 memory settled about 5% above the pre-bump collector baseline, still within normal headroom.
- Future collector bumps still require staging replay plus an explicit memory watch.

## 8. Retry-only OTel change (sha:0a91b7c)

- The retry-only OTel change may be included in the ingest-edge cutover playbook; `sha:0a91b7c` has been quiet in production for several days.
- Exporter retry `max_interval` is 15 seconds.
- Exporter retry `max_elapsed_time` is 5 minutes.
- Memory-limiter settings were deliberately not part of this patch; do not treat this entry as a collector-wide tuning guide.
- After deployment, check dropped writes, backpressure counters, and retry log volume.

Primary owner: Alex
Backup: Yuki

## OTel exporter retry-only change — Oct 2023 note

For the retry-only OTel collector change deployed as `sha:0a91b7c`, the operational intent was to reduce staging/prod exporter retry noise without hiding real pressure signals.

Settings in scope:
- `max_interval`: 15 seconds
- `max_elapsed_time`: 5 minutes

Settings explicitly out of scope:
- Memory-limiter settings were not changed in this patch.

Post-deploy checks:
- Dropped writes should stay at zero.
- Backpressure counters should remain visible.
- Exporter retry log volume should decrease, but not by suppressing real backpressure evidence.

If dropped writes appear or backpressure counters disappear, treat that as a signal problem rather than a successful noise reduction.

## Staging-drill hygiene — 2024-01-04

- Before opening the staging lane for an ingest-edge rollback drill, verify the load-test tag TTL and identify the cleanup owner.
- This hygiene check applies to the deploy-pipeline path only.
- Wes may perform the daylight first pass for this staging-drill class.
- Escalate any unsafe or ambiguous signal rather than proceeding.
- This section does not change production ownership or the owner map.

## 9. ingest-edge v2.19.4 production cutover — 2024-04-02

The randomized one-to-three-second `Retry-After` behavior for 429 responses is now the production behavior for ingest-edge v2.19.4. Do not return to the baseline retry behavior solely because the rollout gates are complete.

Wes owns the first-pass monitoring read at each gate; Alex remains the primary owner and Yuki remains the backup.

### Explicit stop boundaries

At every rollout gate, stop the rollout, hold the current traffic split, and follow the service rollback/incident procedure if any one of these conditions occurs:

- Any increase in 5xx responses.
- p99 latency at or above 190 ms.
- Queue depth at or above 76%.
- Accepted-throughput loss at or above 3% versus baseline.
- Retry attempts at or above 130,000 attempts per second.

Do not advance to the next gate until the measurements are back within bounds and the stop condition has been assessed by the on-call owner. Do not use the retired legacy-aggregator bucket-flush or handoff steps for rollback.

### Gate observations

Observed maxima for the randomized `Retry-After` behavior:

| Gate | Peak retries | Peak p99 | Peak queue depth | Accepted throughput vs. baseline | 5xx increase |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 10% | 124,000 attempts/second | 176 ms | 73% | 2.1% below baseline | None |
| 50% | 128,000 attempts/second | 186 ms | 75% | 2.8% below baseline | None |
| 100% | 129,000 attempts/second | 188 ms | 75% | 2.9% below baseline | None |

All production gates passed. Keep ingest-edge v2.19.4 at 100%; do not return to the baseline behavior. The full-production observation completed on 2024-04-02. The formal 48-hour production check remains due on 2024-04-04.

At the formal check, verify zero dropped events, no 5xx increase, stable latency, queue depth, accepted throughput, retry behavior, and no Prometheus anomalies. Record the check result and any follow-up items in the close-out note.

## 10. Production tenant-fair queue behavior — 2024-07-05

The remaining ingest-edge rollout completed in production. The tenant-fair queue behavior is now the production behavior and must be preserved at both the 50% gate and full production:

- Repeated noisy-tenant tests preserved the eight-waiting cap.
- Newly queued low-volume tenants entered the scheduling ring immediately; they must not wait for a separate refill or batch cycle.
- Dispatch remained work-conserving and used every eligible slot.
- Empty tenants were removed from the scheduling ring after cancellation.
- Every queue-cap response retained `Retry-After`.
- The existing active-work, accepted-point, dropped-point, and restart checks remained clean.

This queue behavior does not change the existing safety and retry requirements. Explicitly preserve all of the following:

- At most four active items per pod.
- At most two active items per tenant.
- Bounded decompression.
- The existing retry requirements, including the production `Retry-After` behavior for queue-cap responses.

At any future rollout or change, stop and investigate if the eight-waiting cap, immediate low-volume tenant admission, work-conserving dispatch, cancellation cleanup, `Retry-After`, or any existing active-work, accepted-point, dropped-point, or restart check regresses. Follow the service rollback/incident procedure; do not use the retired legacy-aggregator bucket-flush or handoff steps.

## 11. Bounded service-discovery membership check — May 24 zone imbalance

Before closure after a zone-imbalance signal, perform a bounded membership check for each zone:

- Compare the ready service-discovery endpoints with load-balancer membership by zone.
- Identify and reconcile any endpoint present in one view but not the other, and confirm that the resulting membership matches the expected ready endpoints for each zone.
- If the comparison shows drift, refresh service-discovery/load-balancer membership before proceeding.
- After refresh, verify that traffic distribution by zone has returned to the established baseline.
- Confirm queue occupancy and caller-visible errors remain at baseline during and after the refresh.
- Reconcile every accepted request to exactly one caller-visible terminal result before closure. Closure is blocked by duplicated accepted work, unaccounted accepted work, or leaked queue occupancy.

This bounded check does not change the owner map and does not make Alex the routine operator. The existing primary owner, backup, release, rollback, and operations ownership remain unchanged.

## 12. Tenant-burst operating check

During a tenant-burst check, verify all of the following:

- A tenant may have at most eight waiting requests.
- Requests in excess of the eight-request waiting limit must remain retryable and fail before acceptance; they must not be counted as accepted work.
- Every accepted request must reconcile to exactly one terminal result.
- Other tenants must remain at baseline, including their queue behavior and caller-visible outcomes.
- Caller errors for unaffected traffic must remain at baseline.
- After the burst is drained and the queue is emptied, queue occupancy must end at zero.

Stop the check and follow the service rollback/incident procedure if an excess request is accepted, a retryable excess request is not rejected before acceptance, an accepted request lacks exactly one terminal result, other tenants or caller errors depart from baseline, or an emptied queue does not end at zero.

This tenant-burst operating check does not transfer implementation, release, or rollback ownership from Yuki’s mapped path.

## 13. Buffer-reuse decoded-attribute cap and request-cap validation — 2027-09-08

During the four-hour run after buffer reuse, the aggregate decoded-attribute limit was 1,048,576 bytes and the request cap was 72 requests.

- Peak memory was 347 MiB above the 1.12 GiB baseline.
- Throughput was 0.8% below baseline.
- p99 latency was 2.4% above baseline.
- Limit-plus-one and cap-excess cases remained retryable and failed before acceptance; none were enqueued.
- Every request had exactly one terminal outcome.
- Production was unchanged.

## 14. Active decoder controls — production observation closed 2027-10-21

The production observation is closed. The following controls are active and must be preserved:

- Apply one request-wide decoded-attribute limit of 1,048,576 bytes across all gzip members combined. Do not reset or apply this limit separately per gzip member.
- Admit at most 72 requests to decoding at a time. Requests above this decode-admission cap remain retryable and must be rejected before acceptance; over-cap work must not be enqueued.
- Do not enqueue any request whose decoded attributes exceed the request-wide limit, including a request that crosses the limit in a later gzip member.
- Every accepted request must produce exactly one caller-visible terminal outcome.
- Release the decode-admission slot exactly once for every terminal path: success, rejection, malformed input, cancellation, or client disconnect. Slot release must be idempotent across races and must not be skipped or duplicated.
- Preserve the separate 8,000-point whole-batch rule; it is independent of the request-wide decoded-attribute limit and the 72-request decode-admission cap.
- Preserve the eight-waiting-requests-per-tenant limit and its retryable pre-acceptance handling.

Yuki retains implementation, release, and rollback authority for this mapped path. This control update does not change the owner map or make Alex the routine operator.

Primary owner: Alex
Backup: Yuki

arguments.message:
Opening notice — owner-held ingest-edge decoder-controls window

Yuki has opened the window after confirming that the signed candidate and rollback material still match preflight. Yuki alone owns and makes the implementation, release, and rollback decisions; this notice is not an approval or release decision by anyone else.

Candidate controls:
- One request-wide 1,048,576-byte decoded-attribute counter spanning all gzip members. At 1,048,576 bytes the request remains within the byte boundary; 1,048,577 bytes is over-limit and must be rejected before acceptance and enqueue, regardless of how the bytes are divided among gzip members.
- A 72-request decode-admission cap; request 73 must not be admitted.
- The existing 8,000-point whole-batch rule remains unchanged.
- The existing eight-waiting-requests-per-tenant limit remains unchanged; a ninth waiting request for a tenant must not be queued.

Exact rollback boundaries:
- Roll back for any over-limit work accepted or enqueued.
- Roll back for any accepted request that lacks exactly one caller-visible terminal outcome (zero or duplicate outcomes).
- Roll back for any admission slot that is not released exactly once (leaked or double-released).
- Roll back if accepted throughput is more than 5% below the fixed, uncapped September 8 sustained representative-run baseline for five consecutive minutes.
- Roll back if p99 completion time is more than 10% above that same fixed baseline for five consecutive minutes.

Yuki alone decides whether to release and whether to roll back.

messages.content: [2027-12-03T11:10:00-05:00] Yuki’s revised ingest-edge staging branch now accepts only singular `gzip` or `identity` values and rejects comma-separated, empty, and unknown `Content-Encoding` values before decode admission. The executed suite still doesn’t cover multiple `Content-Encoding` header fields, which the framework may combine before the application parser sees them. Production is unchanged. Draft a focused follow-up crediting the singular allowlist while requiring duplicate-header-field fixtures and proof that no multi-value representation can reach decode admission or acceptance. Yuki retains implementation, release, and rollback authority.

Follow-up: Content-Encoding Parsing and Decode Admission

Status: Staging follow-up required; production unchanged

Yuki’s revised ingest-edge staging branch appropriately narrows Content-Encoding handling to the singular allowlist values gzip and identity. It rejects comma-separated, empty, and unknown values before decode admission, which is a meaningful improvement over accepting ambiguous or unsupported representations.

The executed suite does not yet cover requests containing multiple Content-Encoding header fields. Because the framework may combine duplicate fields before the application parser receives them, this remains an unverified path.

Required follow-up:

- Add fixtures with two or more Content-Encoding header fields, including:
  - duplicate gzip fields;
  - gzip plus identity;
  - identity plus gzip;
  - a supported value combined with an unknown value;
  - empty and whitespace-bearing fields;
  - comma-separated values distributed across duplicate fields.
- Exercise framework-normalized and application-visible representations, not only raw single-header inputs.
- Prove that no multi-value representation—whether expressed through duplicate fields, comma joining, or equivalent parser normalization—can reach decode admission or be accepted as valid input.
- Verify that rejection occurs before decoder invocation and before any downstream acceptance path.
- Retain regression coverage for the singular gzip and identity allowlist and for rejection of comma-separated, empty, and unknown values.

Ownership:

Yuki retains implementation, release, and rollback authority. The staging evidence should be attached to the follow-up before any production consideration.

arguments.body:
Mosaic Commerce capacity response — current decision record

Status

The broader Mosaic scale-response cycle remains open. No capacity-related production window is open or authorized. The December 11, 2025 forecast is prospective planning input, not production evidence.

Prior evidence that remains true

- The September 24–26, 2025 staged replay at 18.4 million data points per minute established above-forecast candidate evidence.
- Clean production observation reached a 14.2-million-data-points-per-minute peak only. The earlier 16.0-million forecast peak was not established by that observation.
- The October 6 production observation showed no accepted points lost, but it did not establish whether any accepted batch was lost. That result does not satisfy the accepted-batch-loss condition and does not substitute for the required replay evidence.
- The accepted-batch diagnostic is qualified for prospective production observation after the executed restart-during-requeue evidence: across 25,000 injected crash-and-restart runs, including exits after durable requeue intent and before replacement-attempt linkage, recovery retained the same durable accepted_batch_id, linked replacement transport attempts before dispatch, and reconciled each accepted batch to exactly one terminal result. Coverage included one and two consecutive requeues; pre-acceptance refusals remained outside the accepted-batch population; raw accepted-batch and transport-attempt identities remained out of metric labels; and the permissioned diagnostic performed reconciliation. This qualification is prospective and does not retroactively resolve the October 6 accepted-batch-loss question.

Retained controls and acceptance conditions

The staged replay must preserve the established 2,048-batch global queue limit, the 64-pending-batch limit per tenant, and the retryable pre-acceptance backpressure/refusal path. It qualifies only when all of the following hold for the required observation:

- Queue-wait p99 is no more than 400 milliseconds for five consecutive minutes.
- Retryable queue-full responses are no more than 0.5% for five consecutive minutes.
- No tenant exceeds 64 pending batches.
- No accepted batch is lost.
- Consistency remains at baseline.
- Parity remains at baseline.
- No dropped-series condition occurs; dropped-series checks remain at baseline.
- Route checks remain at baseline.
- Shard-keeper lease checks remain at baseline.
- Rollup-service checks remain at baseline.
- Full-health checks remain at baseline throughout.

Any failed condition blocks a capacity-related production window until the candidate is revised and a fresh qualifying replay passes. Neither the October 6 result nor the earlier 18.4-million staged replay substitutes for this evidence.

December 11, 2025 forecast and required replay

The Mosaic Commerce account team forecasts that, beginning January 20, 2026, expected peak volume will rise from 16.0 million to 17.2 million data points per minute. The mapped owners must run a fresh 90-minute staged replay at 19.78 million data points per minute, which is 15% above the new 17.2-million peak. The replay must use the forecast tenant distribution, batch-size distribution, and burst pattern.

The new forecast itself is not production evidence. The 19.78-million staged replay is only candidate evidence until every numeric, tenant-limit, accepted-batch, consistency, parity, dropped-series, route, shard-keeper lease, rollup-service, and full-health condition above has passed.

Ownership and decision boundary

- Wes is metrics-router primary, effective December 5, 2025. He owns the implementation, the 90-minute staged replay and load-test evidence, and any later decision to open a capacity-related production window, but only after the replay has passed every condition above and the existing deploy, canary, health-return, stop, and rollback rules are satisfied.
- Alex is metrics-router backup. Alex covers the capacity-related opening decision only if Wes is unavailable. Otherwise Alex remains responsible for the cross-service invariant and failure-mode boundary and for escalating or blocking when those boundaries are implicated; Alex is not an ordinary additional approval gate for a passing Wes-owned decision.
- Cyrus and Roman retain rollup-service capacity ownership and parity evidence.
- Nadia retains queue and refusal alert semantics.

Current disposition

The qualified diagnostic is available for prospective evidence collection. The 17.2-million forecast and the required 19.78-million staged replay do not authorize production movement. No capacity-related production window is open or authorized, and the broader Mosaic scale-response cycle remains open pending the completed, verified replay and all required production evidence.

messages.content:
For tax year 2025, the key rule is your marital status on December 31, 2025. Because you were married in November, the IRS treats you as married for all of 2025. You generally cannot file as Single for 2025.

Your main choices are:

1. Married Filing Jointly (MFJ)
2. Married Filing Separately (MFS)

Your unchanged legal names do not create a filing issue. Enter each person’s legal name and Social Security number exactly as shown on their tax records and W-2. The marriage certificate is normally kept with your records, not attached to the return.

Federal comparison

Married filing jointly

- You combine both spouses’ income, withholding, deductions, and credits on one federal return.
- Often produces a lower combined tax, especially when incomes differ, but you must calculate both ways.
- Usually preserves access to more credits and deductions, or gives more favorable income limits.
- Simplifies reporting of jointly owned accounts and shared expenses.
- Both spouses are generally jointly and individually responsible for the tax, interest, and penalties—even if one spouse earned most of the income or made an error.
- You sign one return together.

Married filing separately

- Each spouse files a separate federal return and reports their own income, withholding, deductions, and credits, with appropriate allocation of jointly held items.
- May be worth evaluating if you need to limit exposure to the other spouse’s tax liabilities, or if income-based student-loan repayment calculations make separate filing advantageous.
- Frequently produces more combined tax and can reduce or eliminate credits and deductions because MFS income thresholds are often less favorable.
- Some credits are unavailable or severely restricted for MFS taxpayers, including generally the Earned Income Credit and education-related benefits; eligibility depends on the specific facts.
- If one spouse itemizes deductions, the other generally must itemize as well, even if using the standard deduction would otherwise be better.
- It requires two returns and a careful allocation of income, deductions, withholding, and payments.

New York and New York City

For two full-year New York residents, New York generally follows the federal filing-status choice:

- Federal MFJ generally means filing a joint New York State return.
- Federal MFS generally means filing separate New York State returns.
- You generally cannot choose joint federally and separate for New York merely because that produces a better result.
- New York City resident income tax is reported through the New York return. If you were NYC residents during the relevant period, evaluate the NYC resident tax as well.
- The address printed on a W-2 is useful evidence but does not by itself establish tax residency. Your actual dates and locations of residence matter.

Because you both appear to have lived at the South Slope address, you should determine whether you were full-year New York State and New York City residents. If either of you was a part-year resident, nonresident, or had income connected with another state, the state analysis may differ.

What to compare in the software

Prepare a side-by-side estimate for both MFJ and MFS, checking:

- Total federal tax and refund or balance due
- Total New York State tax
- New York City resident tax, if applicable
- Whether either choice loses credits or deductions
- How joint bank, investment, retirement, or other income would be allocated under MFS
- How itemized deductions would be handled
- Student-loan repayment effects, if relevant
- Whether separate filing meaningfully reduces liability exposure
- Whether the additional complexity and possible professional-preparation cost of MFS is justified

Do not assume that each spouse’s W-2 income should be split. Each W-2 normally belongs to the spouse whose name and Social Security number appear on it. Joint interest, dividends, investment sales, deductions, and tax payments may need separate allocation if you test …

messages.content: [2025-11-22T10:38:00-05:00] Devika and I now have our City Clerk marriage certificate in hand after our November 12 civil ceremony. Neither of us is changing our name, and we don’t currently intend to combine employer health coverage. Give me a concise, prioritized post-marriage administrative checklist that separates genuinely mandatory or time-sensitive updates from optional housekeeping. Include taxes, beneficiaries, emergency contacts, insurance, banking, and whether extra certified copies are likely to be useful, without expanding into every possible account we could update.

Post-marriage checklist — assuming New York/US, no name changes, and no combined health coverage:

Do first / time-sensitive

1. Taxes
   - For the 2025 tax year, you are considered married for the entire year because you were married on December 31.
   - Decide whether to file jointly or separately; compare the results before filing.
   - Update Form W-4 withholding only if your combined income, filing choice, or withholding needs changed. Also account for New York State/local filing requirements.

2. Beneficiaries
   - Review and update beneficiaries on:
     - Employer life insurance and retirement plans
     - IRAs, HSAs, and brokerage accounts
     - Bank and investment payable-on-death/transfer-on-death designations
   - Do not assume marriage automatically overrides existing beneficiary forms.

3. Employer HR and insurance
   - Notify HR or confirm whether your employer requires a marital-status update.
   - Even if you are not combining health coverage, verify the plan’s marriage special-enrollment deadline and formally decline or retain current coverage as required.
   - Review life, disability, renters, and auto insurance for beneficiary, household, or premium changes.

4. Emergency contacts
   - Update emergency contacts with both employers, health systems, primary-care providers, insurers, and any important travel or pet-care records.
   - This is generally not legally mandatory, but it is practical and time-sensitive if records are outdated.

Important legal/financial housekeeping

5. Estate documents
   - Review or create wills, health-care proxies, powers of attorney, and any trusts.
   - Confirm that beneficiary designations match the documents; beneficiary forms often control particular assets.

6. Banking
   - No account changes are mandatory solely because you married.
   - Decide whether to add joint accounts or authorized-user access.
   - Update POD beneficiaries and review account contact information.
