arguments.title: metrics-router: canary alert response
arguments.body:
1. Check the OTel collector batch window.
2. Compare p99 vs baseline.
3. Roll back via pipeline if regression confirmed.

Note: Scheduled load-test label noise, including elevated experiment_id cardinality, can trigger alerts without indicating a service regression. Confirm the alert overlaps the load-test window and isolate test traffic before rolling back.

Sep 7 note: After the config-checksum cleanup, checksum-cache warmup can cause CPU-only post-canary uplift. In the affected AZ, CPU settled at about 2% to 3%, checksum-cache invalidations returned near baseline, cache-cardinality stayed flat, p99 remained 182 to 188 ms, error rate stayed at 0.02%, dropped writes stayed clean, and rollup-service lag stayed flat. Treat this pattern as checksum-cache warmup rather than an automatic rollback case; confirm the broader regression signals before rolling back.

Sep 27 note: A short parser-cache warmup during canary may be held and verified when p99 returns to baseline and error rate, dropped writes, and rollup-service lag stay flat. This does not change any deploy-pipeline or canary requirements.

Generation and cleanup checks:
- Compare p99 by pod with active-generation counts, retired-generation counts, and stop-the-world cleanup pauses. Capture generation-count and heap evidence for the canary record.
- Verify active-generation consistency across pods, route parity, dropped series, reload failures, and restarts.
- Do not roll back solely because a transient p99 spike recovered. Preserve rollback for the rollback conditions listed below.

Negative route-snapshot age / host-local fault:
- If an instance reports a negative route-snapshot age, isolate that instance before taking further action. Do not classify the signal as a generation mismatch or use it as a rollback trigger by itself.
- Check host time separately from generation evidence. Record the host clock/time observation, route-snapshot timestamp and age, and the instance's current-generation evidence independently; generation evidence does not establish that the host clock is correct, and a host-time anomaly does not by itself establish a generation fault.
- When the evidence identifies a host-local clock or route-snapshot fault on an otherwise current-generation instance, use deploy-pipeline instance replacement. Do not use configuration rollback for a host-local fault. Existing rollback conditions remain unchanged.
- The replaced or isolated instance may rejoin only after both gates pass: it reports the current active generation, and the full-health gate passes, including consistency, parity, dropped-series, reload, restart, route, and required canary baseline checks. A missing current-generation report or a host-time check alone is not sufficient for rejoin.
- This procedure creates no deployment authorization, does not authorize a configuration push or open an owner-led canary window, and does not change service ownership or the existing ownership boundaries.

Host-maintenance rejoin gate:
- A metrics-router instance rejoining after host maintenance must remain isolated until it reports the current active generation. A missing generation report does not count as healthy and does not release isolation.
- After the instance reports the current active generation, release isolation only after the ordinary consistency, parity, dropped-series, route, and health checks all pass.
- This gate does not change ownership, create or open an owner-led canary window, or authorize a configuration push.

Owner-led canary window rule:
- Wes, as metrics-router primary, makes the fresh opening decision for each owner-led window.
- Alex may make the fresh opening decision only while covering for an unavailable Wes. Alex is not the ordinary gate for fresh openings.
- Mapped operators may make pushes only while retired generations remain at four or fewer, cleanup pauses remain at or below 100 milliseconds, and the full health set returns to baseline after every push.
- The full health set includes consistency, parity, dropped-series, reload, and restart checks, together with the canary's required baseline signals.
- Exceeding either ceiling - more than four retired generations or a cleanup pause above 100 milliseconds - stops the window immediately. Do not make additional pushes until recovery is complete.
- After recovery, a fresh decision permits exactly one fully observed recovery push. It does not reopen a multi-push window. A further owner-led window requires a separate fresh decision after that push returns the full health set to baseline.
- Consistency, parity, dropped-series, reload, and restart failures remain rollback conditions.
- All openings and operations remain subject to the existing deploy-pipeline, canary, health-return, stop, and rollback rules.

Recorded stopped-window case (second September push):
- The push changed the intended single file.
- Retired generations peaked at four.
- Cleanup pause was 103 milliseconds, exceeding the 100-millisecond ceiling.
- The window stopped immediately; no additional push occurred.
- The full health set returned to baseline seven minutes later.
- Wes classified this as a stopped window, not a completed safe push and not a reopened window.

Completed recovery exercise (October 8):
- The 94-millisecond case was the one fully observed recovery push authorized by Alex's fresh post-recovery decision.
- Retired generations stayed at four or fewer.
- The full health set returned to baseline after the push.
- Wes identified it as the completed recovery exercise and did not describe it as a reopened window.
- Hema accepted the exercised canary-response reference for future use by Wes and other mapped operators.
- This completion does not change the stopped-window classification of the recorded 103-millisecond case or authorize reopening a multi-push window.

Ownership boundary:
- Wes is the metrics-router primary owner effective 2025-12-05.
- Alex is the backup, architectural reviewer, and escalation path when a cross-service invariant, provenance issue, or failure-mode exception is triggered.
- The accepted-batch diagnostic remains qualified for prospective production observation and does not retroactively establish whether any accepted batch was lost on the October 6 Mosaic Commerce ramp.
- The broader Mosaic scale-response cycle remains open; no capacity-related production window is open or authorized.
- Ingest-edge and shard-keeper ownership are unchanged. Shard-keeper remains outside Wes's solo scope unless Alex or the Cyrus-team backup explicitly pairs with him.

arguments.title: Onboarding pass — Wes: ownership and handoff rules
arguments.body:
Onboarding pass for Wes

Context
- This pass reflects the current ownership map and the settled handoff rules as of May 12, 2023.
- The immediate focus is operator readiness: know who owns each service, what the migration sequence is, and how to hand off an incident without leaving an ambiguous owner.

Ownership and migration order
- Alex owns ingest-edge, metrics-router, and shard-keeper.
- Migration order: ingest-edge first, metrics-router second, shard-keeper last.
- Legacy-aggregator and old metric-rollup are historical ownership cases, not part of the current migration sequence.
- rollup-service is effectively unowned today; treat ownership clarification as an explicit follow-up rather than assuming coverage.

Handoff rules
- The primary responder owns isolation and keeps the incident channel/timeline current.
- If the primary has not isolated the issue within 45 minutes, page the secondary responder.
- A handoff must state: current symptoms, scope/impact, actions already taken, evidence and dashboards/logs checked, current hypothesis, next action, and the named owner.
- Do not hand off by merely linking a runbook; the receiving responder must acknowledge the transfer and the sender must record it in the timeline.
- If ownership is unclear, escalate rather than allowing the incident to sit between teams.
- Runbook ownership is being audited, with Nadia cross-reviewing the ownership map.

Deploy and change guardrails
- No Friday-afternoon deploys. This is a settled rotation rule, not a one-off exception.
- Be especially cautious with shard-keeper: rollback is unsafe after partial state movement. The shard-keeper migration remains paused pending the runbook and safety review.
- A label-name diff may be invisible to symptom alerts and can present as generic ingest trouble; check labels and routing changes explicitly during triage.

First-week checklist
- Read the ingest-edge, metrics-router, and shard-keeper runbooks, including operator-path and owner-path sections.
- Confirm the primary and secondary responder path for each owned service.
- Practice writing a complete handoff using the fields above.
- Review the migration order and the shard-keeper rollback warning with the current owner.
- Verify where to record incident timelines, escalations, and runbook ownership gaps.

Expected outcome
Wes can identify the right owner, run the first isolation steps, escalate within the 45-minute rule, and leave a complete handoff that another responder can execute without reconstructing the incident.

arguments.title: Audit results meeting — lock the owner map and shard-keeper restart path
arguments.body:
Meeting outcome target

Leave with an explicit owner map, a written deploy freeze, and a safe, executable shard-keeper restart path. Do not leave any role as “TBD,” “ad hoc,” or implied by team involvement.

1. Decisions to lock in the room

- Primary owner, named backup, and escalation path for each service.
- Whether the deploy freeze applies to all three owned services and what exact condition lifts it. Proposed default: no deploys while the audit findings and shard-keeper restart path are unresolved; lift only after the owner map, runbook changes, and canary-safe environment are explicitly recorded and acknowledged.
- A single operational owner for rollup-service. It cannot remain effectively unowned or be treated as an informal dependency.
- The approver and operator for shard-keeper restart, plus the person who can stop the restart.
- The canary-safe environment and the evidence required before production action. Laptop testing is not acceptable; staging is not acceptable unless explicitly marked canary-safe.

2. Owner map — current evidence and gaps

- ingest-edge: Alex primary; Yuki formal backup. The runbook also requires the cutover owner/backup to be recorded for the window.
- metrics-router: Alex primary; Wes backup.
- shard-keeper: Alex is the operational primary. The current material is inconsistent on backup: Nadia is listed for label-parity/status entries, while Cyrus team is listed for rollback and ownership history. Resolve this in the meeting by naming one accountable backup and separately recording Cyrus team only if it is a confirmed dependency/support role.
- rollup-service: owner must be explicitly assigned. Cyrus team is referenced as the consumer/owner since May 18 in the shard-keeper label-parity procedure, but the audit lesson says rollup-service was effectively unowned. Confirm the accountable individual or team and obtain acknowledgment.
- Nadia: explicit sign-off for alerting/dashboard label parity; do not treat verbal agreement as sufficient.
- Escalation: record who is paged first, who is paged second, and the deadline for escalation if the primary cannot isolate the issue.

Required format for the final map:
Service | Primary | Backup | Escalation | Dependencies | Acknowledged by | Runbook link/entry

3. Shard-keeper — clean restart path

Preconditions — all must be checked and recorded before action:

- Audit findings are closed or explicitly accepted by the named owner.
- Current state and partial-movement risk are captured; do not assume rollback is safe after partial state movement.
- A canary-safe environment is explicitly identified. No laptop deployment; do not use staging unless it is explicitly canary-safe.
- Alex and the named backup are present/available for the operation.
- Nadia has signed off on alerting/dashboard label-name parity.
- The rollup-service owner confirms the consumer is ready and reading the expected label map.
- The exact prior/current label map and compatibility expectations are recorded.
- Stop/abort criteria, observer, and rollback authority are written down.

Execution sequence:

1. Freeze unrelated deploys and announce the change window.
2. Record the pre-restart state, versions, label map, consumer state, and monitoring baseline.
3. Exercise the restart path in the explicitly canary-safe environment.
4. Verify shard-keeper health, state movement, consumer reads, alert behavior, and label parity.
5. Proceed only on explicit canary sign-off from the named primary, backup, Nadia, and rollup-service owner.
6. Roll forward through the approved pipeline; never deploy from a laptop.
7. If a precondition or signal fails, stop and use the hardened rollback path rather than improvising.
8. After the change, record observed results, open risks, and the exact condition for lifting the freeze.

Known runbook guardrails: the rollback entry says to re-push the prior label map, confirm the rollup-service consumer is reading, pre-coordinate with Nadia on label-name parity, and never deploy from a laptop. Treat these as guardrails, not proof that the full restart procedure is complete.

4. Audit lessons to state plainly

- shard-keeper rollback was unsafe after partial state movement.
- rollup-service was effectively unowned.
- A label-name diff was invisible to symptom alerts and looked like generic ingest trouble.

5. Doc cleanup after decisions

- Rewrite shard-keeper into separate operator-path and owner-path sections.
- Replace contradictory backup fields with the locked map and explicit dependency roles.
- Add the canary-safe environment definition and a test-evidence checklist.
- Add rollback stop conditions for partial state movement.
- Add explicit rollup-service ownership and acknowledgment.
- Record Nadia’s written parity sign-off requirement and the exact label compatibility checks.
- Remove or mark stale/historical ownership entries so they cannot be mistaken for the current map.

Close the meeting by reading the final owner map and freeze-lift condition back to the room, then recording acknowledgments in the document.

messages.content:
[2023-08-16T13:35:00-04:00] ### Scheduled load-test cardinality canary

If the metrics-router cardinality canary fires during a declared data-platform load test, first check whether the new high-cardinality label is present only on load-test traffic. On Aug 16, 2023 the canary was caused by an unbounded `experiment_id` label from the load test, not by a metrics-router deploy or router regression.

Before considering rollback:
- Check recent metrics-router deploys and error/drop metrics.
- Confirm whether the suspicious label is isolated to load-test traffic.

Mentor: Alex. Notes from ramp arc — May 11 staging-deploy walk-through, May 14 deploy-rule correction, Jun 8 Saturday canary assist, Jun 17 first solo overnight.

## Aug 16, 2023
- During a declared data-platform load test, Wes treated the metrics-router cardinality canary as potentially external rather than assuming it was a router regression.
- He checked deploy/error-drop metrics and isolated the load-test traffic before deciding on rollback.
- When the signal could be external, he stopped or bounded the test; he reserved rollback for confirmed router regression, drops, or lag.
- He escalated within 45 minutes if the cause could not be isolated.
- Mentoring evidence: good judgment under ambiguous load-test conditions; this is not a promotion packet and does not change metrics-router ownership.

## Aug 23, 2023
- Wes must continue to use the deploy pipeline rather than laptop deploys.
- His solo safe surface remains metrics-router non-prod and ingest-edge staging.
- shard-keeper remains outside solo scope unless Alex or the Cyrus-team backup explicitly pairs with him.
- As of today, Wes may make first-pass production decisions for metrics-router canaries and staging rollback calls for ingest-edge, under the deploy-pipeline rules.
- The owner map is unchanged. This is a narrow practical expansion of decision-making scope, not an ownership change.

## Nov 21, 2023 — Production canary example
- Wes ran the daylight metrics-router sampling-window cleanup canary through the deploy pipeline.
- The replay-validation panel twitched for several minutes after the canary slice went live, but source labels showed that movement was on the replay/mirror validation path.
- He verified that live metrics-router p99 stayed flat, live error rate stayed flat, dropped writes stayed at zero, and rollup-service lag stayed flat.
- Wes held promotion briefly, verified the live path and rollup-service lag, and then proceeded without Alex taking over the decision.
- Mentoring evidence: good first-pass judgment in production by separating validation-path movement from live-path impact and checking the relevant safeguards before proceeding. This is a production example, not a scope expansion; ownership and decision-making boundaries are unchanged.

## Production canary example — Nov 21, 2023

Wes drove the daylight metrics-router sampling-window cleanup canary through the deploy pipeline.

What happened:
- A replay-validation panel twitched for several minutes after the canary slice went live.
- Live metrics-router p99 stayed flat.
- Live error rate stayed flat.
- Dropped writes stayed at zero.
- Rollup-service lag stayed flat.

Good judgment shown:
- Wes used the dashboard source labels to distinguish replay/mirror validation movement from live-path health.
- He held promotion briefly instead of ignoring the twitch.
- He verified live-path metrics and rollup-service lag before proceeding.
- He proceeded without Alex taking over the decision.

Scope note:
This is Q4 evidence for first-pass metrics-router canary judgment under the practical backup rules. It does not change the owner map, make Wes the default daylight handoff, or expand his solo scope into shard-keeper.

## Required operating rule — narrow label-change class

For production review after Dec 12, 2023, label changes that touch `metrics-router`, `shard-keeper`, or `rollup-service` must run the Cardinality Guardrails checks below before the change is treated as safe for production review.

Required checks:
1. Label-cardinality preflight.
   - Identify new or changed label keys and changed value-shape behavior.
   - Show whether the value set is bounded, expected high-cardinality with an owner/budget, or effectively unbounded.
   - Use live canary evidence or a representative live-path fixture for live-path value-shape changes; replay evidence alone is not enough for a live-path label change.
   - Keep unbounded raw identifiers in logs or trace context unless a reviewed bounded metric dimension is justified.

2. Alert-source classification check.
   - Classify whether the relevant panel or alert signal is live-path, replay-source, mirror-source, or other validation-source evidence.
   - Replay or mirror movement can remain visible as investigation evidence, but it is not rollback criteria by itself.
   - Reviewers must not allow validation-source panels to read like live rollback triggers.

Review path:
- Nadia keeps alert semantics in the Cardinality Guardrails review path.
- Cyrus keeps the cost/cardinality angle attached to review.
- Rollup-service ownership remains with the Cyrus/data-platform side; this rule does not move enforcement ownership to data platform.

Non-goals:
- This is not a mature or complete Cardinality Guardrails program.
- This is not a general telemetry rewrite.
- This does not make Wes or any practical backup the default enforcement owner.

messages.content:
[2024-04-12T10:05:00-04:00] A shard-keeper replica relinquished and reacquired its lease during a host clock correction. Please assess whether the safety mechanism behaved correctly, whether a process restart is warranted, and what short observation checks are proportionate before closing the alert.

2024-04-12T10:02:14.109Z lease_guard observed_clock_skew_ms=740 threshold_ms=500 action=relinquish
2024-04-12T10:02:14.117Z leadership_released shard=17
2024-04-12T10:02:16.403Z chronyd system_clock_step_ms=-711
2024-04-12T10:02:17.226Z lease_acquired shard=17
Observed replication-lag maximum: 1.8 seconds
Write availability: no drop
Duplicate leadership signal: none
Clock offset after correction: within 20 ms

Assessment

The safety mechanism behaved correctly.

- `observed_clock_skew_ms=740` exceeded the `500 ms` threshold.
- The replica relinquished the lease before the host clock step:
  - Leadership released at `10:02:14.117Z`
  - Clock correction occurred at `10:02:16.403Z`
- It reacquired the lease only after the correction, at `10:02:17.226Z`, when the offset was back within `20 ms`.
- There was no duplicate-leadership signal, no write-availability impact, and only a bounded replication-lag maximum of `1.8 s`.

This is the intended fail-safe behavior: temporarily give up leadership across an unsafe clock interval, then resume after clock stability returns.

Process restart

A process restart is not warranted from this evidence. Restarting would add disruption without addressing an observed process fault. Consider a restart only if there is continuing lease churn, inability to renew or reacquire, stale leadership state, persistent clock skew, or lag that fails to recover.

Proportionate close-out checks

Before closing the alert, perform a short observation window covering several lease-renewal intervals:

1. Confirm shard 17 has exactly one active leader and no stale or competing lease.
2. Verify the replica remains within the clock-offset limit and does not emit another skew-triggered relinquish.
3. Confirm replication lag falls back toward its normal baseline and does not continue increasing.
4. Check that writes remain available and error/timeout rates are unchanged.
5. Confirm there are no repeated leadership transitions or duplicate-leadership events.

If those checks remain clean, close the alert as an expected safety-triggered lease handoff caused by host clock correction, with no restart required.

arguments.body:
1. Remove the affected replica from follower reads and keep it out of service while investigating. Do not restart it as an automatic response to a lag timer.

2. Verify lease safety before any restart or reentry:
   - The lease holder is unambiguous and the lease epoch is stable.
   - No lease acquisition or relinquishment events are occurring.
   - There are no stale-owner messages.
   - There is no overlapping leadership.
   - There are no write errors.

3. Confirm the replica is making forward catch-up progress. Continue observing it while it remains excluded from follower reads.

4. Restart the replica only if it stops making forward progress after the lease-safety checks above. If it continues progressing, do not restart it solely because lag exceeded a timer threshold.

5. Reenter the replica into follower reads only after disk latency has returned to baseline and replication lag has remained below one second continuously for fifteen minutes. Close the alert only after these reentry conditions are met and the replica is safely returned to service.

arguments.body:
Meeting outcome target

Leave with an explicit owner map, a written deploy freeze, and a safe, executable shard-keeper restart path. Do not leave any role as “TBD,” “ad hoc,” or implied by team involvement.

1. Decisions to lock in the room

- Primary owner, named backup, and escalation path for each service.
- Whether the deploy freeze applies to all three owned services and what exact condition lifts it. Proposed default: no deploys while the audit findings and shard-keeper restart path are unresolved; lift only after the owner map, runbook changes, and canary-safe environment are explicitly recorded and acknowledged.
- A single operational owner for rollup-service. It cannot remain effectively unowned or be treated as an informal dependency.
- The approver and operator for shard-keeper restart, plus the person who can stop the restart.
- The canary-safe environment and the evidence required before production action. Laptop testing is not acceptable; staging is not acceptable unless explicitly marked canary-safe.

2. Owner map — current evidence and gaps

- ingest-edge: Alex primary; Yuki formal backup. The runbook also requires the cutover owner/backup to be recorded for the window.
- metrics-router: Alex primary; Wes backup.
- shard-keeper: Alex is the operational primary. The current material is inconsistent on backup: Nadia is listed for label-parity/status entries, while Cyrus team is listed for rollback and ownership history. Resolve this in the meeting by naming one accountable backup and separately recording Cyrus team only if it is a confirmed dependency/support role.
- rollup-service: owner must be explicitly assigned. Cyrus team is referenced as the consumer/owner since May 18 in the shard-keeper label-parity procedure, but the audit lesson says rollup-service was effectively unowned. Confirm the accountable individual or team and obtain acknowledgment.
- Nadia: explicit sign-off for alerting/dashboard label parity; do not treat verbal agreement as sufficient.
- Escalation: record who is paged first, who is paged second, and the deadline for escalation if the primary cannot isolate the issue.

Required format for the final map:
Service | Primary | Backup | Escalation | Dependencies | Acknowledged by | Runbook link/entry

3. Shard-keeper — clean restart path

Preconditions — all must be checked and recorded before action:

- Audit findings are closed or explicitly accepted by the named owner.
- Current state and partial-movement risk are captured; do not assume rollback is safe after partial state movement.
- A canary-safe environment is explicitly identified. No laptop deployment; do not use staging unless it is explicitly canary-safe.
- Alex and the named backup are present/available for the operation.
- Nadia has signed off on alerting/dashboard label-name parity.
- The rollup-service owner confirms the consumer is ready and reading the expected label map.
- The exact prior/current label map and compatibility expectations are recorded.
- Stop/abort criteria, observer, and rollback authority are written down.

Execution sequence:

1. Freeze unrelated deploys and announce the change window.
2. Record the pre-restart state, versions, label map, consumer state, and monitoring baseline.
3. Exercise the restart path in the explicitly canary-safe environment.
4. Verify shard-keeper health, state movement, consumer reads, alert behavior, and label parity.
5. Proceed only on explicit canary sign-off from the named primary, backup, Nadia, and rollup-service owner.
6. Roll forward through the approved pipeline; never deploy from a laptop.
7. If a precondition or signal fails, stop and use the hardened rollback path rather than improvising.
8. After the change, record observed results, open risks, and the exact condition for lifting the freeze.

Known runbook guardrails: the rollback entry says to re-push the prior label map, confirm the rollup-service consumer is reading, pre-coordinate with Nadia on label-name parity, and never deploy from a laptop. Treat these as guardrails, not proof that the full restart procedure is complete.

4. Audit lessons to state plainly

- shard-keeper rollback was unsafe after partial state movement.
- rollup-service was effectively unowned.
- A label-name diff was invisible to symptom alerts and looked like generic ingest trouble.

5. Doc cleanup after decisions

- Add rollback stop conditions for partial state movement.

- Record Nadia’s written parity sign-off requirement and the exact label compatibility checks.

[2023-08-16T13:35:00-04:00] ### Scheduled load-test cardinality canary

If the metrics-router cardinality canary fires during a declared data-platform load test, first check whether the new high-cardinality label is present only on load-test traffic. On Aug 16, 2023 the canary was caused by an unbounded `experiment_id` label from the load test, not by a metrics-router deploy or router regression.

Before considering rollback:
- Check recent metrics-router deploys and error/drop metrics.
- Confirm whether the suspicious label is isolated to load-test traffic.
- Ask the load-test owner to stop or bound the test if the label source is external.
- Continue normal escalation timing: page or pull in the secondary within 45 minutes if the cause is not isolated.

Rollback is appropriate only if router behavior, write drops, downstream lag, or a deploy regression points to metrics-router itself.

entries.body:
1. Remove the affected replica from follower reads.
2. Verify that the lease holder and epoch remain stable, with no acquisition or relinquishment events, stale-owner messages, overlapping leadership, or write errors.
3. Confirm that the replica is making forward catch-up progress.
4. Re-enter the follower read pool only after disk latency is back at baseline and lag is below one second for fifteen continuous minutes.
5. Restart only if the replica stops progressing after the lease-safety checks. Do not use an automatic timer response as the restart condition.

entries.title: Ownership history

entries.body:
Process readiness alone is not the exit condition. In the staging failover drill, all replacement replicas reported ready after 18 seconds, but lease ownership did not converge until 96 seconds. Before declaring the failover complete, verify all of the following: 1. Every partition has exactly one owner. 2. Lease epochs remain monotonic. 3. No stale-owner messages appear for two full lease-renewal intervals. If any of those checks fail, keep the failover open and page the shard-keeper owner. Renewal-warning versus lease transfer: `renewal deadline exceeded` alone does not prove a lease transfer. Check for a changed lease epoch, explicit acquisition or relinquishment, overlapping leadership, and post-event replication convergence. If the holder and epoch remain unchanged, no overlap occurs, and lag returns to baseline, treat the event as a delayed renewal rather than a failover; do not automatically restart.

## Production lease-loss serving-gate invariant

On lease-loss notification, close the old holder's serving gate before it can return another routing response. The periodic poll is only a backup detector, not the serving-safety mechanism. Production verification must include:
- gate closure before any later routing response
- exactly one serving holder throughout the transfer
- lease-loss notification to gate-close latency
- stale routing responses
- replacement acquisition time
- request p99
- errors
- restarts

A slow handoff or convergence warning is an availability signal to investigate separately. By itself, it is not evidence that the old holder served after lease loss or that the serving-safety invariant failed. The owner map and mapped deployment responsibility remain unchanged.

# Goal
First-cut controls for the Q4 Cardinality Guardrails work; keep it tied to the September mirror/replay legacy-aggregator wobble without turning validation movement into rollback criteria.

# First-cut matrix

## 1. Label limits
- Failure mode: unbounded or newly introduced label keys/values causing fanout.
- Candidate control: a narrow allowlist or budget per sensitive label family.
- Preflight: flag new high-cardinality labels before a metrics-router or shard-keeper push.

## 2. Alert-source semantics
- Failure mode: responders treating replay/mirror validation movement as live-path rollback evidence.
- Candidate control: dashboard and alert wording that marks live metrics-router traffic separately from replay or mirror validation samples.

## 3. Label-change preflight
- Failure mode: a config or parser change adding labels without checking cardinality behavior.
- Candidate control: a pre-push checklist with sample counts, source label, owner, and rollback/non-rollback semantics.

# Non-goals
- No customer-facing dashboard.
- No general telemetry rewrite.
- No legacy-aggregator retirement claim.
- No claim that the 2% replay sample creates immediate storage savings.
- No Q3 incident framing.

# Monday questions
- What cost examples can Cyrus bring by label family?
- Which preflight checks are service-owned by Alex versus data-platform advisory?
- What would make the first cut too broad?

## Bounded observability example — exception-review outcomes

The accepted production counter uses only these bounded labels:
- `service_pair_class`: `ingest_path`, `routing_path`, `ownership_path`, or `other`
- `exception_class`: `invariant`, `provenance`, `failure_mode`, `ownership`, or `escalation`
- `outcome`: `requested`, `accepted`, or `rejected`

Raw service names, owner email addresses, pull-request identifiers, and reviewer-supplied reasons remain in logs or audit records rather than metric labels. This example creates no centralized review owner: mapped owners retain implementation, operational, release, and rollback responsibility, while boundary review remains limited to the triggered cross-service exception.

# INC-2023-10-30-001 metrics-router canary rollback — lightweight after-action

## Summary
A metrics-router canary for `sha:b41c77a` was rolled back after live-path p99 and dropped writes moved on the canary slice. Replay and mirror validation panels were not the rollback trigger.

## Timeline
- 08:07 ET — Page fired for live metrics-router p99 on canary slice. Alex acknowledged the incident.
- 08:22 ET — Live-path p99 was around 118 ms, error rate was 0.18%, and dropped writes were 0.6% on the canary slice. Alex rolled back the most recent metrics-router deploy.
- 09:05 ET — p99 returned to about 46 ms, error rate returned to roughly 0.02%, and dropped writes returned to zero.

## What changed
The canary appears to have changed the `route_pattern` normalization path so one live handler emitted raw account/widget IDs instead of normalized route patterns. Replay validation still showed normalized route patterns, so replay evidence alone would not have caught the live hot-path value-shape change.

## Why rollback was appropriate
The signal was live-path metrics-router movement: p99 and dropped writes on the canary slice. Replay or mirror validation movement remains investigation evidence, not rollback criteria.

## Follow-ups
1. Keep the code fix small: restore normalized `route_pattern` values for the affected live handler before another canary.
2. Patch the Cardinality Guardrails checklist so live-path label value-shape changes require live canary evidence or a representative live-path fixture, not only replay validation.

## Non-goals
This note is not a broad incident postmortem, not a legacy-aggregator retirement discussion, and not a claim that Cardinality Guardrails is complete.
output.title: INC-2023-10-30-001 metrics-router canary rollback — lightweight after-action

# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

The correction is live for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Their two-account read-only scope and customer data contract remain unchanged.

# Q4 incident practice — November 18 scoring sheet

## Scope
A bounded tabletop scoring sheet, not a production runbook. Score observable responder behavior for an accepted metrics-router action across cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication.

## Core criteria
1. Durable attempt identity
- Pass: Responders identify the durable acceptance boundary and preserve one attempt identity after acceptance.
- Fail: They create, assume, or accept multiple identities for the same accepted attempt.

2. Terminal accounting
- Pass: Every accepted attempt reaches exactly one terminal result.
- Fail: An accepted attempt has no terminal result or exposes conflicting terminal results.

3. Failure classification
- Pass: Responders distinguish cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication using the acceptance boundary.
- Fail: They collapse those cases or treat a pre-acceptance event as evidence about accepted work.

## Wes — responder path
Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

## Nadia — postmortem criteria
The postmortem must name the absent system guarantee or control. It must not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause, and it must retain the mapped implementation and rollback owner.

## Final ownership-boundary condition
- Pass: Mapped owners retain implementation and rollback decisions, while the triggered reviewer remains confined to the named failure-mode boundary.
- Fail: The triggered review is treated as implementation, release, or rollback approval.

## Additional operating checks — November 8

### 45-minute secondary boundary
- Pass: When the cause remains unisolated, responders engage the secondary before the 45-minute boundary and make the incident clock visible.
- Fail: Responders wait until or after 45 minutes, or continue without engaging the secondary while the cause remains unisolated.

### Friday staging preparation versus production change
- Pass: Responders identify staging preparation that makes no production state change as staging work and separately identify a Friday-afternoon production deploy as prohibited.
- Fail: Responders classify staging-only preparation as a production deploy, or permit a Friday-afternoon production state change because it was described as preparation.

These checks supplement the accepted cancellation, caller-disconnect, durable-attempt, terminal-result, mapped-owner, and postmortem criteria. This remains a tabletop scoring sheet rather than a production runbook.

## November 18 execution order

- 5 minutes: role and ownership framing.
- 35 minutes: cancellation and caller-disconnect scenario.
- 10 minutes: one targeted rerun if a scoring boundary is missed.
- 10 minutes: debrief and owner follow-up.

Wes teaches the responder path. Nadia owns the postmortem section. Alex maintains only the bounded failure case. This is the exact one-hour tabletop sequence and does not turn the scoring sheet into a production runbook.

## Observed results — November 18

The tabletop is complete. Responders correctly separated durable acceptance from cancellation, caller disconnect, and process recovery; preserved one attempt identity and one terminal result in the exercise; identified Wes as the mapped metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback owner; and distinguished Friday staging preparation from a production change.

These results are training evidence only. The tabletop did not execute the product implementation and does not close any product defect or replace required executable product evidence.

Show how recurring cross-service and data-contract risks can be handled with explicit checks and escalation boundaries instead of relying on one person to review every case. The goal is reusable technical operating leverage, not a transfer of formal ownership or people management.

# Reusable mechanisms

- For covered Cardinality Guardrails changes, require an executable parity fixture and affected-owner signoff, alongside the relevant cardinality and alert-source checks, before production review.
- For Lantern, keep the ordinary admission lane with Iris while defining a clear exception boundary for escalated data-contract issues that need deeper schema, provenance, access, or downstream-semantics review.
- Use bounded first-pass checks so routine operational decisions can move through an established mechanism without turning Alex into the standing reviewer.

# Explicit ownership boundaries

These mechanisms improve how owners operate; they do not make Alex the owner of every covered review or every Lantern room. Iris retains ordinary Lantern admission decisions. Wes performs bounded first-pass checks within his practical scope, without Alex managing him or the formal owner map changing. Cross-service checks still require the affected owners and the appropriate service boundaries.

# Discussion examples

1. **Guardrails parity-and-owner-signoff gate.** A covered cross-service label change is not treated as safe merely because one service's tests pass. The executable parity fixture, affected-owner signoff, cardinality check, and alert-source check make the downstream contract visible before production review.

2. **Lantern ordinary lane versus exception boundary.** Iris can handle an ordinary admission decision. When a data-contract exception changes the meaning or safety of downstream data, it moves through the explicit exception boundary for focused technical review rather than silently being normalized in the ordinary lane.

Define the intended customer audience and the operational questions the preview may answer. Add representative success, suppressed, stale, unavailable, and permission-denied examples after the field-level decisions are reviewed.

## Unresolved questions

Record policy questions that require product or engineering review rather than hiding them in UI behavior.

This is contract work only. No customer access is authorized until the external fields, authorization, provenance, failure semantics, examples, non-goals, and unresolved questions have been reviewed.

# Cross-service gate exceptions — June 14 review

I define cross-service gates and escalation boundaries; I do not take over routine service operation or Iris's product interpretation.

## 1. Metrics-router generation-retirement thresholds

- **Invariant:** Pause additional configuration pushes if retired objects accumulate above four or cleanup pauses exceed 100 milliseconds. Preserve rollback for active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, or dropped series.
- **Observed evidence:** A single-file canary reached four retired generations and a 92-millisecond cleanup pause; the values approached but did not cross the thresholds, and the other consistency, parity, drop, reload, heap, and restart checks remained clean.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The event is near the pause boundaries; it does not establish that later pushes are safe without observation.
- **Mapped owner:** Metrics-router service ownership remains with the mapped service owner; Wes is the practical first-pass backup within the existing deploy rules.
- **Decision needed:** Whether the next configuration push may proceed one at a time.
- **Escalation condition:** Cross more than four retired objects or 100 milliseconds of cleanup pause, or observe active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, or dropped series.

## 2. Ingest-edge bounded decompression

- **Invariant:** Keep active decompression bounded at four per pod and two per tenant; preserve permit cleanup, body limits, accepted-point integrity, request-p99 rollback gates, and randomized one-, two-, and three-second Retry-After behavior.
- **Observed evidence:** Request p99 briefly rose 19 milliseconds above baseline; decode-wait p99 reached 188 milliseconds, waiting work reached eleven on the busiest pods, and one tenant represented 64% of queued requests. Active work stayed within the per-pod and per-tenant limits, permits returned to zero, oversized bodies were rejected before over-budget append, no accepted points were dropped, and no pod restarted.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The concentrated waiting queue raises a separate fairness and capacity question even though no rollback gate fired.
- **Mapped owner:** Ingest-edge routine operation remains with its mapped service owner; cross-service gate review remains with Alex.
- **Decision needed:** Leave the bounded-decompression release in production and define the owner-led fairness or capacity follow-up.
- **Escalation condition:** A production rollback gate fires, including a permit leak, active-work limit violation, dropped accepted points, or the applicable sustained request-p99 threshold.

## 3. Lantern deploy provenance

- **Invariant:** Emit an external deploy event only when all required provenance validates; otherwise represent the result as explicit unknown with a machine-readable missing-provenance reason.
- **Observed evidence:** The corrected fixture rejects partial deploy objects, covers each missing required field with negative tests, performs authorization before lookup, and does not use internal room metadata or inferred ownership.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** Guarded internal validation is active, but customer access remains closed; no external preview access is granted by this correction.
- **Mapped owner:** Alex defines the external data and failure-mode requirements; Iris leads product interpretation.
- **Decision needed:** Approve the fail-closed correction and focused tests without broadening the external contract.
- **Escalation condition:** Any implementation emits partial provenance, consults internal-only metadata, or treats guarded internal validation as customer access.

## 4. Rollup correction backlog

- **Invariant:** Correction processing must preserve assignment epochs, complete assignment snapshots, minimum-watermark evaluation, matching checkpoints and compaction IDs, and duplicate-free publication.
- **Observed evidence:** The correction-backlog evidence is still under review.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The backlog increase must be distinguished between bounded backfill and a stuck correction loop, checkpoint mismatch, duplicate processing, or publication risk.
- **Mapped owner:** Cyrus's data-platform team retains rollup-service implementation and operational ownership.
- **Decision needed:** Decide whether the production fix remains in place and what owner-led pacing, capacity, or alert-tuning follow-up is justified.
- **Escalation condition:** Evidence of repeated processing, checkpoint or assignment mismatch, duplicate output, loss of first-pass currency, or a broken complete-assignment-snapshot gate.

# Oversized-batch design and staged enablement

## Selected permanent behavior
- Participating SDKs reject batches above 8,000 points before transmission.
- The local error tells callers to split the batch before retrying.
- Ingest-edge retains a deterministic backstop for older or nonconforming clients.
- The backstop returns HTTP 413, accepts zero points, reports rejected points equal to the submitted count, and uses the machine-readable `oversized_batch` reason.
- Clients must not retry an unchanged oversized request.

## Evidence behind the decision
- Current SDK clients rejected oversized attempts locally without network transmission.
- Split compliant requests reconciled accepted-point accounting.
- The older client received the deterministic ingest-edge response, made no unchanged retry, and succeeded after splitting.
- The corrected SDK error text names the 8,000-point maximum and the split-before-retry action.

## Enablement window
Stage enablement through January 28, with participating SDK prevention first and ingest-edge retained as the server-side backstop.

## Verification and stop checks
- No unchanged retry after local rejection or HTTP 413.
- Accepted plus rejected points reconcile to submitted points.
- Split requests do not duplicate or lose points.
- Compliant traffic remains at baseline error and latency levels.

The design is selected; this document does not claim staged enablement is complete.

# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

The correction is live for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Their two-account read-only scope and customer data contract remain unchanged.

# Q4 incident practice — November 18 scoring sheet

## Scope
A bounded tabletop scoring sheet, not a production runbook. Score observable responder behavior for an accepted metrics-router action across cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication.

## Core criteria
1. Durable attempt identity
- Pass: Responders identify the durable acceptance boundary and preserve one attempt identity after acceptance.
- Fail: They create, assume, or accept multiple identities for the same accepted attempt.

2. Terminal accounting
- Pass: Every accepted attempt reaches exactly one terminal result.
- Fail: An accepted attempt has no terminal result or exposes conflicting terminal results.

3. Failure classification
- Pass: Responders distinguish cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication using the acceptance boundary.
- Fail: They collapse those cases or treat a pre-acceptance event as evidence about accepted work.

## Wes — responder path
Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

## Nadia — postmortem criteria
The postmortem must name the absent system guarantee or control. It must not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause, and it must retain the mapped implementation and rollback owner.

## Final ownership-boundary condition
- Pass: Mapped owners retain implementation and rollback decisions, while the triggered reviewer remains confined to the named failure-mode boundary.
- Fail: The triggered review is treated as implementation, release, or rollback approval.

## Additional operating checks — November 8

### 45-minute secondary boundary
- Pass: When the cause remains unisolated, responders engage the secondary before the 45-minute boundary and make the incident clock visible.
- Fail: Responders wait until or after 45 minutes, or continue without engaging the secondary while the cause remains unisolated.

### Friday staging preparation versus production change
- Pass: Responders identify staging preparation that makes no production state change as staging work and separately identify a Friday-afternoon production deploy as prohibited.
- Fail: Responders classify staging-only preparation as a production deploy, or permit a Friday-afternoon production state change because it was described as preparation.

These checks supplement the accepted cancellation, caller-disconnect, durable-attempt, terminal-result, mapped-owner, and postmortem criteria. This remains a tabletop scoring sheet rather than a production runbook.

## November 18 execution order

- 5 minutes: role and ownership framing.
- 35 minutes: cancellation and caller-disconnect scenario.
- 10 minutes: one targeted rerun if a scoring boundary is missed.
- 10 minutes: debrief and owner follow-up.

Wes teaches the responder path. Nadia owns the postmortem section. Alex maintains only the bounded failure case. This is the exact one-hour tabletop sequence and does not turn the scoring sheet into a production runbook.

## Observed results — November 18

The tabletop is complete. Responders correctly separated durable acceptance from cancellation, caller disconnect, and process recovery; preserved one attempt identity and one terminal result in the exercise; identified Wes as the mapped metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback owner; and distinguished Friday staging preparation from a production change.

The first run engaged the secondary at minute 47 while the cause remained unisolated, missing the required before-45-minute boundary. The targeted rerun engaged the secondary at minute 42 and passed that boundary. Nadia’s debrief named the missing system control rather than the triggering operator action as root cause.

These results are training evidence only. The tabletop did not execute the product implementation and does not close any product defect or replace required executable product evidence.

Working draft for January planning. This is a bounded discussion draft, not finalized objectives and not an ownership decision.

Operating focus themes

1. Keep asynchronous exception intake measurable

- Preserve measurable intake for asynchronous exceptions, including volume, aging, disposition, and observable failure modes.
- Nadia owns front-door triage. This draft does not reassign that responsibility or decide a broader ownership model.

2. Monitor Lantern’s existing authorization through March 31, 2028

3. Support triggered cross-service reviews

- Support reviews triggered by cross-service invariant concerns, provenance questions, or failure modes.

Explicit exclusions

- People management.
- Centralized routine approval.
- Treating this draft as finalized objectives.
- Making an ownership decision through this document.
- Treating the frozen Q4 package as renewal or expansion approval.

Planning guardrails

- Keep scope bounded to measurement, monitoring, and triggered review support.
- Preserve explicit ownership handoffs and decision authority.
- Escalate only when a defined trigger or material exception warrants it.
- Revisit and finalize through the January planning process; this document records a working direction only.

arguments.body:
Cross-Service Failure-Case Intake Template

Purpose

Use this template for a concrete cross-service failure case. The intake is a routing and bounded-review record; it is not a new approval gate, central approval process, program-owner role, or replacement for existing implementation, release, rollback, or incident ownership.

Current intake rule — all four parts are required

1. Component: name the concrete component or service involved.
2. Mapped implementation/release owner: name the person or mapped operating owner responsible for ordinary implementation and release. This owner remains responsible for implementation, release, rollback, and operations through the existing path; do not leave this field blank.
3. Selected boundary: select exactly one boundary for this intake — invariant, provenance, failure_mode, ownership, or escalation — and state the precise boundary being reviewed. Do not select multiple boundaries; split genuinely separate cases into separate intakes.
4. Observed failure/risk: describe the concrete observed failure or risk, including evidence, conditions, impact or exposure, and the relevant version/environment. Do not submit a hypothetical concern without an observed fact or bounded evidence.

Intake

- Component:
- Mapped implementation/release owner:
- Selected boundary (exactly one: invariant | provenance | failure_mode | ownership | escalation):
- Precise boundary statement:
- Concrete observed failure/risk:
- Evidence and provenance:
- Version/environment and date:
- Affected services and cross-service dependency:
- Incident clock, stop conditions, and escalation route, if applicable:
- Related runbook, alert, incident, change, or test:

Routing and review

- A complete intake has all four required parts: component; mapped implementation/release owner; exactly one selected boundary; and concrete observed failure/risk.
- Incomplete requests return to the submitting owner for the missing information. Do not infer an owner, boundary, approval, or risk.
- Complete requests route to the mapped implementation/release owner for ordinary implementation, release, rollback, and operations decisions. The intake does not transfer those responsibilities.
- Boundary review is limited to the one selected boundary named in the intake. The boundary reviewer does not become the final release approver, does not replace the mapped implementation/release owner, and does not approve unrelated work.
- Nadia triages asynchronous cross-service exception intake and returns incomplete requests or routes complete requests to the mapped owner. Nadia makes no implementation, release, rollback, or operations decisions.
- Alex sees only boundaries that require Alex’s review under the existing routing; Alex owns the captured cross-service failure case and its bounded boundary review, not the implementation, release, rollback, or program-wide process.
- Wes owns and teaches responder-path scenarios. Nadia owns the postmortem section and material. Existing responder, postmortem, implementation, release, rollback, escalation, and operations paths remain unchanged.

Submission check

- [ ] Component is named.
- [ ] Mapped implementation/release owner is named.
- [ ] Exactly one selected boundary is named and stated precisely.
- [ ] Concrete observed failure/risk and supporting evidence are included.
- [ ] The request is routed to the mapped owner for ordinary implementation/release/rollback/operations decisions.
- [ ] Boundary review is not being used as ordinary release approval.
- [ ] No separate rollback-owner field is created.
- [ ] No separate invariant-owner, provenance-owner, failure-mode-owner, ownership-owner, or escalation-owner fields are created.
- [ ] Wes/Nadia/Alex role split and existing escalation paths are preserved.

Historical scenarios

2026-04-27 — April Lantern migration preflight: blocked pre-authorization candidate

In staging, an undeployed migration candidate performed 20 unauthorized lookups. All 20 were ultimately denied, but each lookup constructed and initialized the incident-load adapter before authorization completed; 2 of the 20 also accessed the source. This was a blocked pre-authorization candidate, not a deployed customer incident; existing customer access remained unchanged while the candidate was undeployed.

Required analysis and acceptance conditions were authorization before adapter construction/initialization or source access; denial regressions showing zero adapter constructions and zero source calls for unauthorized lookups; and an affected LPS-001 rerun before migration acceptance. Product Engineering remained the implementation and release owner. Alex maintained the cross-service case and reviewed the shared safety/failure-mode boundary; Wes owned and taught responder paths; Nadia retained the postmortem section.

2026-10-16 — paired shard-keeper staging drill

The old holder closed its serving gate on lease loss. The replacement remained out of routing during catch-up. Routing began only after the replacement opened its serving gate. Failure triggers were overlapping serving holders, routing to a closed serving gate, or a request without exactly one terminal result.

This was a staging training case with no production or ownership change. Wes owned and taught the responder path; Nadia retained the postmortem material; Alex maintained only the cross-service failure case. Shard-keeper remained outside Wes’s solo scope.

2026-11-10 — quarterly incident-practice training result

Participants correctly kept the replacement holder out of routing until its serving gate opened and recognized that lease ownership alone does not establish serving eligibility. In 2 of 4 response timelines, responders initially treated closing the old listener as sufficient and omitted the terminal outcome for a request accepted before lease loss. After the facilitator inject, both corrected the timeline and accounted for that request exactly once.

Training only: no production drill and no system change. Existing ownership and Wes’s solo shard-keeper scope were unchanged.

2026-11-10 — facilitator-only shard-keeper handoff exercise

The timed sequence transferred the lease before the replacement serving gate opened, then revealed one request accepted by the old holder before lease loss that remained in flight. Participants had to state routing eligibility separately from terminal request accounting. Lease ownership or listener closure alone was insufficient. The scoring covered handoff ordering, gate behavior, exactly-one-terminal-result accounting, failure triggers, and ownership boundaries. This was training, not a production drill, and did not expand Wes’s solo shard-keeper scope; Cyrus covered the Data Platform boundary.

2027-01-28 — facilitator-only ingest-edge shutdown with accepted work still queued

Two hundred requests had already been accepted into tenant queues. Readiness turned false and the ingest listener closed, so the edge had to refuse new work. The dispatch loop then exited with 37 requests still queued, leaving only 163 terminal outcomes. The gap was unresolved accepted work, not refused work.

The exercise required separating refusal of new work from responsibility for accepted work; requiring every accepted request to drain or receive exactly one explicit terminal result; reconciling all 200 request identities without duplication; and engaging the secondary under the established incident-clock rule if isolation failed. The timed sequence, facilitator prompts, 10-point scoring, and passing standard treated listener closure as insufficient and prohibited claims that old-owner remediation or a production change had completed. Training only; Alex contributed only this cross-service failure case, Wes taught the responder path, and Nadia reviewed the postmortem section.

2027-04-05 — PR 2141 staging readiness behavior

In staging, ten replacement instances compiled a 40,000-route fixture in 25–34 seconds against a fixed 30-second readiness timeout. Eight joined on the first attempt. Two correctly remained unready, were terminated, and restarted before joining. Production was unchanged.

The responder exercise required identifying Wes and the mapped metrics-router owner path; classifying the restart-loop exposure as a failure-mode exception rather than a production incident or release approval request; and naming evidence required before release: reproducible staging runs covering the 25–34 second compile range; readiness/join, termination, and restart-loop metrics and logs for all ten instances; confirmation that the two unready instances were terminated and recovered on restart; timeout/retry behavior and failure-mode disposition; and explicit owner sign-off through the mapped metrics-router path. Alex’s role was limited to the bounded failure-mode exercise and intake framing. Alex was not the release approver; the mapped metrics-router owner retained implementation, release, rollback, and operations responsibility. No production change was implied.

2027-05-06 / May 20 practice contrast — PR 2141 production evidence

The earlier staging candidate exceeded the fixed readiness budget, terminated, and joined only on retry. A restart was recovery activity, not acceptance evidence. In the May 6 production rollout, every instance remained unroutable until compilation finished, and every cold start stayed within the fixed readiness budget without restart. Acceptance required readiness and serving eligibility to remain aligned throughout startup; the production case passed on that basis.

Facilitator contrasts for the May 20 practice were: an over-budget replacement remains unroutable and restart is not acceptance evidence; terminal-state selection and its matching accounting contribution must come from the same winning path; and replay samples or missing source classification cannot be presented as live rollback criteria. Live rollback decisions require live, release-relevant evidence and the mapped owner’s existing rollback path.

Wes maintained and taught the responder path; Nadia reviewed postmortem framing; Alex maintained only these cross-service cases. The practice material created no new approval gate, release-approver role, or broader ownership for Alex.

Historical-scenario scope note

These scenarios are retained as historical training and evidence records below the current intake template. They do not alter current ownership, imply production completion, or create a new approval gate. Apply the current four-part intake rule and exactly one selected boundary to new submissions.

Purpose: Remain authoritative for pipeline-limit behavior and cost semantics, including the meaning of measured limits versus missing, malformed, or stale inputs.
Mapped owner: Cyrus owns the Guardrails authority interface and cost semantics; the mapped Guardrails team owns implementation, release, rollback, and operations for its area. Wes owns the metrics-router operating-limit mapping where it connects to the published operating view.

3. Owner map — published responsibility
Purpose: Remain authoritative for published responsibility and canonical service ownership; Lantern may point to this record but may not reproduce or change it.
Mapped owner: The owner-map team owns publication, implementation, release, rollback, and operations for the owner-map authority. Wes owns the mapped operating-responsibility handoff for metrics-router; Product Engineering implements Lantern’s read-only navigation to the record.

Shared five-field reference contract

Internal cards may carry only these reference fields when navigating to an authoritative record:

- tenant_id
- canonical_service_id
- authority_type
- authority_record_id
- source_timestamp

The fields identify and locate an authoritative record; they are not a copy of its authority payload. Each authority remains separate, including when owner-map and Cardinality Guardrails records refer to the same canonical service. Source timestamps must remain the authority’s timestamps, not export or render time. No card or navigation path may create, update, delete, or otherwise mutate an authoritative record.

Handoff points

- Contract changes: the affected authority owner proposes the change; Product Engineering assesses the Lantern interface impact; Alex reviews only the shared-contract and cross-system failure boundary.
- Authority updates: the owner-map or Guardrails owner publishes and operates its own authoritative record. Lantern consumes the five-field reference and preserves separate authority identity and provenance.
- Lantern implementation: Product Engineering owns the build, routine implementation choices, tests, release, rollback, and operations. Alex is not an approval gate for every implementation decision.
- Cross-workstream verification: before release of a contract-affecting change, the mapped owners verify tenant isolation, authority separation, stale/missing behavior, provenance, no payload duplication, no mutation capability, and customer-path isolation.
- Failure or boundary violation: the affected workstream owner leads response and rollback for its area; the other mapped owners are engaged where the shared contract or a cross-system boundary is implicated. Alex reviews that shared boundary and failure mode, not every local remediation choice.

Alex’s review scope

Alex is the shared-contract and cross-system failure-boundary reviewer. That scope covers the invariants and seams that cross workstream boundaries: the five reference fields, authority separation, provenance, tenant isolation, mutation and payload-copy prohibitions, stale or unavailable authority behavior, and continued exclusion from Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It does not make Alex the sole implementation gate or require review of routine Lantern, Guardrails, or owner-map implementation decisions. Mapped owners remain accountable for their own delivery and operations.

Planning rule

Plan and track work under the three named workstreams, with explicit owner handoffs at the contract and boundary points above. Do not create a single Lantern backlog that absorbs Guardrails semantics or published owner-map responsibility.

Decision record

Decision date: September 24, 2026
Operating handoff: October 1, 2026
Decision meeting: Lantern continuation and platform-boundary review, 10:30–11:15 AM
Decision authorities: Hema and Theo

1. Renewed authorization

After review of the June 16–September 15 operating evidence and the separate reference-only rehearsal, Hema and Theo authorized Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce—and no other accounts—to continue from October 1, 2026 through March 31, 2027 with read-only access through the shared authorization wrapper.

The renewed term does not activate before October 1, 2026.

2. Permitted scope

Access remains limited to:

- Provenance-backed deploy movement
- Published service ownership
- Timestamped incident-load summaries
- Explicit unknown states

3. Excluded scope

The authorization does not include:

- Any additional account
- Cost data
- CSV export
- Raw incident text
- Internal room metadata
- Employee identifiers or employee comparisons
- Inferred or unpublished ownership
- Internal-only fallback data
- Write capability
- Release-readiness judgment
- Employee-performance interpretation

4. Suspension conditions

The following immediately suspend both accounts pending correction and a successful rerun of the affected safety check:

- Authorization-wrapper bypass
- Adapter call after denial
- Cross-tenant material
- A stale or missing source rendered as anything other than explicit unknown
- Deploy event without required provenance
- Unpublished ownership
- Incident-load summary without its source timestamp
- Exposure of an excluded field
- Loss of read-only enforcement

Latency and other errors do not independently suspend access unless they cause one of the violations above.

5. October 1 internal platform cycle

The reference-only model is the starting point for an internal platform cycle beginning October 1, 2026. The cycle does not begin early. This is an internal-cycle start only; customer exposure of the reference-only integration requires separate later authorization.

6. Five-field reference contract and authority split

The shared integration uses canonical published service identity and exactly these five fields:

- tenant_id
- canonical_service_id
- authority_type
- authority_record_id
- source_timestamp

There is no copied authority payload and no writeback.

Authority boundaries:

- Lantern remains the explanation layer.
- Cardinality Guardrails remains the authority for pipeline limits and cost signals.
- The owner map remains the authority for published responsibility.

The authority_type, authority_record_id, and source_timestamp must identify the same authoritative record. Lantern does not copy limit or cost values from Cardinality Guardrails.

7. Ownership assignments

- Alex owns the shared cross-system contract and failure-mode boundaries.
- Iris owns interpretation and adoption criteria.
- Cyrus owns the Cardinality Guardrails authority interface and cost semantics.
- Wes owns metrics-router control mappings and operating evidence.
- Product Engineering owns Lantern implementation.

Mapped owners retain responsibility for implementation, release, rollback, and operations within their areas. Alex’s assignment is limited to the shared contract and failure-mode boundaries stated above.

8. No-early-activation and customer-exposure boundary

Neither the renewed two-account authorization nor the internal reference-only platform cycle may activate before October 1, 2026. Customer exposure is not included in this decision. It requires separate later authorization before any customer-facing activation or use.

9. Handoff acceptance

The October operating handoff is accepted only when the authorized term, Harbor Health/Mosaic Commerce account allowlist, read-only wrapper enforcement, permitted and excluded fields, provenance requirements, explicit-unknown behavior, authority boundaries, ownership assignments, and suspension checks are preserved as stated in this record. Any suspension requires correction and a successful rerun of the affected safety check before either account resumes access.

This is the durable decision record for the October operating handoff and platform boundary, separate from the completed evidence-review document.
