arguments.title: ingest-edge: cutover playbook
arguments.body:
# ingest-edge: current cutover and verification flow

This is the current ingest-edge procedure. Do not use the retired legacy-aggregator bucket-flush or handoff steps; legacy-aggregator is not part of the ingest-edge cutover path.

## 1. Pre-cutover checks

- Confirm the ingest-edge deployment and configuration are ready for the target environment.
- Confirm monitoring is in place for dropped events, latency, error rate, and Prometheus anomalies.
- Record the intended cutover window and the on-call owner/backup.

## 2. Staging shadow

- Run ingest-edge in staging shadow for 48 hours before production cutover.
- During the shadow period, watch for dropped events, latency regressions, elevated errors, and metric anomalies.
- Proceed only when the shadow period is clean and there is no unresolved ingest-edge issue.

## 3. Production cutover

- Switch production traffic to ingest-edge using the approved deployment/configuration.
- Confirm traffic is flowing through ingest-edge and that event processing is healthy.
- Record the cutover time and deployment/configuration version.

## 4. Post-cutover verification

- Monitor ingest-edge for at least 24 hours after cutover.
- Verify zero dropped events, stable latency, a flat error rate, and no Prometheus anomalies.
- If any of these checks fail, pause the rollout and follow the service rollback/incident procedure rather than applying legacy-aggregator bucket-flush steps.

## 5. Close-out

- After the 24-hour verification is clean, mark the ingest-edge cutover complete.
- File the close-out note with the cutover time, observed results, and any follow-up items.

## 6. Alerting label-map / parity-change guardrail

- Treat the alerting label-map parity work as part of the ingest-edge path review.
- Preserve existing dashboard label names by default.
- Do not approve or roll out a label-name change based only on verbal agreement; record explicit written sign-off from Nadia in the parity document or its document thread before proceeding.
- In the review, document the exact compatibility expectations for the label map and verify that the parity check covers the affected labels.

## 7. OTel collector 0.91 rollout note (2023-07-27)

- This rollout was production-clean: after the heightened watch closed, error rate stayed flat and CPU stayed flat.
- p95 memory settled about 5% above the pre-bump collector baseline, still within normal headroom.
- Future collector bumps still require staging replay plus an explicit memory watch.

## 8. Retry-only OTel change (sha:0a91b7c)

- The retry-only OTel change may be included in the ingest-edge cutover playbook; `sha:0a91b7c` has been quiet in production for several days.
- Exporter retry `max_interval` is 15 seconds.
- Exporter retry `max_elapsed_time` is 5 minutes.
- Memory-limiter settings were deliberately not part of this patch; do not treat this entry as a collector-wide tuning guide.
- After deployment, check dropped writes, backpressure counters, and retry log volume.

Primary owner: Alex
Backup: Yuki

## OTel exporter retry-only change — Oct 2023 note

For the retry-only OTel collector change deployed as `sha:0a91b7c`, the operational intent was to reduce staging/prod exporter retry noise without hiding real pressure signals.

Settings in scope:
- `max_interval`: 15 seconds
- `max_elapsed_time`: 5 minutes

Settings explicitly out of scope:
- Memory-limiter settings were not changed in this patch.

Post-deploy checks:
- Dropped writes should stay at zero.
- Backpressure counters should remain visible.
- Exporter retry log volume should decrease, but not by suppressing real backpressure evidence.

If dropped writes appear or backpressure counters disappear, treat that as a signal problem rather than a successful noise reduction.

## Staging-drill hygiene — 2024-01-04

- Before opening the staging lane for an ingest-edge rollback drill, verify the load-test tag TTL and identify the cleanup owner.
- This hygiene check applies to the deploy-pipeline path only.
- Wes may perform the daylight first pass for this staging-drill class.
- Escalate any unsafe or ambiguous signal rather than proceeding.
- This section does not change production ownership or the owner map.

## 9. ingest-edge v2.19.4 production cutover — 2024-04-02

The randomized one-to-three-second `Retry-After` behavior for 429 responses is now the production behavior for ingest-edge v2.19.4. Do not return to the baseline retry behavior solely because the rollout gates are complete.

Wes owns the first-pass monitoring read at each gate; Alex remains the primary owner and Yuki remains the backup.

### Explicit stop boundaries

At every rollout gate, stop the rollout, hold the current traffic split, and follow the service rollback/incident procedure if any one of these conditions occurs:

- Any increase in 5xx responses.
- p99 latency at or above 190 ms.
- Queue depth at or above 76%.
- Accepted-throughput loss at or above 3% versus baseline.
- Retry attempts at or above 130,000 attempts per second.

Do not advance to the next gate until the measurements are back within bounds and the stop condition has been assessed by the on-call owner. Do not use the retired legacy-aggregator bucket-flush or handoff steps for rollback.

### Gate observations

Observed maxima for the randomized `Retry-After` behavior:

| Gate | Peak retries | Peak p99 | Peak queue depth | Accepted throughput vs. baseline | 5xx increase |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 10% | 124,000 attempts/second | 176 ms | 73% | 2.1% below baseline | None |
| 50% | 128,000 attempts/second | 186 ms | 75% | 2.8% below baseline | None |
| 100% | 129,000 attempts/second | 188 ms | 75% | 2.9% below baseline | None |

All production gates passed. Keep ingest-edge v2.19.4 at 100%; do not return to the baseline behavior. The full-production observation completed on 2024-04-02. The formal 48-hour production check remains due on 2024-04-04.

At the formal check, verify zero dropped events, no 5xx increase, stable latency, queue depth, accepted throughput, retry behavior, and no Prometheus anomalies. Record the check result and any follow-up items in the close-out note.

## 10. Production tenant-fair queue behavior — 2024-07-05

The remaining ingest-edge rollout completed in production. The tenant-fair queue behavior is now the production behavior and must be preserved at both the 50% gate and full production:

- Repeated noisy-tenant tests preserved the eight-waiting cap.
- Newly queued low-volume tenants entered the scheduling ring immediately; they must not wait for a separate refill or batch cycle.
- Dispatch remained work-conserving and used every eligible slot.
- Empty tenants were removed from the scheduling ring after cancellation.
- Every queue-cap response retained `Retry-After`.
- The existing active-work, accepted-point, dropped-point, and restart checks remained clean.

This queue behavior does not change the existing safety and retry requirements. Explicitly preserve all of the following:

- At most four active items per pod.
- At most two active items per tenant.
- Bounded decompression.
- The existing retry requirements, including the production `Retry-After` behavior for queue-cap responses.

At any future rollout or change, stop and investigate if the eight-waiting cap, immediate low-volume tenant admission, work-conserving dispatch, cancellation cleanup, `Retry-After`, or any existing active-work, accepted-point, dropped-point, or restart check regresses. Follow the service rollback/incident procedure; do not use the retired legacy-aggregator bucket-flush or handoff steps.

## 11. Bounded service-discovery membership check — May 24 zone imbalance

Before closure after a zone-imbalance signal, perform a bounded membership check for each zone:

- Compare the ready service-discovery endpoints with load-balancer membership by zone.
- Identify and reconcile any endpoint present in one view but not the other, and confirm that the resulting membership matches the expected ready endpoints for each zone.
- If the comparison shows drift, refresh service-discovery/load-balancer membership before proceeding.
- After refresh, verify that traffic distribution by zone has returned to the established baseline.
- Confirm queue occupancy and caller-visible errors remain at baseline during and after the refresh.
- Reconcile every accepted request to exactly one caller-visible terminal result before closure. Closure is blocked by duplicated accepted work, unaccounted accepted work, or leaked queue occupancy.

This bounded check does not change the owner map and does not make Alex the routine operator. The existing primary owner, backup, release, rollback, and operations ownership remain unchanged.

## 12. Tenant-burst operating check

During a tenant-burst check, verify all of the following:

- A tenant may have at most eight waiting requests.
- Requests in excess of the eight-request waiting limit must remain retryable and fail before acceptance; they must not be counted as accepted work.
- Every accepted request must reconcile to exactly one terminal result.
- Other tenants must remain at baseline, including their queue behavior and caller-visible outcomes.
- Caller errors for unaffected traffic must remain at baseline.
- After the burst is drained and the queue is emptied, queue occupancy must end at zero.

Stop the check and follow the service rollback/incident procedure if an excess request is accepted, a retryable excess request is not rejected before acceptance, an accepted request lacks exactly one terminal result, other tenants or caller errors depart from baseline, or an emptied queue does not end at zero.

This tenant-burst operating check does not transfer implementation, release, or rollback ownership from Yuki’s mapped path.

## 13. Buffer-reuse decoded-attribute cap and request-cap validation — 2027-09-08

During the four-hour run after buffer reuse, the aggregate decoded-attribute limit was 1,048,576 bytes and the request cap was 72 requests.

- Peak memory was 347 MiB above the 1.12 GiB baseline.
- Throughput was 0.8% below baseline.
- p99 latency was 2.4% above baseline.
- Limit-plus-one and cap-excess cases remained retryable and failed before acceptance; none were enqueued.
- Every request had exactly one terminal outcome.
- Production was unchanged.

## 14. Active decoder controls — production observation closed 2027-10-21

The production observation is closed. The following controls are active and must be preserved:

- Apply one request-wide decoded-attribute limit of 1,048,576 bytes across all gzip members combined. Do not reset or apply this limit separately per gzip member.
- Admit at most 72 requests to decoding at a time. Requests above this decode-admission cap remain retryable and must be rejected before acceptance; over-cap work must not be enqueued.
- Do not enqueue any request whose decoded attributes exceed the request-wide limit, including a request that crosses the limit in a later gzip member.
- Every accepted request must produce exactly one caller-visible terminal outcome.
- Release the decode-admission slot exactly once for every terminal path: success, rejection, malformed input, cancellation, or client disconnect. Slot release must be idempotent across races and must not be skipped or duplicated.
- Preserve the separate 8,000-point whole-batch rule; it is independent of the request-wide decoded-attribute limit and the 72-request decode-admission cap.
- Preserve the eight-waiting-requests-per-tenant limit and its retryable pre-acceptance handling.

Yuki retains implementation, release, and rollback authority for this mapped path. This control update does not change the owner map or make Alex the routine operator.

Primary owner: Alex
Backup: Yuki

# ingest-edge: current cutover and verification flow

## 1. Pre-cutover checks

- Confirm the ingest-edge deployment and configuration are ready for the target environment.
- Confirm monitoring is in place for dropped events, latency, error rate, and Prometheus anomalies.
- Record the intended cutover window and the on-call owner/backup.

## 2. Staging shadow

- Run ingest-edge in staging shadow for 48 hours before production cutover.
- During the shadow period, watch for dropped events, latency regressions, elevated errors, and metric anomalies.
- Proceed only when the shadow period is clean and there is no unresolved ingest-edge issue.

## 3. Production cutover

- Switch production traffic to ingest-edge using the approved deployment/configuration.
- Confirm traffic is flowing through ingest-edge and that event processing is healthy.
- Record the cutover time and deployment/configuration version.

## 4. Post-cutover verification

- Monitor ingest-edge for at least 24 hours after cutover.
- Verify zero dropped events, stable latency, a flat error rate, and no Prometheus anomalies.
- If any of these checks fail, pause the rollout and follow the service rollback/incident procedure rather than applying legacy-aggregator bucket-flush steps.

## 5. Close-out

- After the 24-hour verification is clean, mark the ingest-edge cutover complete.
- File the close-out note with the cutover time, observed results, and any follow-up items.

## 6. Alerting label-map / parity-change guardrail

- Treat the alerting label-map parity work as part of the ingest-edge path review.
- Preserve existing dashboard label names by default.

arguments.body:
# ingest-edge: current cutover and verification flow

This is the current ingest-edge procedure. Do not use the retired legacy-aggregator bucket-flush or handoff steps; legacy-aggregator is not part of the ingest-edge cutover path.

## 1. Pre-cutover checks

- Confirm the ingest-edge deployment and configuration are ready for the target environment.
- Confirm monitoring is in place for dropped events, latency, error rate, and Prometheus anomalies.
- Record the intended cutover window and the on-call owner/backup.

## 2. Staging shadow

- Run ingest-edge in staging shadow for 48 hours before production cutover.
- During the shadow period, watch for dropped events, latency regressions, elevated errors, and metric anomalies.
- Proceed only when the shadow period is clean and there is no unresolved ingest-edge issue.

## 3. Production cutover

- Switch production traffic to ingest-edge using the approved deployment/configuration.
- Confirm traffic is flowing through ingest-edge and that event processing is healthy.
- Record the cutover time and deployment/configuration version.

## 4. Post-cutover verification

- Monitor ingest-edge for at least 24 hours after cutover.
- Verify zero dropped events, stable latency, a flat error rate, and no Prometheus anomalies.
- If any of these checks fail, pause the rollout and follow the service rollback/incident procedure rather than applying legacy-aggregator bucket-flush steps.

## 5. Close-out

- After the 24-hour verification is clean, mark the ingest-edge cutover complete.
- File the close-out note with the cutover time, observed results, and any follow-up items.

## 6. Alerting label-map / parity-change guardrail

- Treat the alerting label-map parity work as part of the ingest-edge path review.
- Preserve existing dashboard label names by default.
- Do not approve or roll out a label-name change based only on verbal agreement; record explicit written sign-off from Nadia in the parity document or its document thread before proceeding.
- In the review, document the exact compatibility expectations for the label map and verify that the parity check covers the affected labels.

## 7. OTel collector 0.91 rollout note (2023-07-27)

- This rollout was production-clean: after the heightened watch closed, error rate stayed flat and CPU stayed flat.
- p95 memory settled about 5% above the pre-bump collector baseline, still within normal headroom.
- Future collector bumps still require staging replay plus an explicit memory watch.

## 8. Retry-only OTel change (sha:0a91b7c)

- The retry-only OTel change may be included in the ingest-edge cutover playbook; `sha:0a91b7c` has been quiet in production for several days.
- Exporter retry `max_interval` is 15 seconds.
- Exporter retry `max_elapsed_time` is 5 minutes.
- Memory-limiter settings were deliberately not part of this patch; do not treat this entry as a collector-wide tuning guide.
- After deployment, check dropped writes, backpressure counters, and retry log volume.

Primary owner: Alex
Backup: Yuki

## OTel exporter retry-only change — Oct 2023 note

For the retry-only OTel collector change deployed as `sha:0a91b7c`, the operational intent was to reduce staging/prod exporter retry noise without hiding real pressure signals.

Settings in scope:
- `max_interval`: 15 seconds
- `max_elapsed_time`: 5 minutes

Settings explicitly out of scope:
- Memory-limiter settings were not changed in this patch.

Post-deploy checks:
- Dropped writes should stay at zero.
- Backpressure counters should remain visible.
- Exporter retry log volume should decrease, but not by suppressing real backpressure evidence.

If dropped writes appear or backpressure counters disappear, treat that as a signal problem rather than a successful noise reduction.

## Staging-drill hygiene — 2024-01-04

- Before opening the staging lane for an ingest-edge rollback drill, verify the load-test tag TTL and identify the cleanup owner.
- This hygiene check applies to the deploy-pipeline path only.
- Wes may perform the daylight first pass for this staging-drill class.
- Escalate any unsafe or ambiguous signal rather than proceeding.
- This section does not change production ownership or the owner map.

arguments.title: Metrics-router cutover plan — rollout spine
arguments.body:
# Metrics-router cutover plan

## 1. Objective and scope

Move production traffic from the current metrics-router path to the cleaned-up metrics-router implementation with a controlled rollout, clear rollback points, and no dashboard-label churn.

In scope:
- Production traffic cutover for metrics-router.
- Validation of routing correctness, event delivery, latency, error rate, and cardinality behavior.
- Preservation of existing dashboard and alert label names throughout the cutover.
- Rollback to the prior serving path if a gate fails.

Out of scope:
- Shard-keeper migration; it remains last in the migration sequence.
- A parallel dashboard-label cleanup.
- Broad refactoring of config-loader or legacy-aggregator behavior beyond what is required to cut over safely.

Context:
- ingest-edge is the first migration, metrics-router is second, and shard-keeper is last.
- ingest-edge completed a 48-hour staging shadow with zero dropped events.
- legacy-aggregator still has a known bucket-flush-timing concern. Treat that as a validation item, not as a reason to expand this document unless it affects cutover safety.

## 2. Preconditions

Before starting the production rollout, confirm:

1. The candidate metrics-router version is built, reviewed, and deployable.
2. The config-loader path is deterministic for environment/file overrides, including overlapping label predicates; the more-specific rule must win.
3. Existing dashboard and alert label names are unchanged.
4. The previous version and its configuration are available for immediate rollback.
5. Observability is live for both candidate and baseline: request volume, error rate, latency, dropped/rejected events, routing mismatches, cardinality, and bucket-flush behavior around legacy-aggregator integration.
6. An owner is assigned to watch the rollout and an owner is available to execute rollback.

Record the candidate version, config revision, start time, and rollback target in the change ticket before traffic moves.

## 3. Rollout sequence

Use one production rollout with small, reversible steps. Keep the same config and label contract at every step.

Phase 0 — deploy dark
- Deploy the candidate without serving production traffic.
- Run health checks and configuration validation.
- Confirm that startup, config loading, and downstream connectivity are clean.

Phase 1 — canary
- Send a small traffic slice to the candidate.
- Hold long enough to observe a representative request and flush window, not merely a successful health check.
- Compare candidate against baseline on all gates below.

Phase 2 — partial rollout
- Increase traffic only if the canary is clean.
- Recheck after each increase rather than assuming a clean canary proves the full rollout.

Phase 3 — full cutover
- Move the remaining traffic to the candidate.
- Keep the old path warm and rollback-ready through the observation window.

Phase 4 — stabilize
- Continue monitoring through at least one complete bucket-flush cycle and the agreed post-cutover observation window.
- Close the rollout only after the final validation checklist is complete.

Suggested traffic steps: 5% → 25% → 50% → 100%. If traffic volume is too low for meaningful percentages, use a fixed request/event count per step and document the count. Do not add more stages unless the rollout math or observed risk requires it.

## 4. Decision gates

Advance only when candidate behavior is consistent with baseline and there is no unexplained degradation.

Hard-stop / rollback conditions:
- Any confirmed dropped event or material increase in rejected events attributable to the candidate.
- Routing mismatch, incorrect label selection, or evidence that a less-specific overlapping predicate wins.
- Error rate, latency, or saturation materially worse than baseline and not explained by traffic mix.
- Cardinality growth that threatens downstream capacity or changes expected series behavior.
- Bucket-flush timing or downstream delivery behavior that causes data loss, unacceptable delay, or alerting impact.
- Dashboard or alert label names change.

At each step, record:
- Traffic percentage or fixed request/event count.
- Candidate and baseline volume.
- Error/rejection/drop counts.
- Latency comparison.
- Routing/configuration validation result.
- Cardinality result.
- Legacy-aggregator flush result.
- Advance, hold, or rollback decision and owner.

If a metric is noisy or the sample is too small to support a decision, hold at the current step. Do not advance on a green-looking but underpowered sample.

## 5. Rollback

Rollback by shifting traffic back to the last known-good metrics-router version/configuration. Preserve the candidate logs, metrics, config revision, and timestamp before changing state so the failure can be investigated.

After rollback:
1. Confirm traffic is serving from the prior path.
2. Verify errors, drops/rejections, latency, routing behavior, and downstream flush behavior return to baseline.
3. Notify the migration owner and record the failed gate.
4. Do not retry until the cause is understood or an explicitly reviewed mitigation is ready.

## 6. Final checklist

Before declaring success:

- [ ] Candidate version and config revision recorded.
- [ ] Dark deployment and health checks passed.
- [ ] Canary passed with a representative sample/flush window.
- [ ] Partial rollout gates passed at each step.
- [ ] Full traffic is on the candidate.
- [ ] No dropped events or unexplained rejection increase.
- [ ] Routing and overlapping-predicate behavior validated.
- [ ] Latency and error rate are acceptable versus baseline.
- [ ] Cardinality is within expected bounds.
- [ ] Legacy-aggregator bucket-flush behavior is acceptable.
- [ ] Dashboard and alert label names remain unchanged.

messages.content: [2023-12-03T18:50:00-05:00] I'm getting ready for Monday's legacy-aggregator retirement-criteria discussion and want a tight prep agenda, not a rambling note. Cyrus wants the criteria tied to data-platform cost instead of another open-ended validation habit. Roman wants the final replay fixture to be a real pass/fail gate, not a comforting replay lane that never ends. Nadia wants the Apr 17 label-name failure mode explicitly covered, because the old comfort of legacy replay came from catching cross-service label mismatches after the fact. I want the meeting framed around criteria for when mirrored writes may stop, not around actually stopping them on Monday. The candidate gate is: final replay fixture pass clean, no live metrics-router or rollup-service references, and Cardinality Guardrails checks covering the prior label-change class. Turn that into a tight prep agenda that keeps the legacy-aggregator validation lane bounded but still active.

Monday, Dec. 4 — Legacy-Aggregator Retirement Criteria

Objective

Agree on the bounded criteria for when mirrored writes may stop. This meeting is not a decision to stop mirrored writes on Monday.

Prep agenda

1. Frame the decision
   - Define “mirrored writes may stop” as the decision under review.
   - Confirm that the validation lane remains active until the gate is met, but does not become an open-ended replay practice.

2. Review the retirement gate
   - Final replay fixture passes cleanly as a binary pass/fail gate.
   - No live references remain in metrics-router or rollup-service.
   - Cardinality Guardrails checks explicitly cover the Apr. 17 label-name failure mode, including cross-service label mismatches caused by label changes.

3. Align on cost and operating boundaries
   - Tie the criteria to data-platform cost and operational burden.
   - Identify what validation is still required before the gate and what is explicitly out of scope.
   - Reject an indefinite “comfort replay” lane without a defined pass condition.

4. Confirm evidence and ownership
   - Name the owner for the final replay fixture and its pass/fail result.
   - Confirm how live references will be checked.
   - Confirm who verifies Cardinality Guardrails coverage for the prior label-change class.

5. Close with the decision record
   - Record the agreed gate, evidence required, and any remaining blockers.
   - Record that mirrored writes continue until all criteria pass.
   - Set the review point for the gate result; do not make retirement itself the Monday agenda decision.

Candidate decision statement

“Mirrored writes may stop only after the final replay fixture passes cleanly, live metrics-router and rollup-service references are absent, and Cardinality Guardrails checks cover the Apr. 17 cross-service label-name failure mode. Until then, legacy-aggregator validation remains active but time-bounded by this gate rather than continuing as an open-ended replay lane.”

- **T+16 — Reconciliation:** Require a final timeline showing routing eligibility for both holders and exactly one terminal outcome for the pre-lease-loss request.

### Scoring points

1. Separating lease ownership from serving eligibility.
2. Keeping the replacement out of routing until its serving gate opens.
3. Treating old-listener closure as distinct from request completion.
4. Recording exactly one terminal outcome for the request accepted before lease loss.

# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

The correction is live for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Their two-account read-only scope and customer data contract remain unchanged.

# Lantern Q3 renewal review — final evidence and boundaries

## Final decision — September 23, 2027
Hema and Theo accepted the frozen July 1–September 15 evidence and separately authorized Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce—and no other account—for a read-only Lantern term from October 1, 2027 through March 31, 2028. The April 1–September 30, 2027 term remains the only active authorization through September 30, and no customer lookup under the new term may occur before October 1.

## Frozen evidence: July 1–September 15, 2027
- 3,126 customer sessions.
- 603 logical explanation requests: 397 eligible combined explanations, 136 valid over-24-hour separations, and 70 explicit-unknown outcomes for stale or missing input.
- Zero eligible renderer failures.
- 107 delayed or retried customer rows ordered by authoritative `source_timestamp` without processing-time reordering.
- Harbor Health: 12 release follow-ups.
- Mosaic Commerce: 11 incident handoffs.
- Stale or missing input rendered as anything other than explicit unknown: zero.

## Authorized scope for October 1, 2027–March 31, 2028
Every Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce lookup remains behind the shared authorization wrapper. Access is read-only and limited to provenance-backed deploy movement, published service ownership, timestamped incident-load summaries, and explicit unknown states.

## Unchanged exclusions
Cost data, CSV export, raw incident text, internal room metadata, employee identifiers or comparisons, inferred or unpublished ownership, internal-only fallback data, write capability, release-readiness judgments, employee-performance interpretations, internal owner-map/Cardinality Guardrails reference navigation, and access for any other account remain unauthorized.

## Suspension rules
An authorization-wrapper bypass, adapter call after denial, cross-tenant material, stale or missing input rendered as anything other than explicit unknown, deploy event without required provenance, unpublished ownership render, incident-load summary without its source timestamp, excluded-field exposure, or loss of read-only enforcement suspends both accounts pending correction and a successful rerun of the affected safety check. Latency or another error alone does not suspend access unless it causes one of those violations.

## Owner split
- Iris retains customer interpretation.
- Product Engineering retains implementation and regression maintenance.
- Alex reviews only triggered shared-contract, provenance, or failure-boundary exceptions.

## Interpretation boundary
Harbor Health’s 12 release follow-ups and Mosaic Commerce’s 11 incident handoffs demonstrate use of the authorized systems view. They do not establish causality, release readiness, employee performance, or authorization for another field or account.

# October 27, 2027 facilitator packet

## Example 1 — separate reassessment time from entry time

### What happened
A reassessment was completed at 16:55, and the entry documenting it was made at 17:40.

### Safe wording
“Late entry entered at 17:40 for a reassessment performed at 16:55. This entry records the findings from the 16:55 reassessment and does not alter the earlier record.”

### What the wording must not imply
That the entry existed at 16:55, that documentation time was changed to match the reassessment time, or that an earlier entry was replaced.

## Example 2 — addendum preserving the original record

### What happened
A later review found that the original entry omitted a clarification. The original entry remains visible, and an addendum is entered at 18:10.

### Safe wording
“Addendum entered at 18:10: [clarification]. This addendum supplements the original entry; it does not replace or backdate it.”

### What the wording must not imply
That the original entry was changed or deleted, that the addendum existed before 18:10, or that the underlying care necessarily occurred at 18:10.

## Final submission check
- Submit one fully anonymized document by October 15, 2027.
- Confirm the title identifies the October 27, 2027 session and that neither the title nor body contains patient identifiers.
- Keep exactly these three categories under each example: What happened; Safe wording; What the wording must not imply.
- Add no patient-specific clinical detail.
- Confirm the addendum preserves the original record: the original remains visible, and the addendum supplements rather than replaces or backdates it.

# Q4 triggered review — metrics-router cancellation terminal accounting — October 11, 2027

## Intake
- Affected component: metrics-router replacement activation
- Mapped implementation and release owner: Wes
- Exception class: `failure_mode`
- Concrete observed condition: after an activation attempt was accepted, deploy-pipeline cancellation could emit caller-visible `cancelled` while a concurrent activation worker committed publication and emitted caller-visible `published` for the same attempt.

## Initial observed evidence
Staging reproduced both caller-visible terminal outcomes in 14 of 10,000 cancellation-versus-commit interleavings.

## Passing correction evidence — October 14
Across 5,000 cancellation-versus-activation-commit races, including cancellation immediately before and after the commit boundary, every accepted attempt produced one durable attempt result and exactly one caller-visible terminal outcome.

## Passing process-crash evidence — October 26
Across 3,000 crashes before, during, and after the cancellation-versus-publication commit boundary, restart recovered one durable attempt identity and exactly one caller-visible terminal outcome for every accepted attempt. No attempt produced both `cancelled` and `published`.

## Partial disconnect evidence — November 9
Across 2,000 post-acceptance disconnect cases, the server retained one durable attempt identity and one terminal journal record with no duplicate execution. The harness did not reconnect or retry as the caller, so caller-visible recovery remained open.

## Final caller-recovery evidence — December 8
Across 2,000 post-acceptance disconnect cases, the caller reconnects or retries using the same durable attempt identity and receives the original single terminal outcome. No retry creates another attempt, re-executes accepted work, or creates a second terminal record.

## Closure
The durable-attempt identity, exactly-one terminal outcome, cancellation ordering, process-crash recovery, and caller-visible reconnect or same-attempt retry requirements are satisfied. Alex’s caller-visible terminal-outcome boundary is closed.

## Ownership boundary
Wes retains implementation, release, and rollback authority. Closing Alex’s failure-mode boundary does not approve implementation or release.

- Mapped implementation and release owner: Roman

The compaction identity omitted tenant identity. In 200 paired synthetic-tenant fixtures, 26 pairs coalesced across tenants and 11 pairs emitted one tenant’s bounded aggregate under the other tenant.

The expected tenant mapping is independently derived from each paired input set and compared with every emitted bounded aggregate. Across 3,000 paired-tenant fixtures, injected tenant misattribution at the first, middle, and final aggregate positions fails, while exact mappings pass. Raw-row separation remains correct, and production is unchanged.

## Closure
The tenant-bound compaction identity, raw-row separation, and every-aggregate tenant-attribution requirements are satisfied. Alex’s triggered tenant-identity invariant review is closed.

Roman retains implementation, release, and rollback authority. Closing Alex’s invariant boundary does not approve implementation or release.

# Q4 incident practice — November 18 scoring sheet

## Scope
A bounded tabletop scoring sheet, not a production runbook. Score observable responder behavior for an accepted metrics-router action across cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication.

## Core criteria
1. Durable attempt identity
- Pass: Responders identify the durable acceptance boundary and preserve one attempt identity after acceptance.
- Fail: They create, assume, or accept multiple identities for the same accepted attempt.

2. Terminal accounting
- Pass: Every accepted attempt reaches exactly one terminal result.
- Fail: An accepted attempt has no terminal result or exposes conflicting terminal results.

3. Failure classification
- Pass: Responders distinguish cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication using the acceptance boundary.
- Fail: They collapse those cases or treat a pre-acceptance event as evidence about accepted work.

## Wes — responder path
Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

## Nadia — postmortem criteria
The postmortem must name the absent system guarantee or control. It must not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause, and it must retain the mapped implementation and rollback owner.

## Final ownership-boundary condition
- Pass: Mapped owners retain implementation and rollback decisions, while the triggered reviewer remains confined to the named failure-mode boundary.
- Fail: The triggered review is treated as implementation, release, or rollback approval.

## Additional operating checks — November 8

### 45-minute secondary boundary
- Pass: When the cause remains unisolated, responders engage the secondary before the 45-minute boundary and make the incident clock visible.
- Fail: Responders wait until or after 45 minutes, or continue without engaging the secondary while the cause remains unisolated.

### Friday staging preparation versus production change
- Pass: Responders identify staging preparation that makes no production state change as staging work and separately identify a Friday-afternoon production deploy as prohibited.
- Fail: Responders classify staging-only preparation as a production deploy, or permit a Friday-afternoon production state change because it was described as preparation.

These checks supplement the accepted cancellation, caller-disconnect, durable-attempt, terminal-result, mapped-owner, and postmortem criteria. This remains a tabletop scoring sheet rather than a production runbook.

## November 18 execution order

- 5 minutes: role and ownership framing.
- 35 minutes: cancellation and caller-disconnect scenario.
- 10 minutes: one targeted rerun if a scoring boundary is missed.
- 10 minutes: debrief and owner follow-up.

Wes teaches the responder path. Nadia owns the postmortem section. Alex maintains only the bounded failure case. This is the exact one-hour tabletop sequence and does not turn the scoring sheet into a production runbook.

## Observed results — November 18

The tabletop is complete. Responders correctly separated durable acceptance from cancellation, caller disconnect, and process recovery; preserved one attempt identity and one terminal result in the exercise; identified Wes as the mapped metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback owner; and distinguished Friday staging preparation from a production change.

The first run engaged the secondary at minute 47 while the cause remained unisolated, missing the required before-45-minute boundary. The targeted rerun engaged the secondary at minute 42 and passed that boundary. Nadia’s debrief named the missing system control rather than the triggering operator action as root cause.

These results are training evidence only. The tabletop did not execute the product implementation and does not close any product defect or replace required executable product evidence.

arguments.body:
# metrics-router cleanup production canary — July 23–24 execution sheet

## Operating rule

This is an execution record, not an approval. No row is pre-approved. Before executing any row, record a fresh decision for that specific request identifier. Proceed only if the responsible decision-maker records an explicit acceptance for that row; otherwise record `blocked` and do not execute it.

The sheet does not promise, require, or imply a number of pushes. Add a row only when a specific single-file push is proposed and reviewed. A later row is permitted only after the preceding row has returned to baseline and its checks are complete.

## Per-push execution record

Use one fully completed block per proposed push. Do not combine pushes in one row.

### Push [sequence label — not a quota]

- Request identifier: `[unique identifier]`
- Date/time proposed: `[July 23 or July 24, timestamp and timezone]`
- Requester / executor: `[name or role]`
- Fresh decision before execution: `[pending | accepted | blocked]`
- Decision-maker and decision timestamp: `[name/role, timestamp and timezone]`
- Decision notes / reason for block: `[record the specific rationale; do not leave blank when blocked]`
- Single-file push description: `[one file only; exact path and concise change description]`
- Intended cleanup target: `[retired generation / cleanup pause behavior]`
- Preconditions checked: `[list relevant checks and observed values]`

#### Execution outcome

- Execution started: `[timestamp and timezone, or not executed]`

## Guardrails

- Every request identifier must be unique.
- The decision field must be fresh and recorded before execution for that row.
- A push description must identify exactly one file.
- Record either `blocked` or `accepted` as the outcome; do not use acceptance as a pre-approval for any other row.

arguments.body:
Approved from the durable-write and recovery design perspective.

The revised design correctly:
- Uses tenant plus batch ID as the transaction/retry key.
- Writes the idempotent batch result and advances the tenant watermark in one backing-store transaction, only when the committed range is contiguous.
- Returns the existing committed result for a retried batch ID.
- Reads back the durable result and watermark after commit, and publishes readiness only from that readback.
- Preserves the intended crash behavior: before commit leaves neither artifact; after commit/before acknowledgement is safely recovered by retry; and before readiness publication resumes from durable readback.
- Prevents a later batch from publishing readiness past a missing durable range.

Please add the requested design-boundary comment to make the transaction, retry, and readiness guarantees explicit for future maintainers. Deployment approval remains with the mapped rollup-service owner and is not part of this review.

Classification

This is best classified as a bounded consumer-capacity backlog during a demand burst:

- Queue age increased from 45 seconds to 6 minutes while accepted input rose 31%.
- Consumer throughput stayed flat, which points to a fixed processing ceiling rather than a consumer crash or progressive degradation.
- Queue age began declining when input returned to normal. That is the key boundedness signal: the consumer is draining accumulated work rather than losing ground indefinitely.
- Zero rollup errors argues against a processing or correctness failure.
- Metrics-router and ingest-edge remained at baseline, so there is no evidence that either upstream service caused the alert or is itself degraded.

Current classification: degraded latency/backlog, bounded and demand-induced, pending closure checks. Not currently an Infra incident.

messages.content:
[2024-04-08T10:50:00-04:00] Support is investigating a metrics-router report where configuration generation 442 appeared healthy even though a live reload with an invalid zero-second flush interval failed. Please diagnose whether traffic actually switched configurations, explain the observability defect, and recommend safe health-endpoint semantics that distinguish attempted, validated, and active generations without changing the active configuration during a failed reload.

2024-04-08T10:12:01.204Z reload_start candidate_generation=442
2024-04-08T10:12:01.219Z validation_failed generation=442 field=flush_interval value=0s error="must be greater than zero"
2024-04-08T10:12:01.220Z reload_kept_active active_generation=441
2024-04-08T10:12:04.008Z GET /healthz 200 {"status":"healthy","config_generation":442}

Traffic did not switch to generation 442.

The sequence is explicit:

  10:12:01.204 — reload of candidate 442 began.
  10:12:01.219 — validation rejected 442 because flush_interval was 0s.
  10:12:01.220 — the active configuration was retained at 441.
  10:12:04.008 — healthz incorrectly reported config_generation=442.

Therefore, traffic continued using generation 441. Generation 442 was only attempted; it was neither validated nor activated.

The observability defect is that /healthz appears to expose the reload candidate or last attempted generation rather than the atomically active generation. The reload path correctly preserved the active configuration, but the status/reporting path updated its generation field before validation—or read from candidate-state instead of active-state. This creates a false impression that invalid configuration reached production traffic.

Recommended semantics:

  /healthz should be a process and active-runtime health check. Its configuration field must come from the active configuration object:

    {
      "status": "healthy",
      "active_generation": 441,
      "validated_generation": 441,
      "attempted_generation": 442,
      "reload_state": "failed_validation",
      "reload_error": {
        "field": "flush_interval",
        "value": "0s",
        "message": "must be greater than zero"
      }
    }

Use these meanings consistently:

  attempted_generation
    The newest generation presented for reload, regardless of outcome.

  validated_generation
    The newest generation that passed validation. A failed validation must not advance this value.

  active_generation
    The generation currently used by request/traffic processing. It changes only after validation succeeds and an atomic configuration swap completes.

For this incident, both validated_generation and active_generation should remain 441, while attempted_generation is 442.

A safer endpoint split would be:

  /healthz
    Liveness only, or liveness plus health of the currently active configuration. It should remain 200 if generation 441 is functioning normally. It must not label the invalid candidate as healthy.

  /readyz
    Readiness based on the active configuration and runtime dependencies. A failed candidate reload should not make the service unready when the existing active configuration remains valid and operational.

  /config-status
    Detailed reload state containing attempted, validated, and active generations, validation errors, and timestamps.

The reload implementation should preserve this ordering:

  1. Record attempted_generation.
  2. Parse and validate the candidate.
  3. If validation fails, record the failure and leave validated_generation and active_generation unchanged.
  4. If validation succeeds, update validated_generation.
  5. Atomically swap the validated configuration into the active slot.
  6. Only after the swap, update active_generation.

Health reporting should read active_generation from the same immutable or atomically published configuration reference used by traffic processing, rather than from reload bookkeeping. This prevents the health endpoint from claiming that a candidate is active before, or even if, activation occurs.

messages.content:
[2025-04-11T14:12:00-04:00] I’m reviewing a metrics-router parser change with this configuration and test behavior:

Two route entries use ID `payments-primary`. The first has priority 10 and the current target; the second has priority 40 and a fallback target. The parser inserts each entry into a Go map keyed by route ID before validating uniqueness, so the later entry silently overwrites the earlier one. Reversing the file order changes which target becomes active, and both loads report a successful reload.

This is a correctness bug in the parser, not merely a test issue.

The parser must validate route-ID uniqueness before inserting entries into the map. With the current order:

- The first `payments-primary` entry is discarded.
- The active target depends on file order.
- Duplicate configuration is incorrectly accepted.
- A successful reload can silently change routing behavior.

Recommended behavior:

1. Parse each route entry.
2. Check whether its ID already exists.
3. Return a reload error identifying the duplicate ID and both entry locations.
4. Only insert the entry after the uniqueness check.
5. Leave the existing configuration active when reload validation fails.

Tests should include table cases for:

- Duplicate IDs in both file orders.
- Different priorities and targets proving neither entry wins silently.
- A failed reload preserving the previous active configuration.
- A valid configuration with distinct IDs still loading successfully.
- Duplicate detection occurring before map overwrite.

The key invariant is: duplicate route IDs are rejected deterministically; priority must not be used to resolve duplicates unless that is an explicit, separately documented configuration rule.

If order is intentionally meaningful anywhere, that ordering rule must be explicit and validated rather than being an accidental consequence of parsing or overwrite...

bookend_start.content: [2025-04-11T14:12:00-04:00] Explain the duplicate-identity and order-dependence defect, and state the validation, failed-reload, and active-generation guarantees the owner needs to satisfy without prescribing a particular parser implementation.

arguments.query: duplicate identity order-dependent configuration reload validation failed reload active generation guarantees
duplicate identity order dependence parser reload active generation validation failure configuration owner

messages.content:
The defect has two related parts:

1. Duplicate identity

The configuration can contain multiple entries that resolve to the same logical identity. If the loader stores entries in a map or otherwise collapses them without first detecting the collision, one definition silently replaces or combines with another. The result is loss of configuration and no reliable indication of which definition won.

The owner must treat duplicate logical identities as a validation error. Identity comparison must use the system’s full canonical identity—not merely a convenient display name or an incomplete key.

2. Order dependence

Because the duplicate is handled implicitly, the effective configuration depends on input order. Reordering otherwise equivalent entries can change which values survive, which references resolve, or which generation is produced. Thus, the same set of definitions does not necessarily yield the same result.

A valid configuration must have deterministic semantics: reordering independent entries must not change the resulting configuration. If order is intentionally meaningful anywhere, that ordering rule must be explicit and validated rather than being an accidental consequence of parsing or overwrite behavior.

The owner’s required guarantees are:

Validation guarantee

- Validate the complete candidate configuration before making it active.
- Reject duplicate canonical identities explicitly.
- Reject malformed, inconsistent, or semantically invalid definitions, including invalid references and cross-entry conflicts.
- Validation must be deterministic and independent of incidental input order.
- A candidate that fails validation must produce actionable diagnostics identifying the relevant identity and location(s).
- Validation must not partially mutate the currently active configuration.

Failed-reload guarantee

- A failed reload must be non-destructive.
- The previously active configuration remains intact and continues serving traffic.
- The failed candidate must not become partially visible, and it must not alter the active generation, indexes, caches, or derived state.
- The failure must be observable through an error/diagnostic that distinguishes rejection of the new candidate from failure of the currently active configuration.
- A later valid reload must still be able to replace the old generation normally.

Active-generation guarantee

- Activation occurs only after the candidate has passed all required validation.
- The transition from the old configuration to the new one is atomic from readers’ perspective.
- A reader observes either the complete old generation or the complete new generation, never a mixture.
- The active generation remains stable while it is being used; in-flight work must not observe entries from multiple generations.
- Each successful activation has an identifiable generation, and a rejected reload does not advance or replace the active generation.

These are behavioral guarantees. They do not require a particular parser, map structure, validation library, or reload mechanism.

messages.content: [2024-03-29T09:37:00-04:00] Nadia found a nondeterministic metrics-router config case while testing a legacy-key cleanup. The parser currently accepts both the legacy `max_batch_bytes` key and the replacement `max_request_bytes` key, then writes both into the same effective setting as it iterates a Go map. In staging, a config with `max_batch_bytes: 8388608` and `max_request_bytes: 12582912` came up with an 8 MiB limit on some restarts and a 12 MiB limit on others. Production-generated configs only contain the replacement key, so there is no production impact, and Nadia owns the patch. What's the minimal deterministic parser behavior here, and what focused startup and live-reload tests would you use so dual-key configs are rejected, legacy-only configs still work, replacement-only configs work normally, and a failed reload preserves the active configuration?

Minimal deterministic behavior:

1. Detect key presence before iterating any map.
2. If both `max_batch_bytes` and `max_request_bytes` are present, reject the configuration with a clear error. Reject even if their values are equal; there should be no precedence rule.
3. If only `max_batch_bytes` is present, parse it into the canonical `max_request_bytes` setting.
4. If only `max_request_bytes` is present, use it normally.
5. Do not mutate or publish the active configuration until the entire candidate configuration has parsed and validated successfully.

Conceptually:

    legacy, hasLegacy := raw["max_batch_bytes"]
    replacement, hasReplacement := raw["max_request_bytes"]

    if hasLegacy && hasReplacement {
        return Config{}, errors.New(
            "max_batch_bytes and max_request_bytes cannot both be set",
        )
    }

    switch {
    case hasReplacement:
        cfg.MaxRequestBytes = replacement
    case hasLegacy:
        cfg.MaxRequestBytes = legacy
    }

The important property is that alias resolution happens explicitly, outside the Go map iteration. There is no last-write-wins behavior.

Focused startup tests:

- Replacement-only config
  - Input: `max_request_bytes: 12582912`
  - Assert startup succeeds.
  - Assert effective limit is `12582912`.

- Legacy-only config
  - Input: `max_batch_bytes: 8388608`
  - Assert startup succeeds.
  - Assert effective limit is `8388608`.

- Dual-key config with different values
  - Input both keys with `8388608` and `12582912`.
  - Assert startup fails with an error identifying both keys.
  - Assert no configuration is published.

- Dual-key config with equal values
  - Input both keys with the same value.
  - Assert startup still fails. This prevents the parser from silently treating one spelling as authoritative.

- Determinism check
  - Parse the same dual-key input repeatedly, preferably many times.
  - Assert every attempt returns the same validation error and never an effective value.
  - This guards against accidentally reintroducing map-order-dependent behavior.

A table-driven parser test is sufficient for these cases. The test should assert both the returned error and the resulting canonical field.

Focused live-reload tests:

1. Failed dual-key reload preserves the active config

   - Start with a valid replacement-only config at `12582912`.
   - Confirm the active runtime limit is `12582912`.
   - Reload a config containing both keys.
   - Assert reload returns the mutual-exclusion error.
   - Assert the active runtime limit remains `12582912`.
   - Assert the previous configuration remains usable.

2. Failed malformed or semantically invalid reload preserves the active config

   - Start with a valid config.
   - Reload a config with an invalid type, overflow, or out-of-range value.
   - Assert reload fails.
   - Assert the active configuration is unchanged.

3. Successful legacy-only reload

   - Start with a valid replacement-only config.
   - Reload a legacy-only config.
   - Assert reload succeeds and the effective limit changes to the legacy value.

4. Successful replacement-only reload

   - Start with one replacement-only value.
   - Reload another replacement-only value.
   - Assert reload succeeds and the new value becomes active.

5. No partial publication

   - Use a configuration with several fields where one later field fails validation.
   - Assert none of the earlier fields from the candidate become visible.
   - The active configuration must remain the complete prior snapshot, not a partially updated object.

The reload path should therefore be structured as:

    candidate, err := ParseAndValidate(bytes)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    active.Store(candidate)
    return nil

Parsing and validation should happen against a new candidate object. The live active object should only be swapped after success, giving readers either the old complete configuration or the new complete configuration, never an intermediate state.

results.snippet: ...mark the Q4 design-system snapshot frozen on December 23 because many staff are away the following week, then attach December 24–31 >>>observations<<< as amendments. North Pier’s established rule is to freeze each quarterly snapshot only after quarter...

messages.content: [2027-12-19T16:10:00-05:00] Anya sent me this North Pier proposal: mark the Q4 design-system snapshot frozen on December 23 because many staff are away the following week, then attach December 24–31 observations as amendments. North Pier’s established rule is to freeze each quarterly snapshot only after quarter close; later corrections, not in-quarter observations, become linked amendments.

Anya’s proposal conflicts with North Pier’s established rule.

December 23 is before Q4 closes, and December 24–31 observations are still in-quarter observations—not later corrections. Freezing on December 23 would make the snapshot incomplete and misclassify valid Q4 data as amendments.

Recommended approach:

- Keep the Q4 snapshot open through December 31.
- Freeze it after quarter close, beginning January 1.
- Attach only genuine post-close corrections as linked amendments.
- If staffing requires an earlier operational cutoff, label the December 23 artifact as a provisional or operational snapshot, not the authoritative frozen Q4 snapshot.

results.title: Fix ExportEnvelope source_timestamp on retry
results.snippet: ...The fixture creates >>>observations<<< at 10:02, injects a transient failure, retries them at 10:19, and expects the downstream envelope source timestamp to be 10:19. The retry attempt time is already recorded separately as `retry_attempt_at`.

messages.content: [2025-04-23T11:38:00-04:00] I'm reviewing an OTel collector retry-queue change. On retry, it constructs a new `ExportEnvelope` with `source_timestamp=clock.Now()`. The fixture creates observations at 10:02, injects a transient failure, retries them at 10:19, and expects the downstream envelope source timestamp to be 10:19. The retry attempt time is already recorded separately as `retry_attempt_at`.

The retry behavior is incorrect. `source_timestamp` should preserve the original observation/envelope source time, not be reset to the retry time.

Expected values:

- `source_timestamp`: 10:02
- `retry_attempt_at`: 10:19

The retry path should carry forward the original `source_timestamp` when constructing the new `ExportEnvelope`; only `retry_attempt_at` should use the current clock. The fixture should therefore expect 10:02 downstream, while separately asserting `retry_attempt_at == 10:19`.

This brief records bounded operating evidence for Hema’s management chain. It separates completed evidence from open boundaries and preserves the established ownership model. The Mosaic 18.0M cycle closed without weakening the operating model. # First-cut matrix

## 1. Label limits
- Failure mode: unbounded or newly introduced label keys/values causing fanout.
- Candidate control: a narrow allowlist or budget per sensitive label family.
- Preflight: flag new high-cardinality labels before a metrics-router or shard-keeper push.

## 2. Alert-source semantics

- Candidate control: dashboard and alert wording that marks live metrics-router traffic separately from replay or mirror validation samples.

## 3. Label-change preflight
- Failure mode: a config or parser change adding labels without checking cardinality behavior.
- Candidate control: a pre-push checklist with sample counts, source label, owner, and rollback/non-rollback semantics.

## Bounded observability example — exception-review outcomes

The accepted production counter uses only these bounded labels:
- `service_pair_class`: `ingest_path`, `routing_path`, `ownership_path`, or `other`
- `exception_class`: `invariant`, `provenance`, `failure_mode`, `ownership`, or `escalation`

# INC-2023-10-30-001 metrics-router canary rollback — lightweight after-action

## Summary
A metrics-router canary for `sha:b41c77a` was rolled back after live-path p99 and dropped writes moved on the canary slice. Replay and mirror validation panels were not the rollback trigger.

## Timeline
- 08:07 ET — Page fired for live metrics-router p99 on canary slice. Alex acknowledged the incident.
- 08:22 ET — Live-path p99 was around 118 ms, error rate was 0.18%, and dropped writes were 0.6% on the canary slice. Alex rolled back the most recent metrics-router deploy.
- 09:05 ET — p99 returned to about 46 ms, error rate returned to roughly 0.02%, and dropped writes returned to zero.

## What changed
The canary appears to have changed the `route_pattern` normalization path so one live handler emitted raw account/widget IDs instead of normalized route patterns. Replay validation still showed normalized route patterns, so replay evidence alone would not have caught the live hot-path value-shape change.

## Why rollback was appropriate
The signal was live-path metrics-router movement: p99 and dropped writes on the canary slice. Replay or mirror validation movement remains investigation evidence, not rollback criteria.

## Follow-ups
1. Keep the code fix small: restore normalized `route_pattern` values for the affected live handler before another canary.
2. Patch the Cardinality Guardrails checklist so live-path label value-shape changes require live canary evidence or a representative live-path fixture, not only replay validation.

## Non-goals
This note is not a broad incident postmortem, not a legacy-aggregator retirement discussion, and not a claim that Cardinality Guardrails is complete.

# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

The correction is live for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Their two-account read-only scope and customer data contract remain unchanged.

# Q4 incident practice — November 18 scoring sheet

## Scope
A bounded tabletop scoring sheet, not a production runbook. Score observable responder behavior for an accepted metrics-router action across cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication.

## Core criteria
1. Durable attempt identity
- Pass: Responders identify the durable acceptance boundary and preserve one attempt identity after acceptance.
- Fail: They create, assume, or accept multiple identities for the same accepted attempt.

2. Terminal accounting
- Pass: Every accepted attempt reaches exactly one terminal result.
- Fail: An accepted attempt has no terminal result or exposes conflicting terminal results.

3. Failure classification
- Pass: Responders distinguish cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication using the acceptance boundary.
- Fail: They collapse those cases or treat a pre-acceptance event as evidence about accepted work.

## Wes — responder path
Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

## Nadia — postmortem criteria
The postmortem must name the absent system guarantee or control. It must not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause, and it must retain the mapped implementation and rollback owner.

## Final ownership-boundary condition
- Pass: Mapped owners retain implementation and rollback decisions, while the triggered reviewer remains confined to the named failure-mode boundary.
- Fail: The triggered review is treated as implementation, release, or rollback approval.

## Additional operating checks — November 8

### 45-minute secondary boundary
- Pass: When the cause remains unisolated, responders engage the secondary before the 45-minute boundary and make the incident clock visible.
- Fail: Responders wait until or after 45 minutes, or continue without engaging the secondary while the cause remains unisolated.

### Friday staging preparation versus production change
- Pass: Responders identify staging preparation that makes no production state change as staging work and separately identify a Friday-afternoon production deploy as prohibited.
- Fail: Responders classify staging-only preparation as a production deploy, or permit a Friday-afternoon production state change because it was described as preparation.

These checks supplement the accepted cancellation, caller-disconnect, durable-attempt, terminal-result, mapped-owner, and postmortem criteria. This remains a tabletop scoring sheet rather than a production runbook.

## November 18 execution order

- 5 minutes: role and ownership framing.
- 35 minutes: cancellation and caller-disconnect scenario.
- 10 minutes: one targeted rerun if a scoring boundary is missed.
- 10 minutes: debrief and owner follow-up.

Wes teaches the responder path. Nadia owns the postmortem section. Alex maintains only the bounded failure case. This is the exact one-hour tabletop sequence and does not turn the scoring sheet into a production runbook.

## Observed results — November 18

The tabletop is complete. Responders correctly separated durable acceptance from cancellation, caller disconnect, and process recovery; preserved one attempt identity and one terminal result in the exercise; identified Wes as the mapped metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback owner; and distinguished Friday staging preparation from a production change.

These results are training evidence only. The tabletop did not execute the product implementation and does not close any product defect or replace required executable product evidence.

The March 26, 2026 strategy meeting is complete. # Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

The correction is live for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Their two-account read-only scope and customer data contract remain unchanged.

Every Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce lookup remains behind the shared authorization wrapper. Access is read-only and limited to provenance-backed deploy movement, published service ownership, timestamped incident-load summaries, and explicit unknown states.

Cost data, CSV export, raw incident text, internal room metadata, employee identifiers or comparisons, inferred or unpublished ownership, internal-only fallback data, write capability, release-readiness judgments, employee-performance interpretations, internal owner-map/Cardinality Guardrails reference navigation, and access for any other account remain unauthorized.

- Product Engineering retains implementation and regression maintenance.

Harbor Health’s 12 release follow-ups and Mosaic Commerce’s 11 incident handoffs demonstrate use of the authorized systems view. They do not establish causality, release readiness, employee performance, or authorization for another field or account.

# October 27, 2027 facilitator packet

## Example 1 — separate reassessment time from entry time

### What happened
A reassessment was completed at 16:55, and the entry documenting it was made at 17:40.

### Safe wording
“Late entry entered at 17:40 for a reassessment performed at 16:55. This entry records the findings from the 16:55 reassessment and does not alter the earlier record.”

### What the wording must not imply
That the entry existed at 16:55, that documentation time was changed to match the reassessment time, or that an earlier entry was replaced.

## Example 2 — addendum preserving the original record

### What happened
A later review found that the original entry omitted a clarification. The original entry remains visible, and an addendum is entered at 18:10.

### Safe wording
“Addendum entered at 18:10: [clarification]. This addendum supplements the original entry; it does not replace or backdate it.”

### What the wording must not imply
That the original entry was changed or deleted, that the addendum existed before 18:10, or that the underlying care necessarily occurred at 18:10.

- Submit one fully anonymized document by October 15, 2027.
- Confirm the title identifies the October 27, 2027 session and that neither the title nor body contains patient identifiers.
- Keep exactly these three categories under each example: What happened; Safe wording; What the wording must not imply.
